review.title: The U.S. Sets an Unprecedented AI Chip Agreement with China | The Friday Market Wrap!
review.summary: Eisman closes earnings season by explaining thesis checks, management skepticism and balance-sheet analysis. His MLP example links high payouts, external capital dependence and rising leverage to a broken investment model. He remains positive on proprietary AI beneficiaries while warning about cable value traps and possible AI pressure on consulting.
review.assessment: The balance-sheet framework is useful, but its historical illustration overstates a universal MLP payout requirement and labels a simplified cash burden as a complete cost of capital. Circle losses are also explained too casually as normal youth rather than chiefly IPO-related charges. Several macro and AI-disruption conclusions remain hypotheses.
framework_points: Preselect the operating metrics that could falsify the thesis.
Compare management narrative with reported cash flows and balance sheets.
Watch for funding models that require continuously receptive capital markets.
Distinguish a cheap stock from a durable business.
Prefer differentiated products, while retaining valuation and concentration checks.
transcript_cautions: The MLP anecdote does not identify the issuer, date, agreement or analyst; its exact historical details are not independently verified.
Captions repeatedly write H2O; the Nvidia chip is H20.
The wrap concerns August 15 and was uploaded August 16.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman presents; speaker attribution follows the full dialogue.

claims.claim: Use earnings as a thesis check, with particular attention to revenue misses because bottom-line earnings are easier to adjust.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconcile revenue recognition, accruals, cash conversion and adjusted EPS.
claims.reason: This is a research heuristic. Revenue can also be misstated, and the comparative ease depends on the company and accounting choices.
claims.next_check: Reconcile revenue recognition, accruals, cash conversion and adjusted EPS.

claims.claim: Management commentary must be checked against independent evidence, especially when results deteriorate.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare prior statements, filings, cash flows and contemporaneous risk data.
claims.reason: The FCIC documents serious gaps in risk disclosure and governance. This supports skepticism without establishing that every inaccurate forecast is a deliberate lie.

evidence.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, findings and chapters 4, 6, 7, 13
evidence.finding: Investigative evidence documents fragile leverage/funding, fee and ROE incentives, deteriorating underwriting, and securitization dependence. Pages 61-64 describe pay incentives; pages 89 and 125 describe the origination chain; page 281 reports Bear near 38:1 and balance-sheet window dressing. Findings are not proof of a single exclusive cause.

claims.next_check: Compare prior statements, filings, cash flows and contemporaneous risk data.

claims.claim: Managers can be slow to recognize a business-model break, and liquidity may disappear before everyone accepts it.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.reason: This is a conditional risk principle rather than a quantified universal behavioral law.
claims.next_check: Identify financing dependencies and observable thesis-break indicators in advance.

evidence.title: Nvidia fiscal Q2 2026 earnings discussion
evidence.finding: Management described a US expectation of 15% of licensed H20 revenue but no published rule codifying it. The distinction between proposed political arrangement and enforceable implementation matters.

review.title: Industrial Sector Explained: Data Center Growth & Rise of Vertiv | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep. 21
review.summary: Steve Tusa maps industrial opportunities from data-center power and cooling to selected margin turnarounds. Eisman endorses the infrastructure theme and probes the failures of old GE. Later filings support strong Vertiv, GE Vernova and Johnson Controls operations, but do not settle every valuation or causal claim. Tusa cautions against extrapolating AI growth across all industrials and distinguishes Honeywell from GE. Detailed accounting discussion is supported by SEC findings. Revenue-exposure and settlement-size errors are supporting premises, distinct from the major investment theses.
review.assessment: Complete transcript read. Operating evidence supports major infrastructure and JCI themes; stock targets, durable moats and CEO counterfactuals remain separate. The JCI FY2026 directional earnings call is supported. Two revenue-exposure assertions and the guest settlement amount are factual misses, not broad investment failures.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Tusa supplies most industrial analysis. Steve Eisman is identified through questions and explicit agreements; tentative endorsements and disagreements are retained.
framework_points: Separate end-market growth from company exposure and starting valuation.
Evaluate operating margins, incremental returns and cash conversion rather than earnings alone.
Compare the financing structure and customer mix across capital-spending cycles.
Use consolidated balance-sheet analysis to challenge segment-level earnings narratives.
Treat leadership counterfactuals and undated cycle predictions as hypotheses.
tools_and_charts: Data-center revenue shares and construction-spending denominator
GPU rack density and cooling architecture
EBITDA and earnings multiples adjusted for liabilities
Segment margins and return on invested capital
GE contract cost estimates and intercompany receivable sales
transcript_cautions: Opening montage duplicates later discussion.
Captions render Vertiv, Eaton, Hubbell, nVent, AAON and PFAS inconsistently; names are normalized where context is clear.
Electricity demand stated as gigawatts per year is dimensionally ambiguous; no silent numerical correction is made.
Most company recommendations and targets belong to Steve Tusa; Eisman questions are not blanket endorsements.

review.title: Powell Says Nothing & Markets Cheer, Amazon Wins & Target Loses | The Friday Market Wrap!
review.summary: The August 22 wrap questions calendar trading rules and excessive attention to conditional Fed language. Eisman distinguishes weakening traditional retailers from durable franchises and connects weak housing turnover to mortgage lock-in.
review.assessment: The strongest explanation is the housing-finance mechanism. The weakest reasoning uses a single seasonal counterexample as if it disproved average seasonality and treats market capitalization as a complete measure of economic relevance. Several company judgments are dated diagnoses, not price forecasts.
framework_points: Separate business conditions from daily market narratives.
Check housing affordability and mortgage lock-in.
Do not equate an earnings disappointment with universal sector weakness.
transcript_cautions: Some spoken EPS signs and fiscal-year comparisons are ambiguous in automatic captions and are not scored as precise numerical errors.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman presents; speaker attribution follows the full dialogue.

review.title: Tesla vs Waymo: Who Will Win the Robotaxi Race? | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep. 22
review.summary: Itay Michaeli argues Tesla needs product renewal and consumer autonomy, while distinguishing its suburban ambitions from Waymo urban robotaxis. Eisman probes earnings, subsidies, valuation and the practical usefulness of autonomy rather than adopting every bullish forecast. The guest approximate 2025 delivery estimate and cheaper-variant expectation receive support. Broad personal autonomy by summer 2026 did not arrive, although the separate robotaxi service progressed. The review also preserves conditional political-demand reasoning, conventional-auto tailwinds and Aptiv valuation analysis without treating sentiment or hypothetical market size as realized investment returns.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. Most material forecasts are guest views. The broad personal-autonomy summer-2026 expectation misses while the outer 15-month conditional window is still narrowly open at the cutoff. No Tesla stock recommendation is graded from price alone; political and market-size causal stories remain unresolved.
review.speaker_map_notes: Itay Michaeli provides the sector forecasts and recommendations. Eisman asks skeptical questions, states personal preferences and makes limited explicit propositions; guest bullishness is not imputed to him.
framework_points: Distinguish demand deferral from destruction using regional market-share and category data.
Separate assisted driving, restricted robotaxis and general personal autonomous use.
Challenge terminal-market assumptions and product-cycle extrapolation.
Disaggregate supplier outgrowth into technology content, customer share and mix.
Compare earnings definitions and buyback effects before interpreting valuation compression.
tools_and_charts: County-level EV sales and penetration data
Operational design domains and sensor modalities
US mobility market and lifetime revenue capture model
Supplier growth over market, bookings and backlog
Adjusted versus GAAP earnings and price/earnings ratios
transcript_cautions: Opening montage repeats later discussion.
Guest identified by metadata as Itay Michaeli; captions distort his name, TD Cowen, Waymo, Aptiv, Visteon and lidar.
Eisman briefly substitutes states for the guest counties in political-adoption data.
Gross and operating margins are initially conflated but clarified in the dialogue.
Ford announcement dates the discussion near mid-August despite August 25 publication; forecast deadlines are interpreted conservatively.
Personal autonomy is distinct from Tesla restricted robotaxi service and from supervised FSD.

review.title: Trump vs The Fed, U.S. Takes 10% Stake in Intel, Cracker Barrel Cracks | The Friday Market Wrap!
review.summary: The August 29 wrap, uploaded August 30, combines Fed independence and government investment with a detailed tour of sector performance. Eisman links AI spending to semiconductors, power equipment and selected industrials while distinguishing operating quality from stock returns.
review.assessment: The sector disaggregation is useful. Several supporting descriptions are materially wrong: Equinix operates data centers, REITs do not distribute all cash, Mitsubishi is a major gas-turbine supplier, and Deckers is a footwear business. His Fed-removal prediction must be separated from the much narrower interim ruling.
framework_points: Look inside capitalization-weighted sectors.
Trace capital spending into suppliers and bottlenecks.
Separate business quality from realized share performance.
Treat legal allegations, findings and final remedies differently.
transcript_cautions: The episode says August 29 although the listing is August 30.
Nvidia EPS is $1.05 adjusted; the $15 caption is not treated as his financial claim.
A September 5 correction says he previously described Fed creation as a constitutional amendment; that wording is absent from this captured version, so it is not reconstructed as an August 30 claim.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman presents; speaker attribution follows the full dialogue.

review.title: Steve Eisman Answers YOUR Investing Questions | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 23
review.summary: Eisman explains a story-driven investing process grounded in independent data, pricing power, balance sheets and long holding periods. He favors US index exposure and AI, rejects stock compensation as economically free, and revisits MLP financing failures. The housing lock-in mechanism and several accounting principles are sound, but mortgage arithmetic exaggerates the required price decline. His account of deposit rates and the Fed constitutional origin is wrong, and EU trade authority is oversimplified. These explanatory errors are separated from untested long-term portfolio preferences and personal disclosures.
review.assessment: Entire transcript read. Useful company-level accounting and risk principles coexist with weaker monetary/legal explanations. Strong long-term US enthusiasm has no precise return target. The viewer recovery context runs five years, so no premature performance grade is assigned. Unverified anecdotes and portfolio disclosures remain unverified, not adverse grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Require a company story beyond cheap valuation.
Cross-check management narratives with independent operating data.
Analyze cash retention, leverage and security rights together.
Treat stock compensation as an economic transfer.
Recognize personal timing and lifestyle constraints in portfolio design.
Watch for unsupported macro certainty and arithmetic shortcuts.
tools_and_charts: Quarterly earnings calls and management language
MLP distribution coverage, leverage and incentive distribution rights
GAAP versus adjusted EPS and stock compensation
Federal funds rate and yield-curve distinctions
transcript_cautions: Opening montage duplicates later answers.
Viewer questions are quoted and are not Eisman assertions; their hypothetical trades and claims are excluded unless he endorses them.
He corrects Tarullo formal title but incorrectly mentions Chair Powell in the historical explanation; Tarullo left under Yellen.
The broad technology-weight estimate uses an informal sector definition.
Mortgage comparison assumes equal loan terms and proportional down payments for the arithmetic test.
MLP index identity and total-return treatment are unspecified.

review.title: Google Wins Antitrust Case, Is AI The Next Bubble? | The Friday Market Wrap!
review.summary: The September 5 wrap corrects a prior statement about the Federal Reserve, predicts the Supreme Court will uphold emergency tariffs, and interprets Google remedies and Apple policy risks. It then reviews software disruption, Broadcom demand and Lululemon product weakness, ending with a conditional AI-overinvestment scenario.
review.assessment: The clear adverse forecast is the predicted IEEPA win: the Supreme Court later ruled the statute did not authorize those tariffs. Google gained important remedy relief but did not win the underlying case. His AI-bust discussion is explicitly a scenario he was not yet worried about, not a crash prediction.
framework_points: Separate a statutory case from partisan assumptions.
Distinguish operating results from market expectations.
Watch whether cheaper technology weakens established moats.
Treat overinvestment as a conditional mechanism rather than a timed crash call.
transcript_cautions: At 60-82 seconds he corrects a prior Fed constitutional-amendment statement to the Federal Reserve Act of 1913. The earlier captured transcript lacks the erroneous wording, so the correction is documented without inventing a claim in that version.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman presents; speaker attribution follows the full dialogue.

review.title: Steve Eisman’s Masterclass on Financial Literacy | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 24
review.summary: Eisman teaches long-term investing, thesis discipline, short-selling risk, valuation methods, sector behavior and interest-rate transmission. He favors simple US equity-index portfolios, insists on explicit thesis tests, and explains why short exposures grow when prices rise. His sector-based approach is practical, but several definitions and historical explanations need correction, including enterprise value, REIT cash-flow measures, the 2025 drawdown arithmetic and the claim that the Fed controls only one rate.
review.assessment: The most reusable contribution is the distinction between an investment thesis and the emotional reasons for continuing to hold it. Basic short-sale and discounting mathematics are sound when their assumptions are stated. Portfolio preferences are not universal suitability findings, and sector conventions are not valuation laws. The valuation primer contains material technical mistakes, so its formulas should be checked before reuse.
framework_points: Write the investment thesis and the observable facts that would disprove it before becoming attached to the stock.
Distinguish business deterioration, valuation and the funding constraints that can force a short seller to cover.
Learn the metrics used by sector specialists, but reconcile them to cash generation and the balance sheet.
Separate a defensive business from a stock guaranteed to avoid losses.
He distrusts decades-long DCF precision and prefers nearer-term business fundamentals.
tools_and_charts: Forward P/E and dated consensus estimates.
Enterprise value / EBITDA, price / tangible book, DCF and REIT FFO/AFFO.
Position weights, borrow costs, short interest and short-squeeze mechanics.
Sector weights and relative returns during the February-May 2025 selloff and rebound.
Yield curve, net interest margin and discount-rate sensitivity.
transcript_cautions: Read all 1,502 caption segments through the closing disclosure.
Many examples explicitly use June 18, 2025 prices and consensus estimates despite the September 8 listing date; they are not September spot valuations.
Captions corrupt EBITDA, AFFO, company names and some numbers. The drawdown correction uses the stated index levels, so it does not depend on an assumed transcription of an unviewed table.
The sector-weight discussion gives inconsistent rounded weights in different passages; the displayed tables were not independently inspected.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman presents; speaker attribution follows the full dialogue.

claims.claim: Excess leverage and mortgage exposure made the pre-2008 financial system fragile.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare leverage, funding and mortgage exposures before the crisis.
claims.reason: The FCIC documents leverage, fragile funding and mortgage-linked losses. This is a retrospective explanation, not a new forecast win.

evidence.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, findings and chapters 4, 6, 7, 13
evidence.finding: Investigative evidence documents fragile leverage/funding, fee and ROE incentives, deteriorating underwriting, and securitization dependence. Pages 61-64 describe pay incentives; pages 89 and 125 describe the origination chain; page 281 reports Bear near 38:1 and balance-sheet window dressing. Findings are not proof of a single exclusive cause.

claims.next_check: Compare leverage, funding and mortgage exposures before the crisis.

claims.claim: Post-crisis regulation forced large banks to hold more capital and made them safer.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare capital, liquidity, exposures and supervisory coverage over time.
claims.reason: The stress-test framework and capital buffers support improved resilience. They do not establish that all financial risk disappeared or that regulation alone explains every change.

evidence.title: 2025 stress-test results, revised September 30
evidence.finding: Aggregate CET1 13.4% at start, hypothetical trough 11.6%; institution-specific outcomes and separate leverage ratios are disclosed. Results reflect scenario, portfolio and model assumptions, not a direct measure of political intent.

claims.next_check: Compare capital, liquidity, exposures and supervisory coverage over time.

claims.claim: Another GFC-style crisis is unlikely, although a recession remains possible.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: No probability, horizon or operational crisis definition is supplied. Stronger banks do not exclude stress outside banking.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Most individual long-only investors should buy and hold for the long term.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: This is a portfolio-management preference whose suitability depends on horizon, liquidity needs and risk capacity.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Fewer trading decisions reduce mistakes, while panic selling makes it difficult to reenter.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare after-cost investor outcomes and reentry behavior using a defined sample.
claims.reason: The behavioral mechanism is plausible, but neither the frequency of mistakes nor comparative outcomes is measured here.
claims.next_check: Compare after-cost investor outcomes and reentry behavior using a defined sample.

claims.claim: If volatility becomes intolerable, first sell weak theses and trim risk instead of liquidating everything.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: He explicitly allows personal risk tolerance to override a general buy-and-hold preference. It is a decision rule, not a measurable forecast.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Selling appreciated stocks can create a substantial capital-gains tax cost.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Identify account type, basis, realized gain and applicable tax treatment.
claims.reason: The conditional tax cost follows for taxable realized gains; it does not apply identically to tax-sheltered accounts or investors with offsetting losses.
claims.next_check: Identify account type, basis, realized gain and applicable tax treatment.

proof.derivation: For a taxable gain G and effective tax rate t, tax cost is G × t; the rate and exemptions must be established separately.

claims.claim: Most professional active managers fail to beat their benchmarks over long periods.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use survivorship-aware, after-fee results against appropriate benchmarks.
claims.reason: SPIVA supports the broad long-horizon claim in its covered categories. It does not say that every manager or every shorter period underperforms.

evidence.title: SPIVA US Year-End 2024
evidence.finding: No covered category had a majority of active managers outperform over the 15 years to December 2024; shorter periods differed.

claims.next_check: Use survivorship-aware, after-fee results against appropriate benchmarks.

claims.claim: Use SPY, or a combination of SPY and QQQ for greater growth exposure, and invest regularly instead of timing the market.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: These are portfolio preferences. QQQ tracks the Nasdaq-100 rather than every Nasdaq-listed company; the suggested mix remains concentrated in overlapping large holdings.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: The Magnificent Seven represent roughly 30% of the S&P 500, at an unprecedented seven-stock concentration.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Match the seven weights to the June 2025 example date and compare a consistent historical series.
claims.reason: The concentration warning is material, but an exact historical constituent-weight series was not inspected to establish the stated percentage and all-time comparison.
claims.next_check: Match the seven weights to the June 2025 example date and compare a consistent historical series.

claims.claim: Risk limits force many active funds to underweight the largest stocks, helping explain their underperformance.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect fund mandates, holdings and benchmark attribution rather than infer a universal limit.
claims.reason: An underweight can detract when those stocks outperform, but the prevalence of binding limits and their contribution to aggregate underperformance is not established.
claims.next_check: Inspect fund mandates, holdings and benchmark attribution rather than infer a universal limit.

claims.claim: Smaller-cap stocks generally bring more risk and volatility than large-cap indexes.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare matched volatility, drawdowns, liquidity and failure rates.
claims.reason: The comparison needs a defined risk measure, index pair and period; company size alone is not a sufficient individual-stock risk measure.
claims.next_check: Compare matched volatility, drawdowns, liquidity and failure rates.

claims.claim: US equities should continue outperforming developed overseas markets over the long term.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.horizon: long term, no exact end date
claims.test: Define US and ex-US total-return benchmarks, currency treatment and a prospective horizon.
claims.reason: The preference for US dynamism becomes a long-term relative-return thesis, but no completed long-term horizon or precise benchmark is supplied.
claims.next_check: Define US and ex-US total-return benchmarks, currency treatment and a prospective horizon.

claims.claim: A foreign stock gain can be offset by a currency loss for a US investor.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The currency translation mechanism is correct; whether to hedge is a separate portfolio choice.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: USD return = (1 + local return) × (1 + currency return) - 1. A 10% local gain and 10% currency fall produce -1%.

claims.claim: Technology and related firms exceed 40% of the S&P 500, with no comparable developed-country market.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconstruct the stated June 2025 grouping and apply the same classification to other markets.
claims.reason: The broad exposure grouping differs from official GICS sectors, and a consistent international comparison was not inspected.
claims.next_check: Reconstruct the stated June 2025 grouping and apply the same classification to other markets.

claims.claim: Avoid added emerging-market legal complexity and keep individual stocks to a comfortable minority of savings.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: This is a simplicity and concentration preference; it does not establish that foreign diversification or individual securities are inherently inferior.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Young investors with long horizons should do better mostly in stocks than in bonds.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Specify holding period, stock and bond benchmarks, rebalancing and risk-adjusted outcomes.
claims.reason: This is a prospective asset-allocation return expectation without a defined future endpoint. Historical equity premiums cannot guarantee every investor horizon.
claims.next_check: Specify holding period, stock and bond benchmarks, rebalancing and risk-adjusted outcomes.

claims.claim: Investors who need bonds should use simple US Treasury or high-quality corporate exposure rather than overseas bonds.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: The preference reduces some complexity but does not specify duration, credit exposure or currency hedging, which materially affect risk.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Large advisory firms usually assign around half of clients’ money to bonds and overdiversify away good performance.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Measure actual allocations, fees and risk-adjusted outcomes for a representative client sample.
claims.reason: No representative adviser-portfolio sample or definition of decent performance is provided. His experience with selected clients cannot establish the industry-wide claim.
claims.next_check: Measure actual allocations, fees and risk-adjusted outcomes for a representative client sample.

claims.claim: Keep an advised portfolio simple, with no more than about three stock and three bond indexes.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: The number of funds is a simplicity heuristic, not a demonstrated optimum or substitute for examining overlapping exposures.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Thesis creep occurs when the original reason for a purchase fails but the investor invents a reason to keep holding.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: The Capital One example is explicitly hypothetical. It is a useful distinction between updating an evidenced thesis and rationalizing a loss.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: His past Citigroup holding illustrates attachment to cheapness despite a failed management-improvement thesis.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: This is an autobiographical lesson, not a verified trading record. The broad phrase that nothing improved is not treated as an audited statement about every Citi metric.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: If a $4,000 position halves while the total portfolio remains $100,000, its weight falls from 4% to 2%.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The example correctly measures position exposure under its explicit constant-total-portfolio assumption; it does not prove lower business risk.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: 2,000 / 100,000 = 2%; the remaining 98,000 / 24 positions is about 4,083.33 each.

claims.claim: Short selling borrows shares, sells them, then buys them back for return; a lower repurchase price produces a gross gain.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconcile sale proceeds, repurchase price, borrowing charges and distributions.
claims.reason: The basic mechanics are correct. Borrow expense and other obligations reduce gross profit.

evidence.title: Short Selling: Background and Policy Issues
evidence.finding: A short sale borrows shares for later return; losses can be unlimited as the repurchase price rises.

claims.next_check: Reconcile sale proceeds, repurchase price, borrowing charges and distributions.

claims.claim: Borrowing is usually arranged through the desk, but illiquid or heavily shorted stocks can cost 20%-30% a year or more.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect the actual locate, loan agreement, variable fee and recall terms.
claims.reason: The friction is material, but no dated loan quote is supplied to verify the cited fee range for a particular trade. Borrow availability is not guaranteed.
claims.next_check: Inspect the actual locate, loan agreement, variable fee and recall terms.

claims.claim: Buying by shorts covering a rising illiquid stock can amplify a short squeeze.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: This is a conditional feedback mechanism, not a forecast that every crowded short must squeeze.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: If forced covering adds purchase demand while available sell supply is limited, the clearing price must adjust until supply meets demand.

claims.claim: A short initially equal to 4% of the portfolio becomes an 8% position when its stock doubles.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Separate gross liability from net portfolio equity.
claims.reason: Gross short liability doubles, but the equity denominator also falls from the loss unless other gains offset it. With no offset, exposure becomes about 8.33%.
claims.next_check: Separate gross liability from net portfolio equity.

proof.derivation: Start with equity 100 and short liability 4. A doubling creates liability 8 and loss 4, leaving equity 96; 8 / 96 = 8.33%. The stated 8% requires equity to stay 100.

claims.claim: An unhedged short has theoretically unlimited loss, and rising exposure can force risk managers to cover.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: Unlimited price risk is mathematically correct. A particular forced-cover threshold depends on margin, borrowing and internal risk limits.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: For fixed shares N, short profit before costs is N × (sale price - repurchase price); there is no fixed upper bound on the latter.

claims.claim: Valuation matters over the long term, but an expensive stock with intact fundamentals is a dangerous short solely on valuation.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: This distinguishes a valuation concern from a catalyst and is a risk-management rule, not a claim that price never matters.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: The internet bubble broke because recession damaged earnings, rather than because valuation changed.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Distinguish the beginning of the market collapse from later earnings deterioration.
claims.reason: The recession began in 2001, after the 2000 technology-market peak. Later recession damage cannot explain the chronology as stated or establish that valuation had no role.

evidence.title: March 2001 business-cycle peak
evidence.finding: The recession began after the March 2001 business-cycle peak, about a year after the Nasdaq March 2000 peak.

claims.next_check: Distinguish the beginning of the market collapse from later earnings deterioration.

claims.claim: Nvidia’s 2023 earnings revisions made a previously expensive-looking stock retrospectively inexpensive.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconstruct the original forward estimate and subsequent revisions without look-ahead.
claims.reason: Rapid earnings growth can compress a forward multiple, but the claim needs dated prices and contemporaneous consensus revisions. Hindsight earnings do not prove the original price was low-risk.
claims.next_check: Reconstruct the original forward estimate and subsequent revisions without look-ahead.

claims.claim: Market capitalization equals share price multiplied by shares outstanding.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: This is the standard equity-value identity; the approximate Apple value is an illustrative, date-sensitive input.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: Equity market value = price per share × shares outstanding.

claims.claim: Enterprise value equals equity market capitalization plus debt.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconcile equity, debt, excess cash, minority interests and other claims consistently.
claims.reason: That omits cash and other relevant adjustments. It is not a generally correct operating-enterprise-value formula, particularly for cash-rich companies.

evidence.title: Financial ratios and measures: enterprise value
evidence.finding: Operating enterprise value nets cash from equity plus debt and adds minority interests where appropriate; debt plus equity alone includes non-operating cash.

claims.next_check: Reconcile equity, debt, excess cash, minority interests and other claims consistently.

claims.claim: P/E is share price divided by earnings per share; forward P/E substitutes a forecast EPS.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The ratio identity is correct. The reliability of a forward multiple depends on the earnings definition and forecast.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: P/E = share price / EPS for a specified period and accounting basis.

claims.claim: June 18, 2025 forward multiples differ widely: Nvidia 34, Goldman 14, P&G 23, Lilly 36, Lennar 11, Exxon 18 and Eaton 28.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Match each June 18 close to the same-date 2025 EPS consensus and fiscal-year basis.
claims.reason: These are dated consensus examples, not current valuations. The original consensus vendor and exact forecast basis were not inspected.
claims.next_check: Match each June 18 close to the same-date 2025 EPS consensus and fiscal-year basis.

claims.claim: Growth, earnings cyclicality, leverage and stability help explain differing sector P/E ratios.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Control for growth, risk, reinvestment, accounting and the earnings-cycle position.
claims.reason: The proposed determinants are plausible but do not uniquely identify the observed cross-section; multiple factors can move together.
claims.next_check: Control for growth, risk, reinvestment, accounting and the earnings-cycle position.

claims.claim: Sector-allocation mandates force funds into consumer staples and raise P&G’s multiple despite slow EPS growth.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect actual fund constraints and estimate their demand effect separately from durability and risk.
claims.reason: No mandate sample or flow-based valuation attribution is supplied. Some funds have tight sector limits; this does not establish the stated dominant explanation.
claims.next_check: Inspect actual fund constraints and estimate their demand effect separately from durability and risk.

claims.claim: Lennar is valued cheaply because housing earnings are cyclical and rate-sensitive, while Exxon’s earnings depend strongly on oil prices.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare sector cash flows and valuations across rates, commodity prices and the cycle.
claims.reason: The mechanisms identify real exposures, but the size of the valuation discount and relative importance of each factor are not isolated here.
claims.next_check: Compare sector cash flows and valuations across rates, commodity prices and the cycle.

claims.claim: He avoids long-term oil-stock investment because forecasting oil prices is too difficult.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: This is his competence and portfolio preference, not proof that nobody can earn a return in the sector.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Eaton deserves a growth multiple from reindustrialization, and Lilly’s multiple reflects profits expected from its drug pipeline.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Separate realized results, pipeline probabilities and the return implied by the stock price.
claims.reason: These are valuation narratives. The specific high-teens growth and future drug-profit assumptions need matched disclosures and a cash-flow model.
claims.next_check: Separate realized results, pipeline probabilities and the return implied by the stock price.

claims.claim: EBITDA adds interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization back to net earnings.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The unadjusted reconciliation is correct; company-defined adjusted EBITDA may add further items.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: EBITDA = net income + interest expense + tax expense + depreciation + amortization, with consistent scope.

claims.claim: EBITDA per share is always greater than EPS.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect signs and definitions rather than assume every add-back is positive.
claims.reason: Usually positive add-backs make it larger, but the word always fails when net interest or tax benefits outweigh depreciation and other additions.
claims.next_check: Inspect signs and definitions rather than assume every add-back is positive.

proof.derivation: If net income is 100, tax expense is -30 and total remaining add-backs are 10, EBITDA is 80, below net income. Dividing both by the same share count preserves the inequality.

claims.claim: John Malone pioneered EBITDA to show the cash-generating potential of debt-funded telecom expansion.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check contemporary Malone statements and reconcile cash flow, capex and borrowing.
claims.reason: The origin and personal rationale are historical assertions without an inspected contemporaneous source here. EBITDA is not itself cash available after investment.
claims.next_check: Check contemporary Malone statements and reconcile cash flow, capex and borrowing.

claims.claim: EBITDA can give a misleading economic picture by excluding the cost of maintaining capital-intensive assets.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The limitation follows from the metric. This supports a measurement warning, not a verdict on every company valued using EBITDA.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: Adding depreciation back and omitting capital expenditure leaves replacement investment outside EBITDA; identical EBITDA can coexist with very different free cash flow.

claims.claim: Book value per share uses common equity per share; tangible book removes goodwill and other intangibles.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The accounting bridge is correct when common equity, other intangible assets and share counts are defined consistently.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: Tangible common equity per share = (common equity - goodwill - other applicable intangibles) / common shares.

claims.claim: Hidden asset losses make balance-sheet reliability central to bank valuation.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect asset marks, loss allowances, capital and off-balance-sheet exposures.
claims.reason: The financial-crisis evidence supports the importance of unrecognized losses and funding exposures. Tangible book is still an accounting estimate, not a guaranteed liquidation value.

evidence.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, findings and chapters 4, 6, 7, 13
evidence.finding: Investigative evidence documents fragile leverage/funding, fee and ROE incentives, deteriorating underwriting, and securitization dependence. Pages 61-64 describe pay incentives; pages 89 and 125 describe the origination chain; page 281 reports Bear near 38:1 and balance-sheet window dressing. Findings are not proof of a single exclusive cause.

claims.next_check: Inspect asset marks, loss allowances, capital and off-balance-sheet exposures.

claims.claim: JPMorgan trades around 2.4 times tangible book and Citi around 0.7 because JPMorgan earns higher returns.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use the same date and denominator for market value, tangible equity and profitability.
claims.reason: The prices and return measures are date-sensitive, and ROE must not be confused with ROTCE. No matched snapshot establishes these exact multiples or the complete causal explanation.
claims.next_check: Use the same date and denominator for market value, tangible equity and profitability.

claims.claim: DCF values a business by discounting expected future cash flows to present value.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: This is the valuation identity, not a claim that distant forecasts can be known precisely.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: Present value = sum over t of expected cash flow at t divided by (1 + discount rate)^t, plus any consistently defined terminal value.

claims.claim: He prefers researching business fundamentals to building precise decades-long DCF forecasts.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: This is an explicit methodological preference. DCF sensitivity is a reason to use scenarios, not a mathematical invalidation of discounting.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Sector specialists collectively determine the metrics and valuation conventions that markets use for long periods.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Track sector research methods and prices across time, including competing valuation approaches.
claims.reason: The account describes professional practice, but consensus, its persistence and its price-setting power are not measured. It does not make an established convention economically correct.
claims.next_check: Track sector research methods and prices across time, including competing valuation approaches.

claims.claim: Choose valuation tools by business model: P/E for many sectors, tangible book for banks, reserves for oil, pipeline economics for drugs and sometimes DCF for unprofitable growth.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: This is a practical classification heuristic. These are overlapping tools, not exclusive rules, and cash-flow consistency still matters.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: REIT FFO is a cash-flow measure calculated from pretax earnings, adding depreciation and subtracting property gains and interest income.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use the issuer’s reconciliation to the Nareit definition and distinguish cash-flow statements.
claims.reason: The stated bridge conflates FFO with other measures. Nareit FFO begins with GAAP net income, and is expressly not GAAP operating cash flow; interest income is not a universal FFO subtraction.

evidence.title: 2025 supplemental definitions: FFO and FAD
evidence.finding: Nareit FFO starts with GAAP net income, adjusts real-estate depreciation and sale gains/losses, and is not GAAP operating cash flow. The FAD reconciliation deducts recurring capital and leasing costs.

claims.next_check: Use the issuer’s reconciliation to the Nareit definition and distinguish cash-flow statements.

claims.claim: AFFO adds back capital expenditures and then deducts maintenance capex as a standard REIT valuation formula.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect the individual issuer’s AFFO bridge and avoid double-counting capex.
claims.reason: AFFO is not standardized. Recurring capex is commonly deducted from FFO-based measures; capital spending is not generally an expense already removed from FFO that can simply be added back.

evidence.title: Q2 2026 definitions: AFFO
evidence.finding: AFFO deducts recurring capital expenditures and leasing costs from adjusted FFO. Nareit has not standardized AFFO, so company definitions differ.

claims.next_check: Inspect the individual issuer’s AFFO bridge and avoid double-counting capex.

claims.claim: Utilities are often assessed with earnings multiples and dividend yields.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: These are valuation inputs, not an outcome prediction; financing, regulation and investment requirements remain necessary context.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: After the financial crisis, tangible book displaced ordinary book value so completely that only tangible book is used for banks.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect bank research and transaction valuations across book, tangible book, earnings and cash-flow approaches.
claims.reason: The preference for tangible equity is understandable, but the exclusive claim is not established by an exhaustive survey. His own discussion also uses earnings and returns.
claims.next_check: Inspect bank research and transaction valuations across book, tangible book, earnings and cash-flow approaches.

claims.claim: Growth, cyclical and defensive sector labels are useful simplifications but can hide large differences among subsectors.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: He explicitly warns against treating the labels as universal. A defensive business can still have an expensive or risky stock.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: A drop in the S&P 500 from 6,144 to 4,983 is a 16% decline.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Calculate point-to-point return using the starting level as denominator.
claims.reason: The stated levels imply an approximately 18.9% decline. This correction uses his own numbers and does not require an assumed chart series.
claims.next_check: Calculate point-to-point return using the starting level as denominator.

claims.claim: The rebound from about 4,983 to 5,985 is approximately 20%.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Verify the chosen endpoints and whether the return window begins at the April 8 close.
claims.reason: That percentage is arithmetically correct for those supplied levels. The date labels and exact quoted closing levels remain separate verification questions.
claims.next_check: Verify the chosen endpoints and whether the return window begins at the April 8 close.

claims.claim: Defensive sectors fell less during the selloff, while technology and cyclicals rebounded more strongly; healthcare lagged the rebound.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Recalculate all eleven sector indexes for identical starting and ending closes.
claims.reason: The pattern is stated through a table, but the exact sector-return series, total-return basis and endpoints were not independently inspected.
claims.next_check: Recalculate all eleven sector indexes for identical starting and ending closes.

claims.claim: A 20% gain does not recover a preceding 20% loss.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The compounding correction is correct.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: Starting at 100, a 20% fall leaves 80; a 20% rise then leaves 96. Recovery requires a 25% gain.

claims.claim: Defensive sectors can still lose money in a correction even while outperforming other sectors.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: This is the correct distinction between relative defensiveness and absolute capital protection; the specific sample returns remain separately unresolved.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Healthcare missed the rally because Trump made Medicare and Medicaid pay the lowest foreign drug price.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Distinguish announcement, binding implementation, affected products and event-study evidence.
claims.reason: A most-favored-nation initiative was announced, but the order directs targets and possible later rulemaking rather than an immediate universal price substitution. It also does not establish the entire sector’s causal return attribution.

evidence.title: Most-favored-nation drug-pricing executive order
evidence.finding: The order directs price targets and possible later rulemaking if progress is inadequate. It does not instantly replace every Medicare and Medicaid drug price with the lowest foreign price.

claims.next_check: Distinguish announcement, binding implementation, affected products and event-study evidence.

claims.claim: June sector weights show technology dominates the US index and explain why a tech bull should prefer US equities to Europe.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconstruct the same-date weights and compare broad economic exposures under consistent definitions.
claims.reason: The stated weights are not fully consistent across later passages, and the investment conclusion needs valuation and overlap analysis as well as sector share.
claims.next_check: Reconstruct the same-date weights and compare broad economic exposures under consistent definitions.

claims.claim: Within sectors, payments and biotech can be growth businesses while traditional banks are cyclical and staples are relatively defensive.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: The useful lesson is to classify by economics rather than the sector label alone. These are broad conventions with many exceptions, not forecasts for every constituent.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Cord cutting and streaming have damaged the former defensive character of traditional media and cable.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Separate linear-video decline from broadband, connectivity and other segment economics.
claims.reason: The mechanism is plausible, but company-specific cash flow, subscriber trends and valuations determine how much value is impaired.
claims.next_check: Separate linear-video decline from broadband, connectivity and other segment economics.

claims.claim: Celebrity brands and influencers have intensified beauty competition and hurt established companies.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare brand shares, marketing costs and incumbent margins over the specified period.
claims.reason: The industry-change thesis lacks a matched market-share and profit attribution study here.
claims.next_check: Compare brand shares, marketing costs and incumbent margins over the specified period.

claims.claim: Solar is the principal growth exception within the S&P Energy sector.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use official GICS categories when explaining S&P sector weights.
claims.reason: The discussion confuses an energy-related economic activity with index classification. GICS places solar-module and cell manufacturers in Information Technology, with renewable electricity elsewhere.

evidence.title: GICS methodology, Information Technology definitions
evidence.finding: The Information Technology semiconductor category includes manufacturers of solar modules and cells. Solar is not simply a subsector of the GICS Energy sector.

claims.next_check: Use official GICS categories when explaining S&P sector weights.

claims.claim: Higher financing costs and adverse federal policy weakened residential solar demand and stocks.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare financed monthly payments, installations and company-specific demand alongside policy changes.
claims.reason: The proposed channels are plausible, but this passage does not isolate them from pricing, inventories, state policy or company execution. The $30,000 system price is illustrative.
claims.next_check: Compare financed monthly payments, installations and company-specific demand alongside policy changes.

claims.claim: Office REITs lost their former defensive character as office-property values declined.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect vacancies, leases, valuations, debt maturities and actual asset sales.
claims.reason: The broad diagnosis needs dated, property-specific evidence; it does not establish that the downturn is over or that every REIT has the same exposure.
claims.next_check: Inspect vacancies, leases, valuations, debt maturities and actual asset sales.

claims.claim: Regulated utilities have relatively predictable profits and defensive characteristics.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect rate cases, capital plans, recovery mechanisms and financing needs.
claims.reason: Regulation can improve visibility, but allowed returns, cost recovery, debt financing and exceptional liabilities prevent guaranteed profitability.
claims.next_check: Inspect rate cases, capital plans, recovery mechanisms and financing needs.

claims.claim: The Fed controls only the federal funds rate and no other interest rate.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Distinguish administered rates, the funds target and the effective market rate.
claims.reason: It directly administers reserve-interest, reverse-repo and discount rates as well. The useful distinction is between policy instruments and market-determined longer-term yields, not that the Fed sets only one rate.

evidence.title: Ample-reserves monetary-policy implementation
evidence.finding: The Fed sets administered reserve-interest and reverse-repo rates to guide the federal funds market rate. The discount rate is also administered; long-term yields are not directly fixed by the funds target.

claims.next_check: Distinguish administered rates, the funds target and the effective market rate.

claims.claim: Long rates usually exceed short rates because lending for longer is riskier.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Decompose yields into expected policy rates and term premia.
claims.reason: A term premium can contribute, but expected future short rates and changing risk premia also determine the curve. No historical frequency or exclusive causal decomposition is established.
claims.next_check: Decompose yields into expected policy rates and term premia.

claims.claim: For fixed promised bond cash flows, a higher price implies a lower yield.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The inverse relationship is correct when cash flows and maturity are held constant.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: Bond price is the sum of fixed positive cash flows discounted at yield; increasing yield reduces each present value.

claims.claim: Fear of recession can pull long yields below short yields, but inversion does not perfectly predict recession.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare a defined spread and lead window with an official recession chronology.
claims.reason: This is a qualified interpretation rather than a deterministic signal. The passage supplies no specified spread, lead time or false-positive study.
claims.next_check: Compare a defined spread and lead window with an official recession chronology.

claims.claim: A steeper yield curve increases bank net interest margins because banks fund short and lend long.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Model asset and liability repricing rather than use slope alone.
claims.reason: The stylized maturity transformation is useful, but the implication is not automatic: deposit betas, asset repricing, hedges, funding mix and credit losses can offset it.
claims.next_check: Model asset and liability repricing rather than use slope alone.

proof.derivation: Suppose the market short rate is unchanged and the long rate rises 1 point, steepening the curve. If a bank raises previously low deposit rates by 2 points to retain funding while asset yield rises 1 point, its spread falls 1 point. The claimed result requires assumptions about deposit pricing and asset repricing.

claims.claim: Rising long-term rates need not hurt stocks when they reflect stronger growth without excessive inflation.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: He qualifies the usual inverse-rate heuristic. The net outcome depends on earnings revisions and discount rates, so this is a scenario framework.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Inflation-driven Fed tightening caused the 2022 equity decline, although the feared recession did not occur.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Separate price and total returns, realized recession dates and the contribution of earnings versus discount rates.
claims.reason: The rate and earnings-risk channels are plausible, but the attribution is not isolated. The cited roughly 18% decline requires a total-return rather than price-only definition.
claims.next_check: Separate price and total returns, realized recession dates and the contribution of earnings versus discount rates.

claims.claim: With projected positive cash flows fixed, increasing the discount rate reduces DCF value.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: This is correct conditional mathematics. Actual market moves also change growth forecasts and risk premia.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: For each positive future cash flow C at time t, C/(1+r)^t declines as r rises; summing preserves the direction.

claims.claim: Cash flows concentrated farther in the future are more sensitive to discount-rate changes than equally valued nearer cash flows.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The duration mechanism is correct; it does not guarantee that every growth stock underperforms every staple whenever rates rise.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: The proportional sensitivity of a single discounted cash flow is -t/(1+r); later t means larger sensitivity at the same rate.
