review.summary: Glenn Schorr and Eisman distinguish operating businesses from stock valuations across private markets, banks and traditional asset managers. Durable funding, delayed exits, securities runoff and fee pressure offer useful mechanisms. Private-credit reassurance is incomplete: public versus private financing was not a clean distinction in First Brands, and tight public spreads do not logically rule out private-manager weakness. Citi and QQQ illustrate subsequent operational progress without settling every valuation claim.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman interviews Evercore analyst Glenn Schorr. Host restatements are separately recorded where he adopts a substantive proposition.
framework_points: Separate manager equity valuation from credit-portfolio marks and borrower defaults.
Match asset and liability duration without ignoring surrender, leverage and credit risk.
Measure private-equity returns using timing as well as money multiples.
A past mistake can create a forward earnings recovery opportunity at the right price.
Normalize ROE versus RoTCE before comparing banks.
Distinguish settlement technology from underlying asset risk.
Model AUM, flows and fee rates separately.
transcript_cautions: All 1737caption lines were read.
The interview explicitly identifies recording on November 3, 2025, ahead of Apollo's November 4 report; publication was November 10.
Opening montage repeats the interview.
Contemporaneous stock declines are not prospective price targets.
Guest recommendations and guest revision about Fraser are separate from Eisman views.
Claims about fraud or scandals are not treated as adjudicated findings.

Distinguish legacy-business decline from new-business growth.
Use announced deal volume to assess future advisory activity.

review.summary: A publishing panel explains changes in discovery, editorial labor, rights and author compensation, with Eisman mainly asking questions. The material themes are platform dependence, AI substitution of generic information, differentiated author brands and licensing economics. Verified corrections concern Amazon's generated-content policy, the distinction between training and piracy in Bartz, and author-funded costs hidden by headline hybrid royalty comparisons.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman hosts literary agents Regina Brooks and Jennifer Weis, and publisher Anthony Ziccardi. Unclear overlapping turns are explicitly marked uncertain.
framework_points: Follow distribution and discovery power as formats change.
Separate generic information from differentiated author voice and community.
Do not infer legal infringement merely from technical model training.
Compare net contract economics after author-funded costs and rights grants.
Use portfolio economics for hit-driven creative businesses.
Historical data can screen out ideas with no close precedent.
tools_and_charts: Print, ebook and audio revenue versus unit shares
Advance, royalty and author-funded cost comparison
Training rights versus output and acquisition rights

review.title: NVIDIA’S Explosive Growth Can’t Hide the Market’s AI Panic | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: The November 21 wrap separates Nvidia operating growth from market nervousness, highlights Oracle funding needs and compares weak housing retailers with Walmart. It discusses Blue Owl liquidity, fee incentives and Eisman willingness to hold strong business stories through valuation concerns.
review.assessment: Oracle financing dependence and the distinction between supply-chain demand and end-user returns are useful. His dotcom chronology is wrong, and the BDC leverage example confuses debt/equity with assets/equity. The Blue Owl episode concerns liquidity and market discounts rather than proof that loan NAV instantly fell.
framework_points: Follow cash funding, not just bookings.
Separate technological transformation from investor returns.
Check liquidity terms before treating NAV as readily redeemable cash.
Consider manager incentives and valuation discipline alongside an intact thesis.
transcript_cautions: The Next Insurance advertising segment is labeled promotional content and excluded from the investment scorecard.
Reported historical short returns and personal holdings are disclosures, not independently audited performance.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman presents; speaker attribution follows the full dialogue.

claims.claim: Nvidia accelerating revenue confirms continued strong demand for AI infrastructure.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Track recognized revenue, cash conversion and customer returns separately.
claims.reason: The release reports 62% year-over-year and 22% sequential revenue growth. Strong operating demand does not ensure next-day share gains.

evidence.title: Nvidia fiscal Q3 2026 results
evidence.finding: Revenue reached $57 billion, up 62% year over year and 22% sequentially; diluted EPS was $1.30. This supports strong operating demand, not an automatic stock gain.

claims.next_check: Track recognized revenue, cash conversion and customer returns separately.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare intraday news, rates and flows.
claims.reason: He gives a causal opinion rather than an identified event study. Multiple expectations and positioning changes can matter.
claims.next_check: Compare intraday news, rates and flows.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare demand, competition, capital intensity and investor entry prices.
claims.reason: This is a historical analogy reported from Niall Ferguson. It supplies scenarios, not proof that AI must repeat railroad crashes.
claims.next_check: Compare demand, competition, capital intensity and investor entry prices.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Trace incremental external customer revenue and net cash returns.
claims.reason: Supplier revenue and customer net returns are different accounting quantities. Capital outlays can generate supplier profits even when end-user projects later disappoint.
claims.next_check: Trace incremental external customer revenue and net cash returns.

assumptions: Customers buy equipment before receiving uncertain future project cash flows.
proof.proof: A supplier can recognize a valid sale while the buyer later earns a negative NPV. Therefore supplier growth alone cannot establish buyer profitability.
proof.derivation: A supplier can recognize a valid sale while the buyer later earns a negative NPV. Therefore supplier growth alone cannot establish buyer profitability.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.reason: This is expressed as hope, with no specified clarity criterion.
claims.next_check: Define adoption, productivity and profitability evidence before assessing progress.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Track cash flow, capex, debt maturities and customer prepayments.
claims.reason: The subsequent fiscal Q2 disclosure showed six-month capex around twice operating cash flow and over $100 billion of borrowings. The funding gap supports the mechanism, not a prediction of inevitable default.

evidence.title: Fiscal 2026 second-quarter results
evidence.finding: RPO $523 billion, revenue $16.1 billion. Six-month operating cash flow $10.206 billion versus capex $20.535 billion. Trailing FCF negative $13.181 billion. Current/noncurrent borrowings $8.091/$99.984 billion, previously $7.271/$85.297 billion.

claims.next_check: Track cash flow, capex, debt maturities and customer prepayments.

evidence.finding: Primary loan-level research estimates higher market rates relative to existing loans reduce sale probability. Original abstract estimates 1.33 million prevented sales in 2022Q2-2023Q4 and upward price pressure from reduced supply. Estimates support the mechanism, not every December 2025 market statistic.

claims.next_check: Track mortgage cohorts, turnover, affordability and renovation spending.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.reason: The exact quarter was not independently inspected here; a short encouraging start is not a sustained recovery.

claims.next_check: Compare real spending and share by income and category.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.reason: Termination is confirmed. A market-price discount can reduce immediate realizable value, but is distinct from an immediate 20% loss in underlying loan NAV, and exact exchange terms matter.

evidence.finding: The proposed OBDC/OBDC II merger was terminated, with alternatives to be reevaluated. The release cites current market conditions; it does not independently establish every claimed investor motive.

claims.next_check: Compare exchange ratio, NAV, market price and redemption availability.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Define systemic versus issuer-specific deterioration and a time window.
claims.reason: No deadline, materiality threshold or universe is specified. A future isolated adverse story would be an extremely low bar.
claims.next_check: Define systemic versus issuer-specific deterioration and a time window.

claims.claim: Management fees and incentive fees can create conflicts, especially when fees are based on gross assets.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect the actual management agreement and fee base.
claims.reason: A gross-asset fee increases with funded assets even when added assets are financed with debt. Contract details and fee waivers matter.
claims.next_check: Inspect the actual management agreement and fee base.

assumptions: The agreement applies a positive constant fee to gross assets including debt-financed assets.
proof.proof: Increasing borrowing and invested assets raises gross-asset fees without a corresponding increase in investor equity, creating a leverage incentive at the margin.
proof.derivation: Increasing borrowing and invested assets raises gross-asset fees without a corresponding increase in investor equity, creating a leverage incentive at the margin.

claims.claim: At the permitted 2:1 BDC leverage limit, $1 billion equity supports $2 billion of gross assets.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Distinguish debt/equity, assets/equity and asset coverage.
claims.reason: The cited regulatory limit is debt/equity 2:1; $1 billion equity plus $2 billion debt means $3 billion gross assets, subject to applicable coverage rules. His $2 billion example describes 1:1 debt/equity.

evidence.title: BDC asset coverage and leverage
evidence.finding: The 150% coverage regime permits debt/equity of 2:1, subject to approvals and rules. At that limit $1 of equity funds $3 of gross assets, not $2.

claims.next_check: Distinguish debt/equity, assets/equity and asset coverage.

claims.claim: Upside participation can encourage risk, but franchise and career concerns may restrain managers.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect manager capital, fee terms, clawbacks and observed risk taking.
claims.reason: This is a balanced incentive hypothesis. Managers may also invest capital, face clawbacks or high-water marks, so zero downside is not universal.
claims.next_check: Inspect manager capital, fee terms, clawbacks and observed risk taking.

claims.claim: An intact strong business story often matters more to his holding decision than reaching a valuation target.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Track thesis validity and a range of plausible discounted returns independently.
claims.reason: This accurately describes a discretionary process, not a guaranteed return rule. It leaves a vulnerability to overpaying even when operations remain sound.
claims.next_check: Track thesis validity and a range of plausible discounted returns independently.

claims.claim: The internet bubble broke because the 2001 recession first caused technology fundamentals to deteriorate, not because of valuations.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare market peaks, earnings revisions, investment and recession timing.
claims.reason: The Nasdaq peaked in March 2000 and fell substantially before the March 2001 recession peak. The single-cause account reverses important chronology and does not exclude valuation or anticipatory effects.

evidence.title: March 2001 business-cycle peak
evidence.finding: The recession began after the March 2001 business-cycle peak, about a year after the Nasdaq March 2000 peak.

evidence.title: 2000 market and economic developments
evidence.finding: The Federal Reserve describes the technology-market peak in early 2000 and subsequent decline before the March 2001 recession date. This contradicts a chronology in which the recession first broke the bubble.

claims.next_check: Compare market peaks, earnings revisions, investment and recession timing.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Track demand, margins and cash generation separately from price.
claims.reason: The reported growth supports the narrow operating judgment. It does not establish that the stock is attractive at every valuation or will recover on a deadline.

evidence.title: Nvidia fiscal Q3 2026 results
evidence.finding: Revenue reached $57 billion, up 62% year over year and 22% sequentially; diluted EPS was $1.30. This supports strong operating demand, not an automatic stock gain.

claims.next_check: Track demand, margins and cash generation separately from price.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Assess local accounting, regulation, market structure and information access.
claims.reason: This is a scope and competence preference, not a forecast of inferior Indian returns.
claims.next_check: Assess local accounting, regulation, market structure and information access.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Track policy growth, combined ratio, capital returns and entry valuation.

metadata.title: Why It’s So Difficult For Companies to Go Public: A CFO Explains the Process | Real Eisman Playbook

review.summary: Amy Butte explains IPO preparation through NYSE and Navan, emphasizing financial controls, reproducible KPIs and capable teams. Navan provides a concrete AI-support example with later revenue growth and strong gross margins, but the interview does not establish zero hallucination risk or like-for-like labor productivity versus Amex GBT. Butte explicitly declines a profitability deadline, and the career discussion is guidance rather than a quantitative employment forecast.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman interviews Amy Butte, then Navan CFO. Most company execution and AI performance claims belong to the guest.
framework_points: Treat IPO readiness as controls, tax, systems and people work, not merely a financing event.
Demand stable KPI definitions and acquisition integration.
Distinguish an audit concern from proof of fraud.
Separate observed automation, causal savings and durable competitive advantage.
Compare labor at equal service output before inferring productivity.
Distinguish gross margins, adjusted operating income and GAAP profitability.
Do not manufacture a horizon when management declines to forecast one.
tools_and_charts: AI interaction share and gross margin
Support staffing normalized by booking/service volume
transcript_cautions: All 1403caption lines were read.
Opening montage repeats interview claims.
Navan name and Rule 430A are garbled in captions.
NYSEIPOshorthand is explicitly clarified as the Archipelago merger.
The reference to Navan listing two weeks earlier suggests recording preceded publication; no exact recording date is asserted.
Personal health disclosure and biographical details are not investment claims.

review.title: Google Surges Past OpenAI and AI Faces a Bigger Crisis That Could Break the Boom | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman argues that Google has become a serious AI rival to OpenAI, with a stronger funding base. He distinguishes transformative technology from profitable investment, takes depreciation concerns seriously without declaring the AI buildout a failure, and identifies power availability as a constraint. His strongest points concern cash generation and physical infrastructure; sweeping claims about all electricity growth and all chip availability are less secure.
review.assessment: The episode is primarily a business-model and financing analysis, not a dated market forecast. Its power thesis is supported, while the 2028 electricity-share forecast remains open. The Starbucks observation is explicitly about the incomplete turnaround at the time, not a forecast that it could never recover.
framework_points: Separate social or technological value from shareholder returns.
Compare the funding capacity of competitors before assuming the upstart wins.
Find the constraint that prevents demand from becoming usable capacity.
Treat accounting estimates as testable assumptions, not automatic evidence of fraud.
Question CEO reputations with operating results.
tools_and_charts: Forward price/earnings ratios and product differentiation
Operating cash flow, capital expenditure and debt
Asset useful lives and impairment charges
Electricity demand in TWh versus capacity in MW
transcript_cautions: The opening montage repeats later claims and is not counted twice.
Caption errors include Baidu, Digital Realty, STACK, ERCOT, Oklo, Brian Niccol and Jeff Immelt.
Electricity consumption is described as terawatts in speech/captions; the annual quantities require terawatt-hours. This unit slip is flagged rather than treated as a separate major forecast.
The anonymous viewer anecdote is summarized without exposing identifying details.

review.title: Steve Eisman Reflects on 2008, The Big Short & Today’s K-Shaped Economy | The Real Eisman Playbook
review.summary: At a university Q&A recorded October 29 and published December 1, 2025, Eisman explains the financial crisis through leverage, bad underwriting, concentrated ownership and interconnected derivatives. He favors US equities and continued AI spending, expects bank consolidation, and explicitly withholds an opinion on private-credit insurance risk. The historical credit framework is useful; several absolute claims about regulation, investigations and financing need qualification.
review.assessment: The strongest material explanation is the interaction of credit deterioration, leverage and funding. His stated uncertainty on private credit is preserved rather than rewritten as a bearish forecast. Regulatory and due-diligence simplifications are weaker, and an optimistic AI-spending scenario is not an unconditional market target.
framework_points: Study the debt and funding structure behind equity narratives.
Look for a shared hidden assumption, such as permanently rising house prices.
Refresh conviction with recurring operating or loan-vintage data.
Choose an instrument whose carrying cost lets the thesis survive.
Say when the available data do not support an opinion.
Distinguish a sound business or technology from a good investment at the prevailing price.
tools_and_charts: Bank stress tests and capital ratios
Capex guidance and corporate cash flow
Visa spending and bank credit-quality results
transcript_cautions: The introduction dates the event October 29, 2025, although this video was published December 1. Statements about current conditions refer to the recording.
Captions garble company names including Comerica and New Century; obvious names were corrected from context.
The risk-weighted leverage and mortgage examples are simplified, not calibrated models.
Opening montage repeats later passages; ads, personal biography, movie anecdotes and career advice are excluded from material-claim counts.
review.speaker_map_notes: Eisman is the main respondent. Ivy Zelman hosts; students ask questions. Student premises are not assigned to Eisman unless he explicitly adopts them.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the crisis exposure chain in primary investigations.
claims.reason: The FCIC documents the debt-market structures and exposures central to the crisis. This is a historical explanation, not a new successful forecast.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare capital treatment and actual changing underwriting risk.
claims.reason: The incentive mechanism and structured-credit capital treatment are documented in the crisis inquiry. History-based weights cannot guarantee future credit quality.

claims.claim: Banks retained large highly rated mortgage exposures, so securitization failed to disperse the risk safely outside important institutions.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check retained securities, CDO exposures and off-balance-sheet commitments.
claims.reason: The FCIC documents retained senior exposures and concentration. The narrative that excess production alone caused retention is more specific than the evidence establishes.

evidence.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Report
evidence.finding: The report documents leverage, deteriorating mortgage underwriting, retained securitization exposure and derivatives counterparty connections. Chapters 8-10 distinguish these mechanisms from a simple housing-price narrative.

claims.claim: Buying credit protection reduces exposure to the borrower but creates dependence on the protection seller surviving when payment is due.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Identify the protection obligation, collateral and counterparty resources.
claims.reason: This follows directly from the contract structure, subject to collateral and clearing arrangements. It explains counterparty risk rather than proving that every swap increases net system risk.
claims.next_check: Identify the protection obligation, collateral and counterparty resources.

assumptions: A bilateral protection contract without a fully effective independent guarantee.
proof.derivation: The promised payment is valuable only to the extent the protection seller or pledged collateral can satisfy it.

claims.claim: AIG was rescued because failure of its credit-protection business could transmit large losses through the financial system.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Read the AIG failure and intervention account, not only its CDS notional.
claims.qualifications: The remembered $50-70 billion figure is not used as a complete measure of all AIG CDS exposure.
claims.reason: The FCIC records systemic-fragility concerns surrounding AIG and its counterparties. Securities lending and liquidity pressures also mattered.

evidence.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Report
evidence.finding: The report documents leverage, deteriorating mortgage underwriting, retained securitization exposure and derivatives counterparty connections. Chapters 8-10 distinguish these mechanisms from a simple housing-price narrative.

claims.next_check: Read the AIG failure and intervention account, not only its CDS notional.

claims.claim: Synthetic CDOs built around credit-default swaps expanded exposure beyond the underlying cash mortgage bonds.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare synthetic notional with the referenced cash tranches.
claims.reason: The FCIC explicitly documents repeated reference exposures and synthetic issuance as an amplification mechanism.

evidence.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Report
evidence.finding: The report documents leverage, deteriorating mortgage underwriting, retained securitization exposure and derivatives counterparty connections. Chapters 8-10 distinguish these mechanisms from a simple housing-price narrative.

claims.next_check: Compare synthetic notional with the referenced cash tranches.

claims.claim: Without intervention almost every major institution would have failed, and even a successful short seller faced counterparty failure.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Specify a counterfactual funding and resolution model, distinguishing insolvency from liquidity failure.
claims.reason: Counterparty vulnerability is real; the universal no-intervention outcome is an unobservable counterfactual.

evidence.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Report
evidence.finding: The report documents leverage, deteriorating mortgage underwriting, retained securitization exposure and derivatives counterparty connections. Chapters 8-10 distinguish these mechanisms from a simple housing-price narrative.

claims.next_check: Specify a counterfactual funding and resolution model, distinguishing insolvency from liquidity failure.

claims.claim: Off-balance-sheet vehicles could leave banks with economic risk that simple reported leverage concealed.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Include liquidity guarantees, support and retained exposures in leverage analysis.
claims.qualifications: The assessment resolves the economic-risk mechanism only.
claims.reason: The FCIC describes bank support and off-balance-sheet leverage. The additional assertion that regulators knew nothing about these vehicles is not established.

evidence.title: FCIC report, leverage comparisons, printed p.64
evidence.finding: The 2000-2007 ratios varied sharply by bank, including roughly stable ratios at JPMorgan and Wells Fargo. Reported versus off-balance-sheet leverage also differed. This does not establish a uniform tripling from 1997.

claims.claim: Tax refunds seasonally improve borrower payment capacity, so temporary spring credit improvement can mislead an analyst.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use monthly vintage delinquency data and seasonal adjustments around refund receipts.
claims.reason: A testable seasonal mechanism is proposed, but the specific historical price-rally attribution and size of the effect are not independently verified.
claims.next_check: Use monthly vintage delinquency data and seasonal adjustments around refund receipts.

claims.claim: The growth of private credit and insurer ownership is insufficient evidence by itself to conclude that a crisis is coming.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Look for asset, liability, leverage and loss data before forming a crisis forecast.
claims.reason: This is an explicit limit on his knowledge and a research standard, not a prediction of safety or failure.
claims.next_check: Look for asset, liability, leverage and loss data before forming a crisis forecast.

claims.claim: Post-crisis regulation and stress testing materially increased bank resilience by increasing capital and reducing risky exposures.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare consistent bank capital, leverage and risk measures before and after reform.
claims.reason: The Fed confirms a substantial post-crisis capital increase. Exact claims about leverage being more than halved everywhere are not independently resolved.

evidence.title: 2025 stress test background
evidence.finding: Large-bank capital rose substantially after the crisis. Stress testing applies on annual or two-year cycles to covered firms, not uniformly to every bank.

claims.next_check: Compare consistent bank capital, leverage and risk measures before and after reform.

claims.claim: US banks are basically safe under the post-crisis framework.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Define the bank population, loss threshold, scenario and horizon before scoring safety.
claims.reason: He immediately discusses SVB as an exception. Neither a universal safety guarantee nor a precise horizon is stated.
claims.next_check: Define the bank population, loss threshold, scenario and horizon before scoring safety.

claims.claim: SVB essentially just took venture deposits and bought long-term Treasuries; that was its business.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare the year-end 2022 loan and securities balance sheet, including agency mortgage-backed securities.
claims.reason: The description is materially oversimplified. An inspected supervisory account establishes securities and interest-rate exposure, but this review has not yet attached the full asset table needed for a definitive composition grade.

evidence.title: Review of SVB supervision: key takeaways
evidence.finding: Concentrated uninsured deposits, interest-rate risk and weak liquidity management left SVB vulnerable; the securities sale and proposed capital raise preceded a run exceeding $40 billion on March 9.

claims.next_check: Compare the year-end 2022 loan and securities balance sheet, including agency mortgage-backed securities.

claims.claim: SVB failed when interest-rate losses interacted with concentrated deposit withdrawals and the need to monetize assets.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Trace securities losses, liquid resources and deposit outflows.
claims.reason: The Fed review documents this funding and duration interaction. It also identifies governance and risk-management weaknesses.

evidence.title: Review of SVB supervision: key takeaways
evidence.finding: Concentrated uninsured deposits, interest-rate risk and weak liquidity management left SVB vulnerable; the securities sale and proposed capital raise preceded a run exceeding $40 billion on March 9.

claims.next_check: Trace securities losses, liquid resources and deposit outflows.

claims.claim: Large public growth-stock losses imply comparable percentage losses in the private businesses held by venture capital.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Match public and private cash flows, financing terms and valuations before transferring a drawdown.
claims.reason: Public repricing is relevant evidence, but identical percentage changes require matching businesses, terms and starting valuations. No such comparison is supplied.
claims.next_check: Match public and private cash flows, financing terms and valuations before transferring a drawdown.

claims.claim: There are essentially no newly underwritten subprime mortgages in the United States.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Define subprime and compare current originations in that category rather than conflating borrower scores with loan structures.
claims.reason: He softens the literal zero, but does not define subprime as borrower credit quality, product structure or private securitization. Modern low-score government-insured loans are not equivalent to pre-crisis subprime products.
claims.next_check: Define subprime and compare current originations in that category rather than conflating borrower scores with loan structures.

claims.claim: He knows of no mortgage-underwriting regulation; the real constraint is the bank stress test.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect applicable underwriting rules and the population subject to stress tests.
claims.qualifications: He qualifies the first clause as his knowledge, but presents it as the explanation of the regulatory constraint.
claims.reason: Covered mortgage lenders have an explicit ability-to-repay duty under Regulation Z. Stress tests are important but cannot substitute for this underwriting regime.

evidence.title: Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage final rule
evidence.finding: Covered mortgage creditors must make a reasonable, good-faith ability-to-repay determination. Mortgage underwriting rules exist independently of bank stress tests.

evidence.title: 2025 stress test background
evidence.finding: Large-bank capital rose substantially after the crisis. Stress testing applies on annual or two-year cycles to covered firms, not uniformly to every bank.

claims.next_check: Inspect applicable underwriting rules and the population subject to stress tests.

claims.claim: Technology and compliance costs favor scale, and regional-bank consolidation should accelerate.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Track announced and completed regional-bank deals, asset concentration and unit-cost changes against a specified baseline.
claims.reason: A major cited deal subsequently closed. That supports consolidation activity, while one transaction does not prove an industry-wide wave or its causal explanation.

evidence.title: Fifth Third completes Comerica merger
evidence.finding: The announced merger closed, creating a bank with about $294 billion in assets. One transaction supports consolidation activity but does not establish an industry-wide wave or the causal necessity of scale.

claims.next_check: Track announced and completed regional-bank deals, asset concentration and unit-cost changes against a specified baseline.

claims.claim: The Fed is institutionally stronger than alarmist coverage suggests, and the next chair will not pursue uncontrolled easing.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Specify a policy-rate path and an operational independence test.
claims.reason: No threshold for uncontrolled easing or specific policy path is given. This institutional judgment cannot be scored from a single rate decision.
claims.next_check: Specify a policy-rate path and an operational independence test.

claims.claim: Recurring loan-vintage data can sustain conviction when market prices and consensus disagree.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check whether new data actually test and potentially falsify the thesis.
claims.reason: This is a research practice, not a forecast or a guarantee that conviction is justified.
claims.next_check: Check whether new data actually test and potentially falsify the thesis.

claims.claim: Better-than-expected credit performance during rising house prices encouraged lenders to loosen standards repeatedly, creating future losses.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare lending standards, expected losses and later vintage performance.
claims.qualifications: His categorical rejection of any political role is not established by this mechanism alone.
claims.reason: The FCIC documents weak underwriting and incentives within the mortgage boom. This feedback explanation is supported without accepting that policy had no role at all.

evidence.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Report
evidence.finding: The report documents leverage, deteriorating mortgage underwriting, retained securitization exposure and derivatives counterparty connections. Chapters 8-10 distinguish these mechanisms from a simple housing-price narrative.

claims.next_check: Compare lending standards, expected losses and later vintage performance.

claims.claim: Greenspan encouragement of adjustable-rate mortgages helped move lenders toward riskier short-duration loan structures.
claims.speaker: Ivy Zelman
claims.test: Read the original speech and compare lending changes with a defensible causal design.
claims.reason: Zelman offers a causal attribution, but the episode does not establish the incremental effect of that advice versus incentives and other policy conditions.
claims.next_check: Read the original speech and compare lending changes with a defensible causal design.

claims.claim: A debt tranche can express the same bearish thesis with much lower carrying cost than shorting an expensive, high-dividend stock.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare premium, dividend liability, borrow fee, recovery exposure and counterparty risk for the actual trades.
claims.reason: The instrument-selection principle is useful; his personal historical borrow costs are recollections rather than independently verified return records.
claims.next_check: Compare premium, dividend liability, borrow fee, recovery exposure and counterparty risk for the actual trades.

claims.claim: In the simplified waterfall, three 3% layers are exhausted when cumulative pool losses reach 9%.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Apply loss allocation to the stated example.
claims.reason: The arithmetic is correct under the stated sequential-loss structure; real transactions also involve cash flows, triggers and recoveries.
claims.next_check: Apply loss allocation to the stated example.

assumptions: Three successive loss-absorbing layers of 3% each; no offsetting recoveries or excess spread.
proof.derivation: 3% + 3% + 3% = 9%; the third layer is fully impaired at that cumulative loss.

claims.claim: Due-diligence samples revealed deficient mortgages, yet securitizations proceeded with inadequate disclosure of loan quality.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare Clayton results, waivers and investor disclosures.
claims.reason: The FCIC documents sampled failures, waivers and disclosure problems. The account should not be read as proof that every firm followed an identical sample size and procedure.

evidence.title: FCIC report, Clayton due diligence findings, printed pp.165-169
evidence.finding: Clayton rejected 28% of sampled loans; banks waived in 39% of those rejected. Samples and disclosure practices varied; the findings support a serious due-diligence failure but not every universal statement about every firm.

claims.next_check: Compare Clayton results, waivers and investor disclosures.

claims.claim: As far as anyone knows, DOJ never even investigated the mortgage due-diligence conduct referred after the crisis inquiry.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Separate the specific referral, criminal prosecution, civil investigation and settlement outcomes.
claims.reason: DOJ documents investigations and civil resolutions concerning RMBS misconduct. That contradicts a broad impression of no investigation, but does not establish the disposition of every particular FCIC criminal referral.

evidence.title: Goldman Sachs RMBS settlement and admitted facts
evidence.finding: DOJ describes investigations of mortgage securitization misconduct and a $5.06 billion civil resolution. It distinguishes civil liability from criminal charges, which the settlement did not release.

claims.next_check: Separate the specific referral, criminal prosecution, civil investigation and settlement outcomes.

claims.claim: Without bailouts, the crisis would have produced a depression with unemployment near 30%.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use an explicit macro-financial counterfactual model with uncertainty bounds.
claims.reason: The claim is a counterfactual numerical forecast. Neither the observed 2009 recession nor the existence of systemic danger identifies that precise alternative outcome.
claims.next_check: Use an explicit macro-financial counterfactual model with uncertainty bounds.

claims.claim: For-profit education had a structurally poor product sustained by government funding.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare completion, earnings, repayment and public subsidy across named schools and matched alternatives.
claims.reason: This is a broad industry thesis without a defined cohort, outcome measure or new supporting evidence in the episode.
claims.next_check: Compare completion, earnings, repayment and public subsidy across named schools and matched alternatives.

claims.claim: US economic dynamism makes US equities the preferred destination, with little reason to invest abroad.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Specify investable portfolios, currency treatment, starting valuation and horizon.
claims.reason: This preference has no portfolio, benchmark, horizon or valuation constraint. Market-cap leadership alone does not establish future relative returns.
claims.next_check: Specify investable portfolios, currency treatment, starting valuation and horizon.

claims.claim: The economy is increasingly dependent on AI while housing and other segments are weak, and ultimate AI returns remain uncertain.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Separate direct investment contributions from imports and indirect effects; measure sector breadth and realized cash returns.
claims.reason: The direction is a material diagnostic, but the episode does not provide a reproducible decomposition of AI-attributable GDP or a return calculation.
claims.next_check: Separate direct investment contributions from imports and indirect effects; measure sector breadth and realized cash returns.

claims.claim: AI-investment returns may not be clear until 2027; continued capex expansion keeps the current market story alive.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Revisit realized utilization, revenue, capex and free cash flow through 2027.
claims.reason: The explicit 2027 assessment window is unfinished. Alphabet guidance supports continuing investment at the recording date, but not the eventual return on that spending.

evidence.title: Alphabet Q3 2025 earnings call
evidence.finding: Alphabet raised 2025 capex guidance from $85 billion to $91-93 billion and expected a significant further increase in 2026. Management also identified depreciation and energy-cost pressure.

claims.next_check: Revisit realized utilization, revenue, capex and free cash flow through 2027.

claims.claim: Visa spending and healthy reported bank credit quality argue against an imminent broad consumer collapse.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Combine real spending, payment volume, cohort delinquency and labor income; define the forecast horizon.
claims.reason: The inference is material, but aggregate transaction growth and bank portfolios may conceal weakness by income cohort. The episode does not specify an imminent-collapse threshold.
claims.next_check: Combine real spending, payment volume, cohort delinquency and labor income; define the forecast horizon.

claims.claim: The market should keep rising while hyperscalers expand capex; a major capex cut would trigger a large correction.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.horizon: While the AI capex cycle continues; no fixed end date
claims.test: Track comparable capex guidance and market returns around a material spending reversal.
claims.qualifications: The Meta 25% cut is a hypothetical trigger, not a forecast that Meta will announce it.
claims.reason: This is a conditional market scenario without a fixed terminal date. The capex-cut trigger and ensuing return window require definition before resolution.
claims.next_check: Track comparable capex guidance and market returns around a material spending reversal.

claims.claim: Unlike the internet bubble, the current AI buildout is financed from large profitable companies own cash flows rather than leverage.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconcile operating cash flow, capex, distributions, new debt and project financing at the recording date.
claims.reason: Profitable incumbents are an important difference, but the categorical financing claim needs full cash-flow, debt and off-balance-sheet evidence across the named firms. Alphabet capex guidance alone cannot resolve it.

evidence.title: Alphabet Q3 2025 earnings call
evidence.finding: Alphabet raised 2025 capex guidance from $85 billion to $91-93 billion and expected a significant further increase in 2026. Management also identified depreciation and energy-cost pressure.

claims.next_check: Reconcile operating cash flow, capex, distributions, new debt and project financing at the recording date.

claims.claim: Housing is no longer an attractive investment beyond roughly keeping pace with inflation.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Define a property cohort, net total return and holding period.
claims.qualifications: Eisman rejects the investment framing; Zelman supplies the inflation benchmark.
claims.reason: No location, leverage, rent benefit, holding period or maintenance assumption is specified. A blanket investment outcome is not measurable as stated.
claims.next_check: Define a property cohort, net total return and holding period.

claims.claim: He has bought a small amount of crypto despite his longstanding doubts about its rationale.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use only as a disclosed change in exposure unless verified transaction records are supplied.
claims.reason: This is a personal position disclosure, not evidence of a trade price, realized return or unconditional bullish forecast.
claims.next_check: Use only as a disclosed change in exposure unless verified transaction records are supplied.

claims.claim: Crypto often trades like risky technology equities rather than reliably hedging the inflation and fiat-debasement risks used to justify ownership.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Calculate dated rolling correlations and stress-period returns; distinguish inflation shocks from monetary debasement.
claims.reason: A meaningful hedge test must specify regime, asset and horizon. The episode supplies no current correlation calculation, and a long-run debasement thesis does not imply an inverse relationship on every daily move.
claims.next_check: Calculate dated rolling correlations and stress-period returns; distinguish inflation shocks from monetary debasement.

review.title: The Housing Market is Broken: Why Homes Are Unaffordable & What It Takes to Fix It | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman argues that mortgage lock-in, constrained local supply and rising ownership costs explain housing’s weakness despite better-run builders. He distinguishes builders from companies exposed to existing-home transactions and favors supply reforms over buyer subsidies. FHFA loan-level research supports the lock-in mechanism; other quantitative and causal claims need matched evidence. He also discusses AI risks to software franchises, skepticism about crypto valuation and ETF structure. His practical fund comparison is mostly sound, but passive portfolios do change with their indices and not every mutual fund is actively managed.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Separate new-home and existing-home transaction exposure.
Compare earnings deterioration with stock expectations before assuming fundamentals are improving.
Model mortgage payments explicitly and distinguish liquidity lock-in from construction constraints.
Compare demand subsidies with supply elasticity.
Evaluate fund structure, costs and taxes separately from manager skill.
tools_and_charts: Builder and building-product company EPS and share-return tables
Zelman entry-level affordability index including taxes and insurance
Mortgage rate distribution, public builder market share and housing shortage estimates
ETF fees, trading, disclosure and in-kind redemption
transcript_cautions: He corrects an earlier electricity-unit error from terawatts to terawatt-hours.
The mortgage example assumes full financing and excludes taxes and insurance.
Historical and current fund terminology is simplified; mutual fund is a legal structure, not a synonym for active management.

review.title: Inside the Industrial Comeback & AI’s Power Crisis with Nigel Coe | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 37
review.summary: Nigel Coe describes an industrial sector split between AI/power demand and weak consumer-facing markets. He prefers nVent, Wesco and Vertiv, sees a 3M margin turnaround, and is cautious on Eaton revisions, distributors and housing. Eisman endorses the importance of earnings revisions, simple investment narratives, firm power and the scale of grid expansion. Later supplier results support the AI infrastructure and 3M operating theses; Fastenal gross margins weakened but operating margins improved. Conditional housing picks, stock-relative returns and multiyear backlog claims remain distinct from those operating validations.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This episode is strongest in connecting industry structure and physical bottlenecks to operating earnings. Primary results support several guest operating theses, while stock-price causality and categorical valuation rules remain unverified.
review.speaker_map_notes: Nigel Coe supplies coverage-specific ratings, historical calls and most forecasts. Eisman endorses selected mechanisms and discloses GE Vernova ownership; hypothetical housing questions do not turn Coe picks into Eisman recommendations.
framework_points: Segment exposure explains why stocks sharing an AI label can have different earnings paths.
Track earnings revisions and backlog conversion, while separating business growth from multiple expansion.
Power availability can limit deployment even after construction finishes.
Turbine capacity follows a slow supply cycle and coordinated supplier investment.
Value traps and turnarounds require changing the thesis when execution and management change.
tools_and_charts: Supplier order books and backlog duration
Global industrial production and ISM PMI
Manufacturing construction and Dodge Momentum Index
transcript_cautions: Opening montage repeats the full discussion.
Guest explicitly does not cover machinery despite broad host introduction.
Many historical calls are retrospective self-reports.
Eisman ownership of GE Vernova is not a documented realized return.
Energy and power units are verbally mixed around the annual capacity illustration.
Full-year 2026 and beyond-2030 outcomes are not treated as completed.

review.title: Netflix & Paramount’s WBD Fight Heats Up + Oracle Falls as AI Doubts Grow | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman contrasts Oracle’s accelerating AI backlog with its funding deficit, favors Paramount in the Warner Bros. bidding contest, and worries about a possible break in AI model scaling. He remains invested in AI and declines to make a broad bearish call. A viewer describes concrete coding-productivity gains, which Eisman considers insufficient by themselves to justify total infrastructure spending. Oracle’s cash-flow statements validate the funding concern, and Paramount displaced Netflix. The latter outcome does not prove Eisman’s antitrust or political explanation. His claim that almost all GDP growth comes from AI remains inadequately established.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Eisman narrates the wrap and explicitly reads an edited viewer email from Sebastian. Claims in that email remain attributed to the viewer; Eisman separately comments on aggregate ROI.
framework_points: Reconcile headline demand with the cash needed to fulfill it.
Evaluate acquisition integration, regulatory delay and management distraction separately from strategic fit.
State limits of technical expertise while retaining conditional risks.
Distinguish useful AI applications from adequate aggregate returns on infrastructure spending.
tools_and_charts: Oracle RPO, earnings, capex, debt and share-price sequence
Toll Brothers backlog, EPS and revenue
Competing Warner Bros. bid structures and streaming market definition
transcript_cautions: Oracle periods are called third and fourth quarter in speech but the December report is fiscal Q2 2026.
The montage repeats the full discussion.
Sebastian is a viewer whose edited email Eisman reads; its detailed claims are not Eisman’s own measured findings.
AI researcher name is garbled; retained as attributed research commentary without guessing an identity.

review.title: Steve Eisman's Masterclass on the 2008 Financial Crisis (Part One) | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 38
review.summary: Eisman explains the crisis through leverage, deteriorating mortgage quality, concentration of exposures and derivative connections. His strongest analytical lessons are that leverage can masquerade as operating skill, historical loss models can fail when underwriting changes, and like-aged loan vintages reveal deterioration hidden by aggregates. Primary research supports these mechanisms. His account overstates a universal risk-weighting explanation and misdescribes typical subprime introductory rates. Loan-level evidence also complicates his reset-centered causal chain. The blanket claim that real household incomes stopped growing in the early 1990s is contradicted by Census data.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Decompose ROE into asset profitability and leverage.
Treat estimated loan losses as uncertain costs rather than immediately known margins.
Question historical risk weights when underwriting changes.
Compare loan vintages at equal seasoning and account for tax-refund seasonality.
Choose a short instrument with manageable liquidity, borrow costs and capacity.
tools_and_charts: Illustrative banks with $1 billion equity and 1x, 10x and 100x assets/equity
ROA, ROE and risk-weighted capital ratios
Historical bank leverage and subprime origination volumes
Low/no-documentation share and hybrid mortgage refinancing
Monthly securitization delinquency, repossession and loss reports by vintage
transcript_cautions: The opening montage repeats later material.
Illustrative bank balance sheets expressly omit liquidity and hold ROA constant.
He calls 2000 a recession year and gives simplified industry chronology; incidental chronology is not used to judge the investment thesis.
The repeated 3% initial subprime rate is load-bearing in the refinancing explanation and is preserved rather than silently corrected.

review.summary: Eisman reviews 2025 through AI investment, a divided consumer economy, private-credit opacity and affordability. He expects the AI cycle to continue at least six months while identifying power availability and diminishing model-scaling returns as its principal risks. He favors housing supply reform and warns against mechanically buying cheap stocks with damaged franchises. His gross-capex comparison does not establish that AI accounts for nearly all GDP growth. Subsequent Nvidia results support continued infrastructure growth through the stated first-half horizon, without resolving ultimate investment returns or the proposed causal explanations for sector prices.

review.summary: Eisman traces crisis contagion through retained mortgage exposures and CDS, criticizes underwriting due diligence, and argues that post-crisis capital and liquidity rules made large banks safer. He explains SVB as concentrated uninsured funding combined with duration risk, then favors targeted regulatory easing and consolidation. Primary records support the core SVB mechanism and substantial post-crisis recapitalization. Important qualifications concern HTM accounting, blanket bailout protection, nonrandom due-diligence samples and claims that SVB posed no systemic danger. The concluding multi-year bank outlook remains conditional and only partly observable.

framework_points: Examine where distributed credit risk ultimately remains.
A hedge adds counterparty dependence rather than eliminating all risk.
Distinguish asset credit risk, duration risk and liability concentration.
Assess regulation through behavior and unintended consequences, not only stated intentions.
Separate earnings pressure from immediate liquidity failure, while recognizing economic capital losses.
tools_and_charts: Illustrative GE bond plus CDS premium

SVB asset duration, uninsured deposits, unrealized losses and VC cash burn

review.title: 2026 Predictions with Dan Ives and Chris Verrone | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 40
review.summary: The panel favors continued AI investment and broader market participation while debating power constraints, model economics, interest rates and valuation. Ives emphasizes enterprise adoption and specific AI beneficiaries; Verrone prefers bank leadership, contrarian sectors and price trends; Eisman tests financing, housing supply and conditional AI risks. Primary records support Apple’s Gemini catalyst and Eisman’s resistance to rapid Fed-cut expectations. Some bullish supporting premises are overstated, including enterprise adoption, Oracle backlog timing and Palantir’s sales model. Full-year targets remain open, and first-half rotation lacks matched return verification.
review.assessment: Substantive outcomes and reasoning are separated from supporting numeric mistakes. Eisman asks informative falsification questions and explicitly withholds a Tesla investment, but broad enthusiasm does not define a measurable portfolio return. Full-year and multiyear forecasts retain open horizons; elapsed first-half calls remain unresolved where primary return data are missing.
review.speaker_map_notes: Dan Ives discusses technology fundamentals and named AI investments; Chris Verrone discusses market breadth, rotation and charts; Steve Eisman hosts and tests assumptions. Attribution follows extended turns; questions and agreement are scoped narrowly.
framework_points: Keep structural technology adoption separate from equity valuation and drawdowns.
Use bank participation and credit spreads as cross-market checks, while specifying signal rules before backtesting.
Challenge demand forecasts through power availability, monetization and funding.
Separate a conditional downside mechanism from a prediction that it will occur.
Use multi-year cash-flow scenarios without assuming every expensive stock will become a historical winner.
tools_and_charts: Bank stock breadth and credit spreads
Oracle RPO, FCF, debt and CDS
Treasury two/ten-year yields and 2 s 30 s curve
Palantir commercial revenue and FCF scenarios
transcript_cautions: Published January 5, 2026 but explicitly a 2025 year-end review; references to Micron reporting that day suggest late December 2025 recording. Exact date unconfirmed.

review.title: 5 Long-Term Themes You Need to Understand For 2026 | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman explains the widening separation between household conditions and a technology-heavy stock index. He sees tax lock-in, institutional position limits, analyst incentives and passive flows reinforcing concentration, while retaining a role for active price discovery. His conditional risk is an AI or recession shock that reverses flows. PayPal illustrates his preference for durable competitive franchises over cheap earnings multiples. The mechanisms are useful questions, but several universal claims exceed their premises, especially converting fund-flow shares into shares of all stock buying.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Separate the composition of an equity index from the composition of economic output.
Examine taxes, mandates and benchmark incentives before interpreting manager performance.
Consider competitive erosion before treating a low earnings multiple as cheap.
Concentration mechanisms do not by themselves identify a correction date.
tools_and_charts: S&P sector weights in 2015, 2020 and 2025, with GICS reclassification caveats
Largest constituent weights and illustrative five-percent position limits
PayPal price, earnings growth and forward P/E
transcript_cautions: Opening montage repeats later arguments.
Historical sector classifications differ; Eisman acknowledges the comparisons are directional.
The sixty-percent figure concerns fund flows before he extends it to all stock buying.
Individual manager mandates are illustrations, not a documented census.

review.title: The Broken US Healthcare System is Failing Millions of Americans with Warris Bokhari
review.summary: Eisman and Warris Bokhari examine denial incentives, insurer ownership of care delivery, Medicare risk coding, Medicaid selection and ACA affordability. The strongest reasoning distinguishes coverage from affordability, identifies float and duration mismatches, and recognizes that a breakup cannot repair underwriting by itself. Several broad conclusions rely on selected cases or mismatched statistics: physician reimbursement becomes a pharmacy comparison, asset depletion becomes bankruptcy, and review expenses become medical spending. Claimable’s success and disruption claims remain founder assertions. No sector stock-return recommendation is inferred.
review.assessment: Material sector economics and policy mechanisms are retained separately from supporting factual errors. Verified definitions support some reasoning, but neither selected patient harm nor poor stock performance proves a universal deliberate-denial business model. Guest-only allegations are not attributed to Eisman.
review.speaker_map_notes: Warris Bokhari supplies healthcare cases and policy explanations. Eisman asks clarifying questions and sometimes expressly restates conclusions; only those substantive adoptions are recorded as his claims. Claimable is the guest’s own business and creates a relevant commercial interest.
framework_points: Follow the money across insurance, providers and pharmacies rather than looking only at insurance margins.
Separate patient access, approval, payment and ultimate affordability.
Probe incentives with simplified arithmetic, but avoid letting illustrative margins become measured profits.
Anecdotes motivate hypotheses; population denominators and causal counterfactuals remain essential.
tools_and_charts: Medical loss ratio and administrative expense bridge
transcript_cautions: Published January 12 2026 but ACA-subsidy negotiations and references to this year indicate a likely late-2025 recording; exact recording date is unavailable.
Captions switch to HH:MM:SS after one hour; complete 78-minute transcript was read with corrected timestamp parser.
V28 is discussed as CPT code removal although CMS uses diagnosis/HCC risk mapping.
Caption renders some company names and 85 cents per hundred dollars incorrectly; monetary examples are treated as illustrative.
Founder claims, private patient histories and alleged retaliation lack independently inspected case records.
Opening montage repeats later discussion and is not separately counted.

review.title: Why Bank Earnings Are Essential to Understanding the Market in 2026 | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman links technology concentration, unequal household wealth and passive investing, then uses bank earnings to assess the economy. He sees a potential housing-policy trading rally and a regional-bank merger opportunity, while warning large-bank valuations already reflect favorable fundamentals. The episode offers a useful segmentation of bank earnings drivers, but bank credit data alone cannot establish macro safety and blanket yield-curve or passive-flow rules need qualification. Most empirical market and portfolio outcomes remain unverified.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Connect sector weights to economic distribution while distinguishing the index from GDP.
Use bank credit and funding data as a cross-sector diagnostic.
Separate short-term policy trades from lasting supply reforms.
Analyze investment banks, regionals and hybrids differently.
Value banks against sustainable returns on tangible equity, not earnings beats alone.
tools_and_charts: S&P sector weights and passive flows
Mortgage-backed security spreads and mortgage rates
Housing market caps and rate sensitivity
Net interest margin, loan growth and credit quality
transcript_cautions: Opening montage repeats later arguments.
Captions garble unmoored, moribund, company names and ROTE.
Wells Fargo $21.3bn comparison is called net income but likely refers to revenue; the metric needs original-report confirmation.
Gary Marcus and Warris Bokhari views in closing previews are attributed as guest positions, not fully adopted claims.

review.title: Gary Marcus on the Massive Problems Facing AI & LLM Scaling | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 42
review.summary: Gary Marcus argues that LLM scaling faces diminishing returns, unreliable generalization and weak investment economics. Eisman probes the link to GPU demand, explicitly making his spending slowdown and contagion scenarios conditional. The review separates useful reliability and financing questions from categorical claims about cognition and automation. Primary studies narrow the 2.5% automation statistic, contradict the assertion that models never express uncertainty, and demonstrate limited learned world representations. Later executed financing weakens an immediate OpenAI collapse interpretation without settling eventual profitability.
review.assessment: Strongest host contribution is conditional translation of a technical thesis into demand and financing exposures, with explicit admission that GPU end-use shares are unknown. The weakest shared step is treating failure to reach AGI as sufficient to prove poor returns on all current chips. Marcus supplies useful reliability cautions but overgeneralizes narrow automation data and makes categorical technical assertions that inspected research qualifies or contradicts. Undated failure predictions are not assigned invented deadlines.
review.speaker_map_notes: Gary Marcus is the technical guest; Steve Eisman asks business and finance questions. Explicit host endorsements and conditionals are recorded separately. Agreement or silence is not treated as ownership of every guest claim.
framework_points: Translate technical limitations into demand and funding scenarios, but preserve the antecedent before grading the forecast.
Differentiate model capability, economically useful assistance, full job automation and AGI.
Question investment returns and cash runway, while distinguishing cash burn from reported losses.
Expert opinion, researcher departures and anecdotes are suggestive signals, not controlled capability or causal tests.
tools_and_charts: Hyperscaler capex estimate and unknown LLM GPU share
OpenAI funding versus monthly-loss runway arithmetic
Google TPU and internal cash-flow comparison
transcript_cautions: Opening montage repeats later discussion and is not used as independent evidence.
Captions garble names such as Ilya Sutskever and WeWork; normalized only where context is unambiguous.
The 85% survey figure is preserved as stated and evaluated against the actual question and 76% result.
Tesla collision training-data cause is explicitly speculative despite confident subsequent phrasing.
Eisman explicitly endorses the statistical-thinking characterization and Nvidia ecosystem quality; most technical and failure predictions belong to Marcus.

review.title: The “Lone Wolf” Effect: Trump, Burry & a Market on Edge | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman treats Greenland tariff escalation as a market risk, endorses concern about AI equipment depreciation, and warns about private-equity continuation vehicles. He favors a regional-bank consolidation thesis while recognizing CEO resistance. His passive-flow explanation overstates automatic selling mechanics and lacks proof that index funds cause more severe corrections. The depreciation argument identifies a legitimate estimate risk, but a faster new chip does not alone establish the old fleet's economic useful life.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Evaluate influential contrarian views without confusing popularity with proof.
Separate an accounting concern from a near-term catalyst.
Examine related-party pricing and fee resets in private markets.
Tie bank valuations to returns and scale economics.
Distinguish narrative-driven price reactions from fundamental changes.
tools_and_charts: Tariff escalation schedule and Treasury/dollar reactions
Private-equity unsold assets and continuation vehicles
transcript_cautions: Information cutoff is Wednesday January 21, despite Friday publication.
Opening montage duplicates main claims.
Captions garble Rubin, Jensen Huang, Michael Burry and several regional bank names.
Masterworks paid promotion is excluded from the analyst scorecard.
Gary Marcus views are presented as hypotheses and a reason to seek another guest, not fully endorsed forecasts.

review.title: The Mystery of Stablecoins, Visa, & Fiserv’s Collapse with Ken Suchoski | The Real Eisman Playbook
review.summary: Ken Suchoski explains stablecoin reserve economics, cross-border opportunities and the durable advantages of card networks. Eisman focuses on Tether contagion, consumer incentives and preference for Visa/Mastercard. Suchoski favors Circle after its valuation reset and Toast’s restaurant platform, while questioning Fiserv margins and the credit mix at Block. Later disclosures support Circle’s rate sensitivity and Fiserv margin pressure, but Circle’s token-presale revenue complicates apparent operating leverage. The review preserves the guest’s disagreement with Eisman about longer-run benefits from a hypothetical Tether scandal.
review.assessment: The strongest analysis concerns payment incentives, the distinction between rails and full services, and balance-and-yield economics. The Fiserv margin warning has substantial interim support. Weaknesses include overbroad claims that networks grow without paying distribution partners, insufficiently evidenced comparative compliance assertions, and valuation conclusions that need explicit price horizons. Many numerical examples are teaching illustrations and should not dominate the investment-thesis scorecard.
review.speaker_map_notes: Ken Suchoski is the guest analyst; Steve Eisman asks questions and explicitly endorses selected mechanisms. Suchoski’s Circle target, Fiserv skepticism and Block/PayPal ratings are guest views. His disagreement over Tether contagion is preserved.
framework_points: Analyze both sides of a payment network, including consumer incentives rather than only merchant fees.
Separate the settlement rail from compliance, local payout, distribution and workflow integration.
Model Circle with reserve balances, yield and partner sharing rather than transaction volume alone.
Distinguish growth in lending earnings from the valuation and capital risks attached to those earnings.
Use per-employee metrics and customer treatment as possible signs of underinvestment, with normalization.
tools_and_charts: Circle reserve return rate, average USDC balance, RLDC and forward EBITDA multiple
Bottom-up stablecoin use-case supply model through 2030
Network contract lengths and fixed-cost break-even share
Fiserv revenue and EBIT per employee versus FIS and Jack Henry
Block gross-profit mix and short-duration lending
transcript_cautions: Published January 26, 2026, but repeated this-year/next-year language and the stock-performance list clearly refer to a 2025 discussion and 2026 outlook; exact recording date is not supplied.
Opening montage repeats later statements; complete discussion ranges are used.
Captions garble Fiserv, Suchoski, EBITDA and cross-border; normalized where context is clear.
The guest corrects Eisman: incumbent cross-border providers, not stablecoins alone, already perform low-cost netting.
USAT and USDT are distinct; the later US launch uses Anchorage Digital Bank as issuer.
Apple Pay free means no additional wallet surcharge in context, not zero card-processing cost.

review.title: Silver Goes Crazy, United Healthcare is Falling, & AI’s CapEx is Exploding | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman contrasts resilient stocks with metals speculation, argues physical silver tightness may matter, and sees possible broader fiscal-led growth. He warns UnitedHealth requires a deep repair and forecasts 2027 EPS below $19, conditional on weak Medicare pricing. That earnings horizon remains open and final CMS pricing later improved. He favors power bottlenecks, distinguishes supplier growth from AI customer returns, and identifies real Microsoft backlog concentration. His silver explanation overstates the novelty of China exporter controls and leaves key quantities unverified.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Compare different markets rather than infer universal sentiment from VIX.
Differentiate superficial turnarounds from structural business repairs.
Use sector-specific operating metrics such as orders or comparable sales.
Separate good current earnings from future funding and concentration risk.
Permit limited bank-rule changes while preserving post-GFC capital resilience.
tools_and_charts: VIX, Treasury yields and equity versus precious-metal returns
Silver paper/physical ratio and futures backwardation
Medicare Advantage pricing and Optum margins
transcript_cautions: Recorded before the final January session despite language that January closed; end-of-month silver/equity values may describe the recording snapshot, not final monthly closes.
Several captions garble Optum, GE Vernova, Siemens, Citigroup and Daniel Tarullo.
Silver licensing, strategic classification and refining-share claims need separate verification.
UnitedHealth forecast relies on the preliminary 2027 rate announcement, which was not final policy.
Microsoft 45% of $625bn is approximately $281bn; $250bn may confuse a separately announced commitment with total backlog share.

review.title: Jason Trennert on Populism, Policy & a Distorted Market System | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 44
review.summary: Trennert favors industrials, materials, hard assets and financials under a populist fiscal regime; Eisman probes inflation, valuation, private-market opacity and bank scale. Observed growth supports the directional 2026 outlook, while Fed easing had not materialized by cutoff. Their distinction between price levels and inflation rates is sound, as are conditional leverage and valuation-smoothing arguments. Claims that private credit and prediction markets are unregulated overreach. Guest forecasts and holdings remain separate from Eisman’s own views.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Jason Trennert presents Strategas forecasts and personal holdings. Eisman questions and explicitly agrees with selected mechanisms. Backchannel agreement is not treated as adoption of every guest statistic.
framework_points: Separate affordability levels from inflation rates.
Distinguish an asset-price win from correct causal reasoning.
Infrequent marks can conceal economic volatility without reducing it.
Policy-regime narratives need explicit channels and counterfactual tests.
Bank-scale arguments require integration and competition tradeoffs.
tools_and_charts: Bank deposit share and operating scale
transcript_cautions: Recorded January 20, 2026, despite February 2 publication; event-relative references use recording date.
Opening montage repeats later discussion and is not separately counted.
Medical personal history excluded as outside investment audit.
Host reference to Gary Marcus is not endorsement of his scaling-limit thesis.

review.title: Crypto & Silver Collapse, Software Gets Obliterated, & Two Stock Recommendations | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Recorded February 5, this wrap contrasts violent silver and crypto moves with software disruption fears. Eisman introduces new Charter and Meritage positions based on future capex relief, buybacks and possible operating improvement, then examines AI spending and several earnings reports.
review.assessment: The Charter and Meritage theses are unusually explicit about their operating mechanisms, but their multiyear forecasts remain unfinished. Charter later results weaken the early stabilization narrative. The capex-versus-cash distinction is useful; high free-cash-flow yield is not a mathematical bankruptcy signal, and less capex does not directly raise current accounting EPS.
framework_points: A low multiple needs an operating or capital-allocation catalyst.
Separate capital spending from earnings and cash generation.
Watch how competitive narratives change the reaction to good results.
Distinguish a profitable incumbent funding AI from a loss-making firm dependent on new capital.
tools_and_charts: Free cash flow per share and yield
Broadband, mobile and video subscriber changes
transcript_cautions: Local MLX Whisper transcript, no diarization; the host is the sole substantive speaker.
Recorded Thursday February 5 for Friday February 6 publication.
Opening montage duplicates later material.
Forecast tables are described aloud; this audit does not claim a separate visual inspection.
Large currency figures and share prices are retained as reported when no matched price series was independently inspected.
