review.title: Lakshmi Ganapathi on Consumer Stress & the Cracks Beneath the US Economy | The Real Eisman Playbook
review.summary: Eisman tests Ganapathi’s consumer-stress and short-selling theses against stable bank data. She argues that BNPL, loan modifications and securitization conceal deteriorating affordability, then critiques FICO, Digital Realty and private credit. Eisman explains credit waterfalls and yen-carry risks and defends GE Vernova through concentrated gas-turbine supply and expanding power demand. Later company results support that operating thesis. Guest warnings about immediate data-center collapse and FICO displacement face contrary operating evidence, while uneven consumer credit data provide only partial confirmation of a second-half deterioration forecast.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. The strongest host operating thesis is GE Vernova gas equipment demand, supported by subsequent segment results. Guest collapse/displacement language outruns current operating evidence. Consumer stress is distributional and measurement-sensitive, so neither stable aggregate bank losses nor rising stock delinquency alone settles it.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman hosts Lakshmi Ganapathi. Most bearish consumer, FICO and data-center propositions are hers. His questions, paraphrases and hypothetical arithmetic are distinguished from his asserted GE Vernova and credit-mechanics views.
framework_points: Compare reported lender credit with borrower-level data and securitization pools.
Map cash-flow cushions and refinancing dependencies before extrapolating equity outcomes.
Separate a bad segment from the consolidated earnings driver; GE Vernova debate illustrates this.
Avoid shorting cult stocks without a catalyst, according to the guest.
tools_and_charts: Auto and CRE ABS excess-spread waterfalls
transcript_cautions: Opening montage repeats later discussion.
Speaker transitions reconstructed from questions and answers; guest research claims are not automatically Eisman endorsements.
GPI is confused with Genuine Parts in dialogue.
Several numeric claims derive from anonymous sources, unspecified surveys or illustrative examples.
No trade ledger or defined investment horizon for most shorts.
New York Fed Q3 official indexed release inspected; direct page/PDF retrieval failed.

He favors beta as a practical market-exposure measure and contrasts a bullish Charter recovery thesis with bearish PayPal. Molina later remained under earnings pressure, supporting the slow-recovery warning. Charter's organic and cash-flow recovery had not materialized by the cutoff despite acquisition-driven reported growth. His beta arithmetic is useful, but beta does not guarantee a stock's daily move or fully measure portfolio risk.

review.summary: Eisman seeks a second technical view after Gary Marcus. Guetta argues that imperfect present-day AI can create value through representations, retrieval and tools without resolving AGI. The interview contains useful deployment distinctions, but its repeated full-context-recomputation and nearest-word explanations are technically misleading. Eisman leaves the industry return-on-investment verdict open until 2027-2028.
review.assessment: Empirical premises and forecasts are assessed separately. Guest assertions are not Eisman forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal attribution remain unresolved.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman interviews Columbia professor Daniel Guetta. Guest technical assertions and personal coding-view revisions remain guest claims. The host's acceptance of the inference-energy explanation is recorded separately.
framework_points: Separate useful task economics from claims of general intelligence.
Benchmark performance is specific to a task distribution.
Data access, integration and action controls are deployment requirements.
Lower coding cost does not automatically erase workflow and coordination moats.
Use explicit cost and error budgets to evaluate imperfect tools.
Eisman actively seeks a competing expert view and retains a 2027-2028 ROI horizon.
tools_and_charts: Learned embeddings and the Transformer architecture.
KV caching as a correction to the inference-cost explanation.
Reinforcement learning with human feedback and verifiable rewards.

The supplied publisher transcript contains repeated watermark-like lines and multi-second gaps, including parts of the travel and database examples and the closing disruption discussion. Read-complete refers to all available text, not a claim of complete audio recovery.

review.title: George Noble on Gold’s Rise, Crypto Doubts & Tesla’s Struggles | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 47
review.summary: George Noble favors energy, metals and foreign-market rotation while opposing technology, Bitcoin, Tesla and Opendoor. Eisman challenges the timing of dollar-collapse arguments, discloses a Strategy short, and explicitly withholds endorsement of the broad sector call. Their strongest shared analysis concerns gross-versus-net revenue comparisons and the path risks of shorting. Primary filings support Tesla earnings deterioration but challenge the claimed consecutive consolidated revenue declines and show positive nine-month cash generation. The ten-year yield exceeded 5% during 2026, while full-year calls remain open.
review.assessment: Useful analyst-quality signals are the explicit discussion of failed timing, refusal to equate a poor business with an immediately profitable short, and scrutiny of misleading revenue comparisons. Weaknesses include using price action as proof of fundamentals, broad social-substitution explanations without flow evidence, and speculative valuation analogies. Several guest forecasts have explicit calendar-year horizons that remain open at the cutoff. The host’s Strategy short is distinct from his explicit refusal to short Tesla.
review.speaker_map_notes: George Noble is the buy-side guest. Steve Eisman’s challenges, specific endorsements, Strategy disclosure and closing reservations are separately attributed. The closing recap is essential to avoid treating the whole guest portfolio as Eisman’s.
framework_points: Require a why-now catalyst rather than repeat a longstanding macro vulnerability.
Separate a company’s economics, valuation and the timing constraints of a short position.
Normalize gross-versus-net revenue and inventory exposure before comparing valuation multiples.
Treat market-price confirmation as feedback, not independent proof of a causal thesis.
Reserve-currency network effects can resist displacement without guaranteeing unchanged purchasing power.

review.title: Trump Tariff Turmoil, Private Credit Risk Grows, & AI’s Software Fears | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman treats tariff policy as disruptive but unlikely by itself to overwhelm US resilience. His main concerns are AI capital returns, software-heavy private credit and insurance links. He distinguishes payment-network moats from exposed software, remains skeptical of solar and Warner Bros valuation, and finds Netflix more interesting. Nvidia and Circle operating growth is supported, while Circle reserve interest is dominant rather than its sole revenue. Private-credit transaction ownership, insurance leverage and loss forecasts require further primary verification.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Focus on growth, funding and related-party incentives across private credit and life insurance.
Use network effects to distinguish payments from software-disruption fears.
Separate reported earnings strength from market narrative and valuation.
Recognize that institutional information advantages do not guarantee outperformance.
tools_and_charts: Private-credit fund discounts and redemption restrictions
transcript_cautions: Recorded February 26, published February 27.
Montage repeats the later qualified UBS default scenario; Eisman expressly says he does not know whether 15% is realistic.
Kuvare Asset Management ownership is not automatically ownership or legal control of Kuvare Insurance.
Viewer GDP/PCE figures are not silently attributed to Eisman.

review.title: The Next Financial Crisis? Private Equity, Private Credit & Life Insurance | Real Eisman Playbook
review.summary: Eisman and forensic accountant Tom Gober argue that private-equity ownership, complex assets and affiliated reinsurance could conceal life-insurer leverage and threaten policyholders. Eisman explicitly adopts this warning in his closing summary. Primary evidence supports growth in structured exposure and the reality of PHL’s financial failure, but several premises are overstated: Bermuda statutory disclosures exist, its capital regime is not GAAP alone, and funding agreements cannot simply be treated as callable deposits. The systemic crisis forecast remains conditional and open; opacity is a reason to investigate, not proof of a quantified industry capital hole.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. Useful focus on legal-entity solvency and recoverability is weakened by categorical secrecy claims and untested funding assumptions. The case for further scrutiny is stronger than the case that a system-wide capital hole or inevitable crisis has already been established.
review.speaker_map_notes: Tom Gober is the forensic-accountant guest. Eisman asks many explanatory questions but expressly adopts hidden-leverage, portfolio-risk, analyst-blindspot and regulatory-inaction claims in his final monologue. The private-credit defense is presented hypothetically.
framework_points: Inspect statutory legal-entity accounts and reinsurance recoverability in addition to consolidated GAAP.
Separate affiliate origination, affiliate ownership and direct obligations of the parent.
Model contract maturities, collateral calls and surrender rights before asserting a run.
A benign credit cycle cannot demonstrate safety under adverse losses.
A specific failure is a warning example, not automatic proof of identical industry-wide insolvency.
tools_and_charts: Statutory annual statements and Schedule S Part 3 Section 1
GAAP versus statutory and economic capital
transcript_cautions: Opening introduces a conditional scandal, not a dated crisis prediction.
Closing monologue explicitly endorses core guest concerns.
Several numerical captive examples are unnamed or based on temporarily public documents not available here.
Mutual insurance is not synonymous with charitable nonprofit status.
All offshore no disclosure and GAAP-only descriptions fail for inspected Bermuda example.
Funding-agreement classifications alone do not establish short maturity or immediate withdrawal rights.

claims.claim: Private-equity involvement in life insurance, captive reinsurance and private credit could become the next major financial crisis affecting policyholders.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.horizon: one day; no date, conditional on credit losses and funding stress
claims.test: Establish whether the stated insurance future crisis proposition holds using matched primary disclosures; retain its conditions and separate causal explanations from price movements.
claims.qualifications: Repeated and explicitly adopted by Eisman at 2340-2420 and 2720-2900; not merely a guest thesis.
claims.reason: A contingent industry-wide crisis has no specified horizon and is not established by the inspected record. Individual failures do not resolve the systemic forecast.

evidence.title: Rehabilitator Third Accounting and Status Report
evidence.finding: Combined PHL/Concord/Palisado surplus was negative $2.236bn at September 2025. Rehabilitation began May 2024. Commissioner removed an admitted prepaid-expense asset, with $91.7m remaining at September 2025; report also documents reserve adjustments and payment limits. This supports a real failure, not a blanket extrapolation to large insurers.

claims.next_check: Obtain primary evidence matching the stated metric, period and conditions before assigning an outcome grade.

claims.qualifications: State regulatory architecture is factual; comparative competence is a broad judgment. Specific staffing, enforcement and capital outcomes are not matched.
claims.reason: Regulatory action is documented, but its adequacy and incentives cannot be established from the existence of rules alone.

evidence.finding: Inspected actions section documents acquisition-review guidance since 2013, 13 macroprudential considerations, cross-border reinsurance monitoring and enhanced annual-statement investment disclosures. evidence.title: Private Equity-Owned U.S. Insurer Investments Increased at Year-End 2024
evidence.finding: Annual-statement data show PE-owned insurer investments more than doubled since 2018. ABS/other structured securities were 31% of their bond holdings versus 13% industry-wide; 95% of their structured holdings had NAIC 1/2 designations. Complex exposure is established; realized inferior credit quality is not.

review.title: Iran War Volatility, Private Credit Fears Grow, & Solar Continues to Crash | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman attributes market swings to changing war and credit narratives, flags retail and institutional redemption pressure, and remains cautious on solar and health insurance. The Elevance regulatory problem was real, but the threatened sanctions were conditional and later recorded as corrected. He explicitly leaves AI-driven mass unemployment and life-insurer credit losses unproven. His categorical no-credit-cycle-since-GFC statement is too broad; evidence of market anxiety is distinct from realized systemic loss.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Distinguish a narrative reversal from new realized losses.
Look for loan growth and weak diligence before credit trouble.
Follow financing costs and subsidies in solar.
Separate duration matching at insurers from asset credit and hidden leverage concerns.
tools_and_charts: Medicare Advantage sanctions and star ratings
transcript_cautions: Recorded March 5, published March 6.
Opening montage duplicates later excerpts.
The MongoDB guidance sentence lacks a verb in captions; context describes weak guidance.
MFS is identified as Market Financial Solutions in this episode.
Viewer criticism of asset-manager ownership is not an assertion by Eisman.

review.title: Private Credit Cracks, The AI "Boogeyman" & Why Crypto is for Boomers | The Real Eisman Playbook
review.summary: Eisman, Glenn Schorr and Dwight Collins distinguish private-credit losses from fundraising pressure, debate software disruption and favor durable payments networks. The senior-debt cushion argument is conditionally valid, but current equity valuations and refinancing capacity remain unverified. Later Blue Owl filings show meaningful repayments, worsening residual credit metrics and continued parent fundraising. The dialogue reverses the public/private Blue Owl merger entities. Visa operating resilience is supported, while permanent immunity, price-causality and cross-asset incompatibility claims are overstated.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Glenn Schorr handles private markets and credit; Dwight Collins covers investor sentiment, brokers, payments and SoFi. Turn-taking inferred from named prompts. Host closing explicitly adopts selected points; other guest forecasts remain separate.
framework_points: Separate manager equity, fund liquidity, loan credit and sponsor equity.
Check realizable enterprise value and refinancing, not just original equity contribution.
Challenge AI displacement by examining customer integration and workflow.
Use credit spreads as a comparison signal, not proof that unrelated equities must be mispriced.
tools_and_charts: Blue Owl BDC merger and asset-sale waterfall
transcript_cautions: Public and private entities are reversed in the merger discussion; filing resolves the error.
Recording predates publication: last week references February Blue Owl transaction.
CQS insurer name is uncertain ASR, likely Kuvare.
Guest loan-to-value near 35% becomes about 25% debt in host closing; neither treated as verified industry aggregate.

review.title: The Iran War Crisis: Ex-CIA Analyst Helima Croft on Oil Shock & Energy Risk | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman frames the Iran war as a dominant source of market uncertainty and reiterates Oracle’s funding risk. Guest Helima Croft explains why blocked shipping, limited storage, LNG dependence and vulnerable bypass routes make a prolonged conflict economically damaging. Subsequent physical-market evidence supports her warning about persistent supply stress and alternative-route vulnerability. These are Croft’s forecasts, not Eisman’s. The interview usefully distinguishes military targets from economic normalization, but private-source interpretations of leaders’ intentions and exact war timelines remain unverified. Neither a price move nor a politician’s statement establishes a durable reopening.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman narrates the first four minutes and then interviews Helima Croft. Croft supplies most physical-market and geopolitical analysis. Questions, acknowledgments and praise are not treated as Eisman endorsing each guest claim.
framework_points: Eisman distinguishes uncertainty-driven trading from ordinary earnings analysis.
He asks the guest to explain physical mechanisms and disclose experience-based biases.
Croft separates military objectives, shipping normalization, storage exhaustion and production restart.
Scenario duration and alternative-route security matter more than a single oil-price headline.
tools_and_charts: Oracle revenue, non-GAAP EPS, RPO and funding plan
Hormuz daily vessel and oil-flow estimates
SPR inventories and hypothetical depletion arithmetic
Regional shut-ins, storage capacity, LNG restart constraints
Saudi East-West pipeline and Red Sea alternatives
transcript_cautions: Wrap recorded March 12, interview recorded March 11, upload March 13.
Opening montage repeats the interview.
Captions render shale as shell and stockpile as stock power.
Most geopolitical and energy predictions are Croft’s; Eisman’s questions and brief acknowledgments do not imply adoption.
Oracle historical quarter/peak chronology is imprecise, while the current report is fiscal Q3 2026.

review.title: Mark Cuban on the Broken Drug Pricing System & How PBMs Really Work | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 50
review.summary: Mark Cuban explains Cost Plus, PBM incentives and direct employer healthcare, while Eisman explicitly adopts several conclusions in his closing. Concentration and specialty-drug markups have primary support. The summary conflates rebates reaching plans with PBMs retaining them; the claims that PBMs exist only in America and only Cost Plus publishes pharmacy prices are contradicted. Company savings, retaliation and healthcare reform claims largely lack matched causal evidence. Cuban’s cash position and flow-driven equity theory remain guest views.
review.assessment: Material drug-pricing critique has empirical support, but several adopted premises are overstated. No investment-return win is inferred from business-model praise. Regulatory allegations are distinguished from established universal causation.
review.speaker_map_notes: Dialogue context identifies Mark Cuban as guest. Host closing is clearly Eisman and supplies explicit adoption; earlier questions alone do not. Market allocation and entrepreneurial forecasts remain Cuban views.
framework_points: Map payments among patients, plans, manufacturers and intermediaries before attributing profits.
Strong concrete mechanism questions, followed by insufficient challenge to categorical guest assertions.
Closing paraphrase can become stronger than what the guest actually said.
Patient cost and manufacturer list price are different benchmarks.
tools_and_charts: Public-company count and retirement fund flows
transcript_cautions: Ads around 18:30-22:15 excluded.
ASR brand spelling in the Stelara biosimilar example is uncertain; annual versus per-dose prices are not directly comparable.
Guest corrects always cheaper to almost always cheaper.
Closing rebate-retention description differs from guest employer-pass-through explanation.

review.summary: Eisman separates war-driven inflation risk from AI capital returns and private-credit stress. He distinguishes retail fund liquidity from underlying credit quality, but overstates the absence of prior credit cycles and treats SoFi securitization access as indispensable despite its deposit-funded bank. Software refinancing and related-party asset transfers are material concerns whose magnitude remains unresolved. He endorses transparency and incentive reform in drug pricing without endorsing price controls.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Separate liquidity constraints from realized credit losses.
Follow fast credit growth and sector concentrations.
Stress the financing waterfall rather than just headline asset value.
Distinguish AI supplier spending from eventual investor returns.
Demand transparency in both credit marks and healthcare incentives.
tools_and_charts: Private-credit market growth and software exposure
PBM rebates and Cost Plus markup
transcript_cautions: Recorded March 19, published March 20.
Opening montage repeats later statements and is not separately counted.
Caption names Treasury Secretary Mnuchin; contemporary identity needs checking before attribution.
MFS is called MFS Investment Management here, whereas the March 6 episode identifies Market Financial Solutions; do not transfer fraud allegations to the unrelated asset manager.
SoFi illustrative 10%/5% rates are annualized yields, despite monthly wording.
Viewer drug-pricing argument is a question, not automatically Eisman endorsement.

review.title: The Only Health Insurance Stock You Can Own with Michael Ha | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 51
review.summary: Michael Ha argues that UnitedHealth’s coding exposure and fragmented acquisitions outweigh a simple repricing recovery, while Medicaid may remain difficult until 2027-2029. He favors Alignment’s care model and discusses PBM fee flexibility. Eisman adopts broad sector caution but expressly has not researched Alignment. Subsequent evidence is mixed: UNH segments recovered, Molina remained strained, and Alignment grew while cutting profit guidance. Eisman’s specific expectation that final Medicare Advantage rates would not improve was wrong. Longer Medicaid timing and Alignment’s five-year target remain open, and clinical/coding causality requires more than raw company comparisons.
review.assessment: Full transcript read. Strong focus on segment economics and policy mechanics, but the host political-rate forecast failed and broad caution underweighted the possibility of company-level recovery. Primary results support selective rather than universal conclusions; unverified coding and clinical comparisons remain unresolved.
review.speaker_map_notes: Michael Ha is the Baird analyst guest. Eisman supplies hypothetical explanations and explicitly adopts overall sector caution/integration critique. Investor repricing counterarguments are exploratory, and Alignment targets belong to Ha alone.
framework_points: Use CMS cohort data to test coding exposure, but control for population composition.
Separate insurance repricing from provider-service economics.
Rate-setting lags and selection can move medical costs faster than premiums.
Vertical ownership does not automatically establish operational integration.
Compare clinical outcomes on risk-adjusted populations and consistent denominators.
Map all PBM compensation channels before forecasting profit effects of regulation.
tools_and_charts: CMS risk-score cohorts and acquisition timing
Optum segment margins and recast comparisons
Medicare Advantage advance and final rate notices
Medicaid acuity, redeterminations and rate lags
Medical loss ratios and star ratings
PBM formulary, rebate and fee economics
transcript_cautions: No opening montage; introduction references prior Claimable and Cuban interviews.
Life-insurance advertisement at roughly 1110-1205 is excluded from analyst claims.
ASR repeatedly spells Optum as Optim or Optimum; names normalized.
Ha corrects 80 hours per week to per month.
Host adoption is strongest in closing, but ALHC remains the guest recommendation.
Final CMS policy changed after the interview; distinguish rejected proposed calibration from continuing coding controls.
Admissions and denial rates are not comparable without denominator and risk-mix controls.

review.summary: A short credit update precedes a full Meritage CEO interview recorded March 6. Eisman acknowledges his housing recommendation has suffered as rates rise, but retains a below-book, improving-capital-efficiency thesis. Philippe Lord describes affordability constraints, mortgage subsidies, local fees and the cost-benefit tradeoff in land options, then sets multiyear operating targets. Those targets belong to the CEO. Eisman separately endorses potential upside from higher ROE and a 1.5x book valuation, with rates and execution still decisive.

Analyze land ownership, options and financing costs together.
Connect operating margins, asset turns and ROE.
Distinguish CEO targets from independent analyst forecasts.

review.summary: Recorded March 23, Steven Cook distinguishes tactical military damage from strategic success. He expects a messy outcome with a surviving Iranian regime, continuing containment and greater Gulf defensive spending. Eisman questions whether Trump truly seeks an exit, then reports Cook's forecast without adopting a firm regime-change prediction. June EU evidence supports continued Iranian leverage over Hormuz, but military damage, private intentions, opposition polling and uranium accessibility remain insufficiently verified.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman hosts Steven Cook. Cook provides most regional and military analysis; Eisman's questions, disagreements and final reported takeaways remain separately identified.
framework_points: Define strategic success separately from battlefield damage.
Separate official policy, private interlocutors and public opinion.
Keep nuclear enrichment distinct from an operational nuclear weapon.
Preserve short forecast horizons even when evidence is missing.
Assess energy sanctions licenses by their actual scope.
transcript_cautions: Full transcript read in two contiguous parts including closing recap.
Explicit recording date March 23, one week before publication.
Captions mangle Mojtaba Khamenei into ordinary words; no claims are built from that transcription artifact.
Casualty figures and intelligence claims are attributed guest assertions, not established findings.

metadata.title: John Spencer on What the Headlines Get Wrong About the Iran War | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 55

review.summary: Recorded April 6, this interview presents John Spencer’s case that military degradation can achieve U.S. objectives without regime replacement and may strengthen broader deterrence. Eisman emphasizes those potential market implications. The audit distinguishes stated goals, tactical damage and uncertain strategic outcomes. Continued Hormuz coercion and nuclear verification gaps prevent a victory grade; postwar stability remains conditional, and claims about secret knowledge or Chinese decision-making remain unresolved.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman interviews John Spencer. Spencer provides the military analysis. Eisman’s closing recap begins around 3750 seconds.
framework_points: Evaluate strategic outcomes against explicitly defined political goals.
Separate capability destruction from compliance, governance and durable security.
Distinguish launches, interceptions, impacts and intended targets.
Do not treat official belligerent claims as independent battle-damage verification.
A counterfactual deterrence claim needs more than an event not occurring.
Direct import exposure does not determine exposure to global commodity prices.
tools_and_charts: Postwar investment, arms sales and deterrence scenarios.
transcript_cautions: Interview explicitly says April 6, 2026; YouTube publication is April 14.
Full transcript read through closing and disclaimer.
Precise battlefield counts and classified intelligence claims remain unverified.
Political and moral preferences are not graded as objective predictions.
Guest claims and Eisman’s reporting of those claims are explicitly separated.
No tactical advice is extracted from discussion of military options.

review.summary: Eisman uses bank credit supplements to distinguish localized private-credit stress from a broad recession signal. He argues that senior protections and capital should contain future bank losses, evaluates earnings quality bank by bank, and relates sustainable returns to book multiples. He discourages using regional banks as a simple private-credit hedge and explains why new lending opportunities do not rescue legacy funds. The macro direction is supported by later expansion, while the systemic-loss forecast remains open.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman delivers a solo monologue; inserted advertisements and opening montage are excluded.
framework_points: Compare sequential and annual credit trends across broad lenders.
Separate recurring earnings from tax and trading effects.
Connect bank book multiples to sustainable returns and risk.
Match a hedge to actual exposure.
Evaluate new-vintage loans separately from legacy portfolios.
tools_and_charts: Four-bank consumer and commercial nonaccrual table.
Bank return on tangible common equity versus price/tangible book.
transcript_cautions: Full transcript read including all three mailbags.
Nonaccrual is not universally synonymous with 90 days delinquent.
All-non-Treasury-debt-yields-higher is an overgeneralization, separated from the useful spread-risk explanation.
NDFI private-credit estimates are explicitly uncertain.

review.summary: Jeffrey Hirsch presents seasonal market rules, including the midterm cycle, winter strength, January signals and sector windows. Eisman accepts parts of the framework while asking for causal explanations. The audit preserves the guest's explicit warnings about unstable signals, small Bitcoin samples and combining disciplines. Statistical claims remain unresolved without the original tests. Eisman's supporting assertions about a universal mutual-fund cash ceiling and nearly all credit growth occurring outside banks are contradicted by primary filings and Fed tables.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.

Compare conditional success rates with the market's unconditional upward bias.

metadata.title: Apollo's Private Credit Exposure: Chris Edson Weighs In | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 57

review.summary: Apollo's Chris Edson distinguishes broad asset-backed lending from leveraged software finance and argues that customized origination, long liabilities and insurer ownership improve risk management. Eisman accepts Apollo's relative diversification while retaining his software-credit warning. The filing supports business breadth, but common ownership does not remove conflicts and low fund leverage does not establish that every migration from banks reduces systemic risk. Loan-level disclosure and low software exposure require further look-through verification.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman interviews Chris Edson. Guest responses are separately attributed; Eisman's final recap supplies his own endorsed conclusions.
framework_points: Separate direct lending from the broader private-credit universe.
Test cash-flow and collateral underwriting against enterprise-value assumptions.
Distinguish credit loss from liquidity mismatch.
Do not infer absence of conflicts from common ownership.
A disclosed redemption limit is not a default event.
tools_and_charts: Apollo origination and AUM segment tables.
Statutory investment schedules and BDC holdings.
transcript_cautions: Full transcript read in two contiguous parts, including closing takeaway.
Chris Edson is the Apollo guest; most industry claims are his assertions, not Eisman forecasts.
Eisman explicitly retains a software-credit-cycle view after accepting greater differentiation within private credit.

review.summary: Eisman defends and adds to Charter after acknowledging a failed early turnaround signal, relying on future capex declines, buybacks and convergence. He sees continued AI infrastructure strength, uneven consumer conditions and a challenge to FICO pricing power. Charter's operating setback and the UAE's OPEC exit are verified. The multiyear Charter payoff and 2027 scoring transition remain open; private-software valuation extrapolations and broad causal market stories remain unresolved.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman delivers a solo monologue; inserted advertisements and opening montage are excluded.
framework_points: Avoid changing a thesis merely because the stock moves.
Cheapness needs operating improvement or a cash-return catalyst.
Separate current loan performance from future refinancing exposure.
Distinguish aggregate consumer spending from individual household stress.
tools_and_charts: Charter capex schedule, free-cash-flow yield and buyback capacity.
Hyperscaler cloud growth and capital budgets.
transcript_cautions: Full transcript read, including extensive Charter update.
Forecast valuation multiples depend on future cash flows and ignore changing capital structure unless separately modeled.
Captioned hyperscaler revenue figures may omit or substitute segments; exact totals are not silently repaired.

review.summary: Chris Verrone and Todd Sohn interpret the rebound as a return to AI, power and bank leadership, with faster risk-taking than in 2025. They discuss gold's changing behavior, software capitulation, credit versus geopolitical risk and passive semiconductor concentration. Verrone expects a possible melt-up; Eisman reports that view and emphasizes benign bank credit. Their technical indicators are hypotheses requiring defined, independent price tests. Energy's prewar uptrend explicitly challenges an exclusively war-driven account.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman hosts; Chris Verrone provides most market-regime and trend interpretations; Todd Sohn provides ETF, flow and concentration observations. Joint guest attribution is used for short ambiguous exchanges. Closing melt-up statement credits Chris explicitly.
framework_points: Use price behavior to challenge intuitive macro narratives.
Oversold is a condition, not an automatic purchase signal.
Inspect look-through sector concentration in passive funds.
Separate financial contagion from geopolitical headlines.
Retain false signals and changing market structure when using historical analogies.
tools_and_charts: ETF net inflows versus trading volume.
Gold correlations and precious-metal ETF turnover.
Software trend lines and relative performance.
Sector relative strength and ETF launches.
transcript_cautions: Full transcript read in two contiguous parts, including long advertisement break.
Recording date explicitly April 27, earlier than May 4 publication.
Chris Verrone is sometimes transcribed as Ferrone; Todd Sohn has distinct flow/ETF comments.
Where rapid guest exchanges make exact attribution uncertain, joint attribution is used and excluded from Eisman scoring.

review.title: Conspiracy of Credit Part 1
review.summary: Eisman places private credit in an early contraction phase, emphasizing redemption pressure, software concentration, bank links and life-insurer exposure. Blue Owl filings confirm striking tender demand, and supervisory evidence supports stronger bank capital. However, gross redemption requests do not equal forced asset sales or net outflows. Claims that virtually all post-2008 lending growth was private, all subprime mortgages were securitized, and rates fell in 2018 are overstated or wrong. The aggregate CDO multiplier and software exposure require tighter definitions. His smaller-than-2008 crisis thesis remains unresolved, with explicit insurer caveats.
review.assessment: The episode identifies meaningful liquidity and concentration vulnerabilities but blends supported examples with universal claims and stock-flow confusion. Preserve the cautious systemic comparison and separate a sector credit cycle from an economy-wide credit-led recession. Captions contain genuine incomplete sentences; no missing AI prediction is reconstructed.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_00 is Steve Eisman throughout the solo lecture, established by opening self-identification. No guest views are present.
framework_points: Separate sector credit cycles from recession causes.
Measure net outflows and liquidity resources alongside gross tender requests.
Trace bank financing of ostensibly nonbank credit.
Compare common borrower exposures rather than labels.
Use consistent stocks, flows, notionals and net losses.
Stress insurer liabilities and assets together.
Treat ratings as opinions and test shared assumptions independently.
tools_and_charts: Blue Owl OCIC and OTIC tender requests and caps
Subprime originations and CDO exposure comparison
Software sector classifications and subscription revenues
transcript_cautions: Several sentences are interrupted or missing endings, including the second regulatory action, named fraud list, and an AI sentence around 1040 seconds. Missing content is not invented.
Cryptocurrency near 230 seconds appears to be a caption error in a credit-crisis sentence; it is not treated as a cryptocurrency forecast.
Standard deviation approaching one appears to confuse correlation and volatility.
The $1.8 trillion annually wording confuses an outstanding market-size stock with a flow.
Blue Owl request percentages refer to outstanding shares, whereas the transcript says assets; portfolio assets and NAV differ.
The transcript says software companies owned by private credit, although the surrounding buyout explanation concerns private equity.

review.title: A Conspiracy Of Credit Master Class: Part 2
review.summary: Eisman introduces bond contracts, yields, duration, taxation, ratings, credit analysis and amortization while warning about private-credit leverage and insurer connections. Several basic relationships are useful, but two central teaching claims fail: the five-year bond example confuses current yield with yield to maturity, and ratings do not mechanically set bond prices or equalize all same-rated yields. His four-C framework and acknowledgement of investors anticipating downgrades restore some missing judgment. Private-credit opacity has official support, while the scale and timing of eventual losses remain unresolved.
review.assessment: The lecture contains a material mathematical error and an overstated ratings-driven pricing model, rather than merely harmless terminology slips. The correct inverse price-yield relationship survives the incorrect numerical example. Distinguish conditional systemic-risk concerns from completed forecasts and unregulated from less prudentially regulated.
review.speaker_map_notes: This is a solo Steve Eisman lecture, established by self-identification at the opening. Brief SPEAKER_00 fragments within sentences are diarization errors, not a guest; the closing disclaimer is separate narration and not claim evidence.
framework_points: Read debt contracts and cash-flow timing before relying on labels.
Separate coupon, current yield and yield to maturity.
Treat ratings as one credit opinion rather than a price algorithm.
Trace leverage through portfolio companies, funds and insurers.
Assess capacity, collateral, covenants and character.
Distinguish maturity from duration and promised from realized return.
tools_and_charts: Treasury yield curve and high-grade/high-yield comparisons
transcript_cautions: Solo lecture has occasional SPEAKER_00 fragments that continue the same sentence.
The $1,250 example is coherent spoken arithmetic but incorrect finite-bond valuation; it is not silently corrected as a caption error.
Duration is repeatedly used where the conventional yield-curve axis is maturity.
Risk-free Treasuries are explicitly an assumption for the lecture.
Later discussion of investors anticipating downgrades qualifies earlier mechanical price-setting rhetoric.

claims.claim: For a fixed set of promised cash flows, bond prices fall when the required yield rises and rise when it falls.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Hold default assumptions and embedded options constant.
claims.reason: The inverse relationship is valid with fixed cash flows and a common discount-yield change.

evidence.title: Understanding bond yield and return
evidence.finding: Current yield divides annual coupon by market price; yield to maturity discounts all remaining coupons and principal. A typical yield curve slopes upward.

claims.next_check: Hold default assumptions and embedded options constant.
claims.deductive_proof: P(y)=sum(CFt/(1+y)^t). For positive fixed cash flows and y greater than -1, dP/dy=-sum(t*CFt/(1+y)^(t+1)) is negative.

proof.derivation: P(y)=sum(CFt/(1+y)^t). For positive fixed cash flows and y greater than -1, dP/dy=-sum(t*CFt/(1+y)^(t+1)) is negative.

claims.claim: A five-year $1,000 bond paying $50 annually must rise to $1,250 when comparable yield falls from 5% to 4%.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Discount all five coupons plus redemption at 4%.

claims.deductive_proof: Assume annual coupons, five full years remaining, no default or options, and 4% annual yield. Price=sum(t=1..5,50/1.04^t)+1000/1.04^5=1044.518223. 50/1250=4% is only current yield; a perpetual $50 stream would justify $1,250, but the stated five-year bond does not.

metadata.title: Why This Market “Melt-Up” is Making Me Nervous | The Weekly Wrap

review.summary: Eisman reduces exposure after a rapid technology-led rally, emphasizing speculative positioning, war risk and producer inflation while maintaining his no-recession view. He separates healthier banks from a risky private-credit cycle, prefers network moats in payments, and continues to favor AI infrastructure and Meritage while short FICO. Cisco results support the supplier thesis. His near-term Coinbase profit prediction is ambiguous because GAAP losses persisted while adjusted EBITDA was positive.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman delivers a solo monologue; inserted advertisements and opening montage are excluded.
framework_points: Distinguish risk reduction from predicting recession.
Watch funding conditions at lenders as well as borrower defaults.
Separate strong reported growth from demanding expectations.
Disclose positions and specify the actual business thesis.
tools_and_charts: Sector index weights and retail option positioning.
FSK sponsor capital and credit facilities.
Cisco AI orders and Meritage tangible book.
transcript_cautions: The substantive private-credit lecture excerpt is retained; routine subscription promotion and sponsor advertisement are omitted.
Coinbase profitability metric is unspecified and must not be graded with a selectively chosen accounting definition.
Eisman explicitly acknowledges uncertainty in market timing and his FICO short.

review.summary: Bob Brackett explains why near-term oil cash flows, forward curves and producer equities can diverge. He favors disciplined commodity exposure, dry-gas producers, Exxon, Diamondback and Cheniere while remaining tactically cautious on copper. Eisman adopts a cyclical entry-and-exit framework. review.title: A Conspiracy of Credit, Part III: How the Greatest Fraud in Human History Happened - and What It Means for Private Credit Today
review.summary: Eisman explains securitization and mortgage-era due-diligence failures, then argues that software concentration, retail liquidity promises and insurer links create private-credit vulnerabilities. Documented underwriting misconduct supports his central historical concern, but several absolutes fail: MBS predates the 1980s, Denmark has a substantial 30-year fixed mortgage market, some due-diligence samples expanded, and consumer mortgages can be modified. Civil RMBS enforcement contradicts broad claims that nothing happened without settling particular criminal-referral outcomes. The 2027-2028 refinancing scenario remains unfinished; universal private-software valuation losses and undated credit-cycle predictions remain unproved.
review.assessment: Substantive article review with paragraph references. Distinguishes persuasive mechanisms from overgeneralized history, unverified market estimates, normative judgments and actual future deadlines. The specific criminal-accountability claim remains unresolved rather than rebutted with unrelated originator cases.
review.speaker_map_notes: Signed solo article by Steve Eisman. No guest attribution or inferred dialogue.
framework_points: Trace cash flows and loss seniority through securitization.
Separate collateral risk from repackaged security notional.
Inspect sampling design before extrapolating defects.
Distinguish civil enforcement from specific criminal referrals.
Match liquidity promises to underlying loan liquidity.
Separate public equity prices from private enterprise values.
Track maturity cohorts and sponsor equity support.
Include affiliated insurers in exposure mapping.
tools_and_charts: Clayton due-diligence samples and underwriting exceptions
transcript_cautions: This source is the complete substantive signed-in article, not an episode transcript. No player or full video transcript was available.
Use paragraph_references and source_locator; the normalization placeholders at zero are not speech timestamps.
Illustrative building and coupon figures are not treated as universal historical deal statistics.
The criminal-accountability discussion concerns Wall Street due-diligence conduct; scope is preserved.
Market-size, software and maturity estimates lack identified original datasets in the article.

review.title: Inside the Hidden Consumer Crisis with Lakshmi Ganapathi
review.summary: Lakshmi Ganapathi argues that inflation, BNPL dependence and opaque credit structures reveal strain hidden by benign bank statistics. She connects these concerns to shorts in FICO, Wingstop, AutoZone, Group 1 and DoorDash. Eisman challenges the missing bank-loss evidence, adopts selected Wingstop and refinancing explanations, and distinguishes near-term noise from future software-loan maturities. Inflation and several BNPL figures are supported, while claims about universal borrower distress, payment-network invisibility and automatic private-company markdowns overreach. Most company-specific causal claims remain unverified, and 2027 refinancing outcomes are genuinely unfinished.
review.assessment: Useful tension between household surveys and reported bank outcomes, with several independently verified premises. Neither survey dependence nor public-equity drawdowns alone establishes hidden bank losses or a universal private valuation decline. Guest positions, Eisman's probing questions and his explicit recap endorsements are kept separate.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 is Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_00 is Lakshmi Ganapathi, inferred with high confidence from the introduction, questions, replies and final recap. Dialogue determines brief interjections.
framework_points: Separate household hardship from bank loan performance.
Distinguish payment status, expected-loss provisions and realized charge-offs.
Use consistent survey denominators and distinguish any use from dependence.
Trace private-credit funding, guarantees and retained exposure.
Compare private companies with public peers without assuming identical equity and enterprise-value changes.
Make maturities and sponsor incentives explicit.
Demand cohort evidence for immigration and affordability explanations.
tools_and_charts: Bank earnings calls and nonaccrual balances
CPI, PPI, energy inflation and real wages
Warehouse lines and synthetic risk transfers
Software equity drawdowns and loan maturity ladders
Receivables, invoice factoring and used-car auction observations
transcript_cautions: The episode was published May 27, 2026; references to released April inflation data imply recording after May 13, without establishing an exact day.
The speaker immediately corrects HSBC billions to millions; the corrected amount is used.
The Wingstop demographic denominator changes from customers to store locations and is not silently reconciled.
Technology and food-delivery survey percentages differ from the inspected originating survey; delivery is not exclusively DoorDash.
Public software equity losses are not identical to enterprise-value losses.
Statements about corporate fraud remain allegations unless adjudicated.
The opening promotional summary is not used in place of the complete discussion.

review.title: The SpaceX IPO: Science Fiction or Serious Investment? | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Recorded May 28 and published May 29, this wrap challenges SpaceX proposed valuation using segment economics, index mechanics and a comparison with established technology businesses. It also discusses Salesforce accounting, Dell demand and the contrasting economics of banks and ratings agencies.
review.assessment: The segment-level skepticism and insistence on treating stock compensation as a real cost are useful. The claim that Nasdaq conspired to guarantee success is not established, and the float cap is described without its full-cap weighting context. Bank of America margin improvement regardless of Fed policy is also too categorical.
framework_points: Read the S-1 rather than rely on a mission statement.
Separate current profitable segments from speculative addressable markets.
Use comparable growth and margins alongside valuation.
Treat stock compensation and funding needs as economic costs.
transcript_cautions: Publisher transcript contains several genuine gaps and corrupted numerical phrases, including TAM and comparative multiples. Only clear recoverable claims are evaluated.
Recorded Thursday May 28 for the May 29 wrap.
The quoted SpaceX loss around $1.9 billion is operating loss, not the much larger loss before taxes; the transcript does not clearly specify the measure.
The mailbag is abridged by the host; listener assertions are separated from his response.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman presents; speaker attribution follows the full dialogue.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare price per completed task, compute costs and free allowances.
claims.reason: Costs and subsidies vary by vendor, model, workload and contract. A broad claim needs a matched pricing and cost series.

claims.reason: The general methodology change and three-times-float cap exist, but the cap limits weighting relative to full capitalization. The public consultation and general eligibility rules do not establish conspiracy or guaranteed success.

evidence.title: Nasdaq-100 methodology update
evidence.finding: The May 1 change followed consultation, replaced the 10% minimum float requirement and added a general Fast Entry pathway for top-40-sized listings. The three-times-float mechanism is a cap relative to full capitalization, not evidence of a private agreement guaranteeing an IPO return.

claims.next_check: Apply the actual methodology to shares, float, liquidity and eligibility dates.

metadata.title: The AI All-You-Can-Eat Buffet Is Ending with Gary Marcus | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 62

review.summary: Eisman maps AI beneficiaries, software risks, financing concentration and physical bottlenecks before interviewing Gary Marcus. Marcus accepts useful coding and brainstorming while emphasizing reliability limits, tool-driven progress and uncertain unit economics. Eisman questions profitable demand rather than treating failure to achieve AGI as sufficient evidence of a bubble, and declines an immediate short despite concern. Several supporting claims require correction or restraint, especially CPU ratios, automatic private-valuation losses and speculation about Anthropic's compute discount.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman delivers the opening investment map and interviews Gary Marcus. Marcus supplies technical critiques; Eisman states separate financing risks, willingness to be wrong and reluctance to short current growth.
framework_points: Separate useful specialized AI from AGI claims.
Analyze a model together with its tools and verification environment.
Trace revenue, compute cost, funding and customer concentration separately.
Differentiate announced capacity from paid utilization.
A bubble thesis needs a mechanism and catalyst, not just high spending.
Test price elasticity when subsidized usage becomes metered.
tools_and_charts: Hyperscaler capex and free cash flow.
transcript_cautions: Entire supplied public transcript read in two contiguous parts.
Public episode ends with a premium invitation mid-answer; read_complete refers to the complete supplied public source, not an unavailable premium continuation.
Guest is Gary Marcus. His technical and economic assertions are not automatically Eisman predictions.
Intro conflates CPU and memory; later question confuses inference with internet retrieval and is corrected by the guest.
Pentium date and cost anecdote appears garbled and is incidental to the material reliability thesis.
NVIDIA result reference places recording after May 20; exact recording date is not stated.

metadata.title: The AI Semiconductor Boom and What Could End It with Stacy Rasgon | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 63

review.summary: Stacy Rasgon describes AI demand spreading from GPUs into CPU, memory, networking and equipment bottlenecks. He upgrades AMD, remains constructive on Broadcom and NVIDIA, and distinguishes Intel's improved narrative from proven manufacturing economics. Eisman owns NVIDIA and endorses the continuing infrastructure cycle. They reject simplistic immediate GPU obsolescence while identifying weak eventual returns and power limits as risks. Later supplier earnings support demand acceleration, but long-horizon revenue, EPS and investment-return claims remain open.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Stacy Rasgon supplies technical explanations, analyst ratings and numerical forecasts. Eisman asks questions, discloses NVIDIA ownership and gives the closing endorsement; guest upgrades are not attributed to Eisman.
framework_points: Distinguish earnings revisions from multiple expansion.
Inspect bottlenecks across the entire supply chain.
Treat reported margin changes separately from impairment base effects.
Use GPU rental prices and utilization to assess useful life.
Separate temporary digestion from permanent ROI failure.
Treat management language, warrants and capex announcements as evidence requiring interpretation.
tools_and_charts: SOX forward earnings and P/E decomposition
CPU/GPU rack ratios and agent workload illustration
AMD EPS scenarios and warrant milestones
transcript_cautions: Rasgon corrects Eisman's gross-margin comparison in real time; the correction is preserved.
Rasgon explicitly says fixed CPU/GPU attachment ratios are an imperfect heuristic.
The $600 AMD warrant threshold is a vesting condition, not an unconditional price target.
May 25, 2023 refers to market reaction; the earnings release was the prior evening.
Qualcomm and Intel rumors remain unconfirmed in the extracted claims.

review.title: Citigroup: A Story of 20 Years of Mediocrity - and One CEO - Jane Fraser - Who Changed Everything
review.summary: Eisman credits Jane Fraser's simplification for Citigroup's improving returns while arguing that a weak US retail deposit franchise imposes a lasting disadvantage. He distinguishes exceptional trading quarters from normalized profitability and evaluates each business against ambitious management targets. Reported Q1 divisional returns and subsequent improvement support parts of the story. However, Corbat-era returns were not always below 10%, the cited dividend cut occurred in January 2008, and the estimated four-point funding penalty is unverified. Rerating causality, permanent peer underperformance and the feasibility of long-term targets remain separate unresolved or unfinished propositions.
review.assessment: A nuanced operating-turnaround thesis beneath an overstated historical narrative. Reported segment numbers are largely accurate, but Q1 capital-allocation changes complicate direct return comparisons. Citi still retained 51% of Banamex in Q3. The 2027-2031 target path is unfinished, while current normalized-return estimates are testable with interim results rather than automatically too early.
review.speaker_map_notes: The PDF labels the solo speaker Gavin Leighton, but the opening explicitly self-identifies Steve Eisman and the content consistently recounts his career. All substantive claims are attributed to Eisman. Caption name variants are normalized to Jane Fraser, Sandy Weill, Michael Corbat and Citigroup.
framework_points: Combine management incentives with financial analysis.
Reconcile segment recasts before inferring operating trends.
Track leverage and off-balance-sheet recourse.
Separate retail and institutional funding economics.
Normalize exceptional trading income rather than annualizing one quarter.
Distinguish company guidance from the analyst's forecast.
Model business-specific growth and capital allocation.
tools_and_charts: Long-term stock chart adjusted for reverse split
Return on tangible common equity and price/tangible book
Wealth client investment assets and competitive comparisons
transcript_cautions: Publisher PDF is mislabeled Gavin Leighton; opening self-identification establishes Eisman.
Timestamps are the real coarse PDF blocks. Claims share block ranges because more precise speech timing is unavailable.
The PDF has an embedded 16:53 marker within a larger block; precision is not invented for individual claims.
The sentence linking dilution and the 2011-2024 price period is garbled; no precise dilution date is inferred from it.
Citi's 2011 reverse split must be accounted for in historical per-share comparisons.
The 50-75 basis-point funding and four-point RoTCE penalties are explicitly guesses.
Company targets and qualitative culture statements are distinct from independently demonstrated outcomes.

review.summary: The wrap develops Eisman's thesis that AI is shifting funding risk onto public shareholders through equity issuance and higher capital intensity. He contrasts strong Oracle demand with its cash burden and questions model moats and future IPO absorption. He also warns about a 4.5% Treasury threshold, concentrated earnings growth, addiction-related litigation and private-market illiquidity. Primary records support the large financing packages, inflation figures and filed lawsuit while leaving causal market explanations and most forward returns unsettled.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman delivers a solo monologue; inserted advertisements and opening montage are excluded.
framework_points: Compare cash demands with reported earnings and backlog.
Separate headline aggregate growth from sector concentration.
Assess illiquidity and benchmark crowding as distinct risks.
Treat equity issuance and long payoff horizons as investor burdens.
tools_and_charts: Treasury yield range and index drawdowns.
Alphabet financing terms, Oracle capex/FCF/RPO and Super Micro proposed issuance.
Private-equity holding periods and unrealized assets.
transcript_cautions: Montage omitted; full discussion used.
At about 160 seconds captions say the Fed will not be raising rates and might raise them; later discussion clearly distinguishes cuts and hikes.
Google equity history changes from 2004 here to 2005 in the following wrap; do not silently resolve it.
Allegations about addictive design are not adjudicated facts.

review.summary: Tom Gallagher offers a less alarmed second opinion on private-equity-owned insurers, emphasizing differences between large platforms, smaller insurers and retail private-credit funds. They examine asset liquidity, reinsurance, legacy liability guarantees, weak public valuations and capital allocation. Eisman acknowledges the more reassuring analysis but remains unenthusiastic about public life-insurance stocks. Lincoln's later buyback resumption supports improving capital flexibility, while sector-wide solvency and future merger benefits remain unproven.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Tom Gallagher provides insurance analysis and forecasts. Eisman poses challenges, states buyback preferences, and explicitly describes his changed comfort level in the closing monologue.
framework_points: Seek a second expert view when an earlier interview creates a strong conclusion.
Separate investment yield from credit, liquidity and concentration risks.
Trace where reinsurance moves risk and capital.
Compare accounting earnings with distributable capital before recommending buybacks.
Treat gross annuity sales separately from net flows.
tools_and_charts: Traditional versus alternative insurer private-credit yield comparison
Top 30-40 private holdings inspection described by guest
Forward P/E comparison across life insurers
Annuity asset yield and liability runoff
transcript_cautions: The acquisition-history discussion confuses American Equity with Aviva and associates Carlyle with Corebridge before later naming Blackstone. No ownership table is inferred from these captions.
The comment dating Alzheimer's recognition to the early 2000s is incidental and unreliable; the material duration-risk explanation is retained without that history.
GE reserve funding and accounting charges are not treated as identical.
Advertisements are excluded.

review.title: The Lawsuits That Could Change Social Media Forever w/ Ben Zipursky
review.summary: Benjamin Zipursky separates negligence, consumer fraud, product liability and public nuisance in social-media litigation. He favors ordinary negligence while criticizing expansive nuisance theories and emphasizing federal defenses and appeals. Eisman identifies lasting legal exposure and possible product changes. Later multistate settlements, New Mexico remedies and continuing trials support material risk, but do not establish every causal allegation. The guest misstates the California damages split; Eisman overstates the absence of related appellate precedent and assumes all cases will be appealed. The New Mexico court later rejected direct algorithm redesign while ordering other safeguards and abatement funding.
review.assessment: The central warning about prolonged and potentially substantial exposure has meaningful support. Legal opinions about the proper scope of nuisance are normative, not failed forecasts because a trial judge ruled differently. Preserve the distinction between alleged harm, adjudicated facts, settlement obligations and final appellate outcomes.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 is Steve Eisman; SPEAKER_00 is Fordham tort scholar Benjamin (Ben) Zipursky, established by introduction and legal answers. Short embedded interjections are attributed from dialogue.
framework_points: Classify cause of action, plaintiff and remedy before assessing exposure.
Separate third-party publication from a platform's independent design duties.
Distinguish complaints, jury findings, judgments, settlement and appeals.
Consider aggregated state exposure rather than only one verdict.
Separate a normative legal critique from a prediction of judicial outcomes.
Preserve alternative causes and uncertainty about technical implementation.
Update legislative pessimism when state activity supplies contrary evidence.
tools_and_charts: Negligence, strict product liability and consumer-protection claims
First Amendment and Supreme Court review
Corporate cash flow versus aggregate litigation exposure
transcript_cautions: Publication is June 17, but discussion says the May 4 bench trial began last week. Recording in early May is an inference, not an exact verified date.
Ziperski is normalized to Zipursky from the named Fordham scholar.
Eisman briefly says Arizona while repeatedly discussing New Mexico; the substantive case mapping uses the established New Mexico context.
The guest explicitly has not carefully read the New Mexico pleadings and gives tentative accounts of jury motives and plaintiff history.
The spoken California damages split of $4 million compensatory and $2 million punitive conflicts with the filed $3 million compensatory award.
A no-appellate-decisions statement is narrower when applied to the new verdicts than when applied to related Section 230 design issues.
The court's August algorithm-relief rejection is distinct from its other product safeguards and abatement award; Meta later reported a stay.

review.summary: Eisman balances ongoing AI infrastructure growth against heavier capital needs, weak model moats, usage-based pricing and construction constraints. He argues suppliers may retain better economics than model providers while acknowledging their dependence on continued spending. The Anthropic suspension and Alphabet equity package are real, but the suspension was temporary and the financing headline includes future capacity. Other themes include rate-sensitive homebuilders, private-credit liquidity, payment competition and the limits of geographic diversification.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman delivers a solo monologue; inserted advertisements and opening montage are excluded.
framework_points: Distinguish technological transformation from investment returns.
Compare suppliers' economics with capital-intensive customers.
Track pricing and usage after subsidies decline.
Treat higher rates as a key housing and valuation transmission channel.
tools_and_charts: NVIDIA revenue growth and hyperscaler capex.
Alphabet equity financing and cash flow.
Meritage tangible book and acquisition multiples.
Regional index sector weights and company market caps.
transcript_cautions: Opening montage duplicates later claims and is excluded.
The transcript says airlines are not notoriously bad businesses, but surrounding sentences clearly describe weak airline economics; retain this as a caption/negation caution.
Amazon motive is explicitly speculative.
Announced equity capacity is distinguished from completed funding.

metadata.title: The Consumer Stocks To Own & Avoid with Evercore's Top Analysts | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 65

review.summary: Three Evercore analysts separate consumer income pressures from company strategy. They favor value retail, selected restaurant recoveries and Ralph Lauren, while warning about Nike, Lululemon and legacy packaged foods. Eisman adopts the cautious food view and highlights Walmart. Subsequent results support operating dispersion, Walmart membership growth and packaged-food stress, but many causal explanations, valuations and longer-horizon recoveries remain unresolved.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Eisman interviews Michael Binetti on apparel, David Palmer on restaurants and food, and Greg Melich on big-box retail. The closing recap from about 3902 seconds is Eisman.
framework_points: Separate income-cohort demand from brand-specific execution.
Distinguish accumulated price levels from current inflation.
Track transactions, ticket, comparable sales and margin separately.
A good company or rising sales does not automatically imply an attractive valuation.
Gradual distribution changes can preserve customer and wholesale relationships.
Differentiate completed earnings recovery from anticipated operating leverage.
tools_and_charts: Apparel same-store sales and off-price comparisons.
Starbucks and Chipotle price charts and earnings expectations.
Housing lock-in estimates and pro-market size.
Ralph Lauren AUR and product mix.
transcript_cautions: All transcript segments including the hour-plus ending were read.
Company results reported after the conversation are outcome checks, not evidence known to the speakers at recording.
Sponsorship claims and the separate premium-content advertisement are excluded.
Several figures are proprietary analyst estimates rather than disclosed company data.

review.title: Why Cannabis Rescheduling Changes Everything for Glass House Brands
review.summary: Jonathan DeCourcey argues that medical rescheduling can transform Glass House by opening higher-priced markets, lowering taxes and enabling a US listing. Eisman explicitly adopts the speculative margin thesis in his recap. The NYSE listing and first European hemp sale occurred, while the guest's pre-fall broad-rescheduling deadline failed. Export permits and state rules remain material, European cultivation already exists, and the proposed Medicare market is overstated. Eisman also converts a production-cost target into a current figure and confuses illustrative gross margin with operating margin. The larger earnings opportunity remains conditional.
review.assessment: The successful listing and hemp export are distinct from unproven interstate medical-cannabis economics. Guest errors are recorded separately; Eisman is responsible only for his explicit claims and closing adoption. The investment thesis remains unresolved, while its legal, cost and margin premises contain identifiable errors.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 is Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_00 is Jonathan DeCourcey, identified as Glass House head of investor relations. Very short interjections are occasionally embedded within the other speaker's segment; attribution follows the surrounding question and response.
framework_points: Compare a restricted local market with potential expanded-market economics.
Separate current operations, installed capacity, targets and realized production.
Treat legal reform, licensing and distribution implementation as distinct milestones.
Use price-volume-cost scenarios while retaining incremental expenses.
Separate a successful exchange listing from investment returns and operating success.
Disclose ownership and distinguish speculative opportunity from modeled valuation.
tools_and_charts: Greenhouse footprint and annual biomass capacity
Cost per pound and wholesale prices
California versus US medical and European market pricing
Reverse stock split and exchange-listing conditions
transcript_cautions: The publication is June 24, but the guest refers to May 26 as current and April changes as roughly a month earlier. Treat late-May recording as an inference, not a verified exact date.
DeCorsi is normalized to Jonathan DeCourcey from the identified company role.
The guest repeatedly says April 18; the inspected medical rule was issued April 23 and published April 28.
The 1920-second can/cannot institutional-ownership interjection is ambiguous and is not silently corrected.
The guest initially says target selling price then explicitly corrects to target production cost.
Eisman's closing operating-margin language differs from the guest's gross-margin calculation.
Publication follows June retail deconsolidation; original interview figures describe the earlier business perimeter.
The first completed European transaction was hemp; it is not evidence of unrestricted marijuana exports.

review.title: The Q2 2026 Report Card: Who Won, Who Lost, and Why | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman reviews a technology-led second-quarter rally already showing signs of reversal. He favors scarce semiconductor and power capacity over capital-hungry model builders, questions weak consulting and consumer turnarounds, and discusses financial-sector leadership. He criticizes Greenspan's regulatory legacy and argues that greater US economic dynamism favors US investments over Europe.
review.assessment: Full transcript reviewed. Empirical claims without inspected primary outcome evidence remain unresolved; guest claims are separate from Eisman attribution. Primary outcome verification is incomplete for claims marked unresolved; these are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman hosts the episode; guest turns are inferred from introductions and conversational context.
framework_points: Look inside sector returns to distinguish scarce suppliers from the buyers funding their growth.
Capital intensity requires durable competitive protection to generate acceptable returns.
Separate social-policy preferences from investment-return judgments.
tools_and_charts: S&P 500, Nasdaq and eleven sector returns through June 24
Micron earnings, forward P/E and supply outlook
Capital raising and business-model comparison for hyperscalers
transcript_cautions: Quarter review is explicitly an incomplete-quarter snapshot, not final June 30 performance.
Micron EPS is rendered $251; primary disclosure is $25.11, so the caption numeral is unreliable.
Captions render moat as moes and MOU as anou.
Greenspan is repeatedly said to have retired in 2005; Federal Reserve history says January 31, 2006.

review.title: The Market's Biggest Warning Signs Right Now with Todd Sohn | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 66
review.summary: Todd Sohn reviews stock trends, ETF flows and the concentration of index, quality and momentum exposures in technology. He favors the relative charts of Alphabet and GE Vernova, is cautious on software and several mega-caps, and warns about leveraged and thematic products. Eisman adopts the hidden-concentration lesson and emphasizes an AI-led market. Daily leverage mechanics are verified, but proprietary flow charts and stock-selection returns were not independently reproduced. Strong risk diagnosis should be separated from unproved timing and causal explanations.
review.assessment: Full transcript reviewed. Empirical claims without inspected primary outcome evidence remain unresolved; guest claims are separate from Eisman attribution. Primary outcome verification is incomplete for claims marked unresolved; these are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman hosts the episode; guest turns are inferred from introductions and conversational context.
framework_points: Inspect underlying holdings across funds rather than count fund labels.
Separate overbought trends from automatic sell signals.
Use flows as observed positioning, not a deterministic forecast.
Distinguish daily leverage from long-horizon returns.
tools_and_charts: Relative strength and equal-weight sector returns
ETF flow percentiles and cumulative flows
Thematic maximum drawdowns and Sharpe ratios
transcript_cautions: Recording explicitly refers to June 15 despite June 29 publication.
Caption socks refers to SOXX; sharp ratio means Sharpe ratio.
Chart attachments and underlying proprietary datasets were not independently reconstructed.
Some stock-chart observations are conditional and contain no entry price, stop level or horizon.
Historical 15% industry-weight exchange is internally imprecise about which cases failed.
