review.title: Steve Eisman Reveals His Personal Portfolio: Every Position Explained
review.summary: Eisman explains his concentrated long portfolio through AI suppliers, electricity infrastructure, low-valued turnarounds, established franchises and speculative cannabis. He sells capital-intensive platforms while monitoring AI financing and power bottlenecks. NVIDIA growth and the infrastructure backlog support current demand, but most valuation and recovery theses remain undated or conditional. Charter and Meritage still face operating pressure. Apple already had its own models, Microsoft had raised debt since its IPO, and Progressive did not invent direct insurance. Glass House upside rests on unproven market access, prices and margins; scenario arithmetic is separated from investable outcomes.
review.assessment: A useful statement of holdings, catalysts and falsifiers, with several factual errors in supporting premises. The central multi-year and conditional investment theses should not be graded as completed returns. Capital-intensity rotation has evidence, while stock-specific valuation claims lack point-in-time consensus reconstruction. Cannabis rescheduling is real but narrower than an automatic opening of every market.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_00 is Steve Eisman throughout this solo portfolio discussion, established by first-person holdings and self-identification.
framework_points: Write the initial thesis and sell when it fails rather than rationalizing thesis creep.
Distinguish growth stories from fundamentals and recognize uncertainty at regime changes.
Separate AI suppliers from buyers bearing the capital-spending burden.
Use cash flow, buybacks, book value, ROE and backlog to identify catalysts.
Model speculative outcomes with explicit margins and dilution rather than a single target.
State concrete evidence that would reduce portfolio risk.
tools_and_charts: Sixteen-position portfolio grouped into five themes
AIG ROE and tangible book value
Glass House price-volume-margin and enterprise-value scenarios
transcript_cautions: All captions identify one speaker. Company spelling and tickers are normalized only where context is clear: Novo Nordisk, Meritage/MTH and Taylor Morrison/TMHC.
Publication is July 1 but references to an upcoming NYSE listing likely reflect earlier recording; Glass House began NYSE trading June 30.
Position counts are not portfolio market-value weights.
Several forward EPS multiples and growth figures lack stated price dates or GAAP/adjusted conventions.
The Glass House valuation chart is discussed but its complete debt and share-count inputs are absent from the transcript.
The brief sentence near 1419-1429 seconds is incomplete, so no missing comparison is reconstructed.

review.title: Who Wins the Midterms & What It Means for Markets with Dan Clifton | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 67
review.summary: Dan Clifton links midterms, tariffs, fiscal stimulus and Fed balance-sheet reform to markets. He expects a Democratic House but leans against a Senate takeover, emphasizes an underpriced data-center backlash and favors defense technology. Eisman challenges the moderate-Democrat scenario and expects a prolonged Iran conflict. Several long-term forecasts remain open; election outcomes require primary tally confirmation. The Supreme Court tariff ruling is verified, while causal macro and political explanations remain substantially unresolved.
review.assessment: Full transcript reviewed. Empirical claims without inspected primary outcome evidence remain unresolved; guest claims are separate from Eisman attribution. Primary outcome verification is incomplete for claims marked unresolved; these are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman hosts the episode; guest turns are inferred from introductions and conversational context.
framework_points: Use institutional control and budget leverage, not just election labels.
Track the change in fiscal/tariff impulse rather than gross tariff announcements.
Distinguish speculative motives from observable policy.
Treat data-center local costs and tax benefits together.
tools_and_charts: Fed balance sheet and bank deposits
transcript_cautions: Captions confuse Warsh with Walsh and IEEPA with IAPA.
Several recorded timing references precede the July publication date.
Opening and closing summaries repeat guest views; summaries are not automatic host endorsement.
Eisman corrects 2028 to 2026 during a midterm discussion.
Election horizons have passed by the audit cutoff; missing official evidence means unresolved, not too early.

review.title: The Bearish Case for Oil and Gold with Queen Anne's Gate Capital
review.summary: Kathleen Kelley argues that war-driven demand destruction and new supply will create severe oil surpluses, potentially pushing prices into the twenties. Nancy O'Flynn sees crowded gold positioning and prefers silver. Eisman mostly reports their views, adding conditional consumer and equity implications plus a separate critique of crypto. Chinese refinery weakness and delayed reserve replenishment have support. However, contemporaneous Gulf supply shortfalls and falling onshore stocks contradict assertions of fully offset disruption. Long-run oil balances remain future-dated, while renewed central-bank gold buying weakens the proposed demand-exhaustion mechanism.
review.assessment: The central oil forecast is conditional on restored flows and extends beyond the cutoff. Current physical-balance claims deserve different verdicts from that future scenario. Eisman does not unconditionally adopt the guest $20 oil target; his closing $40-50 framing is his interpretation, not a second explicit guest target.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_00 is Steve Eisman, SPEAKER_02 is Kathleen Kelley and SPEAKER_01 is Nancy O'Flynn, established by named introductions, backgrounds and the explicit handoff to Nancy near 1545 seconds. The publisher captions spell Kelley as Kelly; attribution uses the identified Queen Anne's Gate economist.
framework_points: Build commodity balances from supply, consumption, trade and inventories.
Separate final consumption from stockpiling and refinery demand.
Distinguish crude availability from refined-product bottlenecks.
Test geopolitical narratives against routes, capacity and realized output.
Separate positioning, prices and causal explanations.
Preserve conditional forecasts and the time required for retail price pass-through.
tools_and_charts: Strategic reserve release and refill schedules
Gold ETF flows and commitments of traders
Oil price moving averages and inflation lags
transcript_cautions: Publication is July 8; an exact recording date is not stated. References to a ceasefire and oil in the seventies locate a particular interim market regime.
Kelley and O'Flynn spellings are normalized; speaker assignments are supported by introductions.
A Saudi export statement combines inconsistent component totals; do not silently reconcile them.
Demand is sometimes used for refinery demand, final consumption and apparent demand interchangeably.
The closing recap says oil where context clearly means gold.
Nancy locates $5,200 in early 2026; Eisman later incorrectly places it at 2025 year-end.
The closing $40-50 oil base-case suggestion is Eisman interpretation; Kelley explicitly discusses possible twenties.

review.title: Beyond Ozempic: The Next Wave of Biotech Winners with Boris Peaker
review.summary: Peaker explains trial costs, early-stage selection risk, China sourcing and why oncology and orphan diseases attract development capital. He highlights pancreatic-cancer RAS inhibition, immune resets, gene editing and muscle-preserving obesity therapies, while questioning rapid AI-driven productivity gains. Eisman adopts several explanations in his recap. Daraxonrasib efficacy and subsequent approval are verified, but the recap misstates the control treatment. FDA rules do not categorically require all pivotal patients to be American. GLP-1 lean-mass data need careful interpretation, and Lilly commercial strength does not establish permanent victory over Novo.
review.assessment: Useful development-economics framework with several factual overstatements. Clinical benefit, commercial attractiveness and stock returns are kept separate. Most company-specific long-run commercial outcomes remain unresolved or genuinely future-dated.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 is Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_00 is Boris Peaker, established by named introduction and dialogue. Several SPEAKER_00 blocks contain short Eisman prompts; standalone assertions are assigned from conversational context.
framework_points: Evaluate trial economics by disease, endpoint and time to informative data.
Early selective samples may not predict broad population outcomes.
Separate statistically significant benefit from cure and normal life expectancy.
Distinguish clinical development, regulatory approval and commercial value.
Test AI productivity through failure rates and full development cycles.
Consider patent expirations and acquisition proceeds as capital-recycling drivers.
tools_and_charts: DXA body composition versus functional outcomes
Biotech IPO, secondary and venture financing
transcript_cautions: Introductory audio/captions skip from about 77 to 96 seconds and several later phrases are incomplete.
Peaker, daraxonrasib, retatrutide, Novo Nordisk and PCSK9 are misspelled in machine captions.
The $1.3 billion acquisition-capacity statement is explicitly corrected to $1.3 trillion.
Phase/stage terminology is colloquial; cancer stage must not be confused with trial phase.
The pancreatic trial involved previously treated metastatic disease and chemotherapy controls, not all newly diagnosed patients or an untreated control.
Lean mass and skeletal muscle are not interchangeable measurements.
HeLa historical details are incidental and omitted from material claims; they should not be relied on as a scientific chronology.

review.title: Bank Earnings Just Gave the Market a Much Needed Confidence Boost | The Weekly Wrap
review.summary: Eisman interprets strong bank earnings and benign credit quality as evidence against an imminent bank-led recession, while shifting his macro attention toward AI and private credit. He sees AI infrastructure spending crowding out software budgets, payment incumbents challenging Circle, and investment banking benefiting from AI financing. He distinguishes earnings beats from the guidance expectations that move shares.
review.assessment: The inspected IBM and JPMorgan disclosures support important operating observations, with qualifications about causality and adjusted results. The absolute claim that short Treasury values do not fluctuate is contradicted by the reserve-fund risk disclosure. Many other quarter-specific and causal claims remain unverified rather than being awarded accuracy credit. Primary outcome verification is incomplete for claims marked unresolved; these are not adverse accuracy grades.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman hosts the episode; guest turns are inferred from introductions and conversational context.
framework_points: Use nonaccrual trends at diversified banks as a concurrent credit indicator, while acknowledging that private credit and AI may lead the next downturn.
Compare returns on tangible common equity with price to tangible book.
Distinguish reported operating results from market expectations and forward guidance.
tools_and_charts: JPMorgan, Citi, Wells Fargo and Bank of America consumer/commercial nonaccruals for 2Q25, 1Q26 and 2Q26
Company quarterly EPS, revenue, guidance and share reactions
transcript_cautions: The brief biotech guest clip is a promotion, not a full attributable analysis.
Caption numerals around Goldman ROTCE and bank EPS are malformed; exact numbers require source audio or filings.
Eisman presents adjusted JPMorgan EPS and ROTCE without consistently naming the adjustment.

review.title: AI Has a Power Problem: Why the U.S. Power Grid Can't Keep Up | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 69
review.summary: Kallo describes power, grid equipment and skilled labor as bottlenecks to AI construction and favors GE Vernova's long order cycle. He discusses Tesla autonomy and storage, predicts a potential SpaceX-Tesla combination, and explains tariff-driven solar uncertainty. Eisman owns GE Vernova, questions Tesla's valuation and autonomy promises, and adopts the power-and-labor constraint thesis without endorsing all guest forecasts.
review.assessment: Full transcript reviewed. Empirical claims without inspected primary outcome evidence remain unresolved; guest claims are separate from Eisman attribution. Primary outcome verification is incomplete for claims marked unresolved; these are not adverse accuracy grades.

Identify speed-to-power and firm capacity rather than nominal generating capacity alone.
Value long-cycle equipment with backlog, service revenue and delivery timing.
Separate an EV business valuation from autonomy and robotics optionality.

review.title: Payments Industry - Fear and Reality
review.summary: Eisman and Ken Suchoski distinguish fears of AI disruption from early payment adoption. Both emphasize card-network distribution, consumer protections and the potential to integrate agents and stablecoins. Suchoski sees value in Toast's integrated model while identifying PayPal pricing and Fiserv execution problems; Eisman ends by favoring only Visa and Mastercard for long-term ownership. Primary disclosures support Visa services growth, agent infrastructure and Toast memory-cost pressure. Permanent network safety, stablecoin adoption shortfalls and stock-price causality remain unproved. PayPal has revenue and volume growth despite profit pressure. Time-relative figures require caution because the recording appears earlier than publication.
review.assessment: Full locally transcribed interview and closing lessons reviewed. Guest forecasts are separated from Eisman's explicit views. Corporate disclosures verify reported products and results, not all management promises or investment causality. The central incumbent-network thesis is plausible but undated and therefore unresolved, not automatically too early.
review.speaker_map_notes: No diarization is available. Opening identifies Steve Eisman and recurring Autonomous Research analyst Ken Suchoski. Host questions, personal Visa disclosure and solo closing lessons establish Eisman; technical answers are inferred as Suchoski with medium attribution confidence. Where Eisman explicitly adopts a proposition, the claim records him and notes shared origin when relevant.
framework_points: Separate discovery, authorization, execution and settlement in agentic commerce.
Test payment adoption through realized volume rather than narratives.
Compare consumer protection, rewards and switching costs.
Distinguish relative-value shorts from outright bearish forecasts.
Use network distribution and two-sided adoption costs in moat analysis.
Avoid equating low earnings multiples with low intrinsic value.
Model hardware acquisition cost against recurring lifetime gross profit.
Account for leverage when comparing earnings and cash-flow valuations.
tools_and_charts: Autonomous agentic-commerce report and delegation table
PayPal rack rates versus negotiated merchant pricing
Toast hardware costs and recurring gross profit
Fiserv unlevered free-cash-flow valuation and debt
transcript_cautions: On-device MLX Whisper transcript has no speaker markers. Ken Sahowski is normalized to Ken Suchoski using publisher metadata.
Fiserv is occasionally transcribed as Pfizer; Mastercard and Adyen also have harmless name errors.
Publisher date is July 22, but the interview calls Lyons' June 15 departure this week and Monday. An earlier recording is likely; exact recording date is not established.
Time-relative prices and latest-quarter comparisons are not silently reassigned to the publication date.
The transcript ends with complete closing lessons and disclaimer.
Incumbent-network safety is an undated thesis, not a completed outcome.

Question crowding and update when counterparty funding changes.
Translate backlog into funded, delivered, margin-generating revenue.

Distinguish technology adoption from shareholder returns.

review.title: The Real Estate Brokerage War, For-Profit Education, & the Art of the Short with Brad Safalow
review.summary: Safalow favors Zillow over Compass, expects housing affordability to improve with lower rates, and argues that AI weakens Google advertising and education economics. He revisits shorts in Trupanion, Freshpet and Kinsale. Eisman explicitly shares selected education and pet-insurance concerns while disclosing Google ownership. Primary records confirm Washington listing restrictions, computing-enrollment declines and Kinsale premium softness, but challenge zero-growth pet insurance and simple Freshpet deterioration. Several private channel checks, liability accusations and valuation claims remain unresolved. The interview was recorded June 11, well before publication.
review.assessment: The episode offers differentiated mechanisms but many causal claims depend on private research. Keep Safalow stock calls separate from Eisman ownership and explicit endorsements. Subsequent operating results are mixed rather than uniform confirmation of the short theses.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 is Eisman and SPEAKER_00 is Brad Safalow, established by the introduction and sustained question-answer roles. Embedded interviewer prompts are attributed by dialogue. Recording date June 11 is explicitly stated near 2110 seconds.
framework_points: Separate listing access from brokerage brand and lead generation.
Trace commission incidence and agent-broker splits.
Compare housing supply with household formation by region.
Distinguish price, revenue growth, dilution and cash generation.
Test insurance pricing with cohort aging and adverse selection.
Distinguish advertising claims from product safety.
Treat private research and management guidance as hypotheses requiring independent checks.
tools_and_charts: Broker commission splits and leverage multiples
Mortgage-rate buckets and household-adjusted housing turnover
State building permits and home-price changes
Zillow EBITDA, free cash flow, EPS and stock compensation
Enrollment by field, Pell share and graduate-loan exposure
Pet cohorts, churn, acquisition cost and premiums
Freshpet refrigerator placements and retail distribution
Insurance statutory closed-claim data and court searches
transcript_cautions: Published July 29 but explicitly recorded June 11, 2026.
Captions variously misspell Safalow, Reffkin, MLS and Homes.com.
The commission split is 80/20 from context; one caption renders 20/20.
Graduate PLUS and Parent PLUS wording is occasionally conflated; claims retain the graduate-financing context.
New Jersey is one of four large Trupanion states, not alone 40-45% of the business.
Closing summaries distinguish Eisman assertions from his reports of Safalow views.

review.summary: Adrian Wooldridge surveys American capitalism from Hamilton through industrialization and financial crises. The main investment lesson is that transformative infrastructure need not reward its investors. Eisman independently challenges the book GFC account, emphasizing leverage rather than housing policy alone. Primary commission evidence supports that emphasis while limiting stronger claims about a single regulatory cause and a panic-free counterfactual. Long-run AI and institutional analogies remain unproven; the claimed Roosevelt inauguration timing is contradicted by a contemporaneous record.

review.title: Streaming Hits Hollywood Hard: Here's Why with Producer Peter Hoffman
review.summary: Eisman argues that streaming maturity and migration from legacy margins weaken entertainment investments, especially Disney and debt-heavy Paramount. Hoffman describes presale financing, production risk and changing independent-film economics, using his own films as examples. Netflix reported the cited EPS slowdown, but its next quarter rebounded sharply. Disney historical margins support a difficult transition without proving permanent stock stagnation. Hoffman prosecution narrative is kept separate from Eisman views and checked against court opinions that preserve the convictions while acknowledging disputes over actual and intended loss.
review.assessment: The quarterly earnings comparison is accurate, but extrapolating it into permanent streaming weakness requires more evidence. Historical margin differences are real but heterogeneous. Private production anecdotes and legal accusations remain distinct from established financial or judicial facts.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 is Eisman solo introduction; SPEAKER_02 is Eisman in the interview. SPEAKER_00 is Peter Hoffman. Brief interviewer questions embedded in SPEAKER_00 runs are inferred from dialogue and not treated as guest endorsements.
framework_points: Separate film quality, theatrical receipts and producer profit.
Presale contracts can transfer demand risk and support financing.
Financial capacity determines tolerance for creative overruns.
Past talent success reduces uncertainty only probabilistically.
Separate current quarterly growth from durable maturity.
Distinguish actual loss, intended loss and elements of fraud.
tools_and_charts: Disney and AMC historical stock charts
Film production budgets and territorial presales
State film tax-credit spending and court outcomes
transcript_cautions: Opening 60-230 seconds contains original substantive Eisman investment commentary, not a repeated montage.
Technical difficulties are disclosed and several phrases disappear around 580-612, 627-664, 964-980, 1107-1126 and 2007-2021.
Speaker labels split Eisman across two IDs and sometimes merge questions into guest answers.
Rambo 2 and Terminator 2 writing credits are conflated around 1410-1460; omitted as incidental film trivia.
Basic Instinct worldwide rank and stock-price comparisons require independent verification.
Hoffman is discussing his own contested prosecution; interviewing him does not make Eisman endorse his legal allegations.

review.title: Why the Iran War Is Stuck & What Comes Next with Steven Cook
review.summary: Cook explains the Iranian regime survival, contested Hormuz navigation and fragmented regional responses. He expects the conflict to remain stuck three to four months after the July 28 recording. Early November maritime reports support that persistence forecast. Eisman endorses the impasse and challenges confidence in Iranian promises. The discussion also covers Saudi transformation, Syrian incentives for accommodation, Lebanese disarmament and Turkish influence. Private motives and military inventories remain largely unverified; a new UAE pipeline reduces crude-export exposure without establishing economic immunity.
review.assessment: The central dated guest forecast has observable support. Most causal claims rest on private contacts or strategic interpretation, so they remain unresolved. Eisman closing endorsements are separately coded. Legal custom is distinguished from constitutional text.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 self-identifies as Steve Eisman; SPEAKER_00 is introduced as Steven Cook. Long SPEAKER_00 runs include interviewer prompts and assent, so attribution follows substantive answer context. One production comparison has medium attribution confidence.
framework_points: Separate tactical destruction from strategic capitulation.
Identify regime survival incentives rather than assuming civilian economic pain changes leadership behavior.
Distinguish material depletion from having no stock remaining.
Analyze regional states separately rather than as one bloc.
Use infrastructure alternatives to assess commodity exposure without assuming complete immunity.
tools_and_charts: Hormuz transit restrictions, blockade and proposed tolls
UAE bypass pipeline and OPEC membership
Regional military coalitions and security agreements
transcript_cautions: Published August 12 but explicitly recorded July 28; forecast horizon starts from recording.
Long gaps and incomplete phrases around 165-179, 305-316, 341-371, 474-491, 832-852, 883-913 and 1340-1374 seconds prevent reconstruction of omitted content.
Speaker diarization repeatedly puts both questions and answers under SPEAKER_00.
Dan Kane denotes Dan Caine; commander names near 601-609 are garbled and not silently resolved.
Ahmed Osada and related variants are inferred to refer to Ahmed al-Sharaa.
Closed Hormuz is colloquial for severely restricted or unsafe navigation, not verified zero vessel traffic.

review.title: The AI Trade, Rising Rates, and Why the Market Is Still Standing | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 73
review.summary: Jason Trennert and Chris Verrone contrast concentration and AI financing risk with improving market breadth, strong growth and bank leadership. They prefer Japan to Europe and increasingly favor healthcare. Eisman emphasizes hidden long-short thematic leverage, hyperscaler capital intensity and dependence on frontier labs. Cash-flow evidence supports the capital-intensity concern; the Alphabet funding number mixes completed issuance and capacity. Japan governance reform is real, but the asserted ROE/PB delisting rule is incorrect. Most market-selection and conditional year-end forecasts remain unresolved or open.

framework_points: Measure shared factor exposure across both sides of a long-short book.
Compare market breadth with headline index concentration.
Separate AI demand growth from shareholder returns and financing costs.
Use financial-sector strength as a signal while recognizing that prices can miss risk.
Distinguish actual listing rules from capital-efficiency reform requests.

400 days likely means trading days; calendar interpretation would be misleading.

review.title: Why Europe Can't Fix Itself & Why It's Getting Worse with Wolfgang Munchau
review.summary: Munchau attributes European stagnation to industrial dependence, weak capital-market integration, regulation and fragmented political authority. Eisman endorses the structural concern and highlights failed fighter cooperation. The discussion distinguishes falling profitability from continued production and wealth from growth, but sometimes turns these into sweeping claims. Primary records show positive European GDP growth, positive but declining BMW profits, lawful routes for AI data use, and a nuclear phase-out completed after the Ukraine invasion. Defense-program failure is supported in part; exclusive capability and political motives remain unverified.
review.assessment: A coherent structural thesis with useful institutional mechanisms, but many absolute statements exceed the inspected evidence. Near-zero potential growth is not the same as no measured GDP growth. Guest policy and cultural explanations are kept distinct from Eisman explicit endorsements.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_00 self-identifies as Steve Eisman and introduces Wolfgang Munchau; SPEAKER_01 supplies the substantive guest responses. Closing solo comments explicitly endorse selected claims.
framework_points: Separate production volumes from economic profits.
Analyze capital-market institutions alongside regulation.
Distinguish spending amounts from capability purchased.
Separate wealth levels, current GDP growth and structural potential growth.
Trace political incentives that block collective action.
tools_and_charts: Automotive profitability and China market share
GDPR data use and retention rules
Draghi investment requirements and EU budget share
Nuclear closure dates, gas imports and coal use
Fuel cost per liter and gallon
transcript_cautions: Missing phrases around 355-369 and 859-879 seconds; do not reconstruct omitted claims.
Google Mind likely refers to DeepMind.
At 2420-2514 the caption says more independent despite surrounding text arguing greater dependence.
Nuclear closure chronology is compressed inaccurately.
700 miles and five-minute charging are not supported by a named vehicle or charge amount.
Potential growth, observed GDP and productivity are different measures throughout the conversation.

review.title: The Juiciest Corporate Scandals with Becca Platsky
review.summary: Eisman and Platsky use fraud cases, media mergers, prediction markets and FIFA to discuss oversight and executive accountability. Platsky corrects her Frank customer counts during the interview. Eisman favors the Paramount combination and challenges weak corporate governance, but makes overbroad claims about the absence of financial-crisis prosecutions. Official records verify the Javice case and contemporaneous merger delay, correct Immelt tenure, and contradict claims of universal executive impunity. Many psychological explanations, private anecdotes and current corruption allegations remain unverified.
review.assessment: Valuable governance questions with uneven factual precision. Preserve explicit corrections and distinguish subjective criticism from legal findings. Guest allegations are not Eisman views by silence. His broad enforcement language conflicts with documented prosecutions, while the narrower accountability of leading Wall Street executives remains unresolved.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_00 repeatedly self-identifies as Eisman and introduces Becca Platsky, who answers as SPEAKER_01. Dialogue clarifies occasional embedded short interjections.
framework_points: Compare public executive statements with filings and actual conduct.
Separate fraud identification from short-sale timing.
Distinguish buyer due diligence failures from perpetrator culpability.
Test board independence and relevant expertise.
Use pressure, opportunity and rationalization as risk questions, not proof of guilt.
Distinguish allegations, charges, convictions and policy preferences.
tools_and_charts: Acquisition customer data and due-diligence verification
transcript_cautions: Platsky explicitly corrects initial Frank figures at 888-903 seconds; retain the revision.
The acquisition is briefly misstated as $177 million; the surrounding account and official record use $175 million.
FAFSA is an application for financial aid, not a standalone loan type.
Captions contain missing passages around 769-792, 1377-1386 and 1527-1542 seconds.
Carr is called an FTC commissioner, but is FCC chairman.
Blazer role and Immelt tenure are misstated.
Discussion of future trial and merger fees predates the September settlement; do not retroactively treat the original procedural claim as false.

review.title: The Art of the Short with Lakshmi Ganapathi: FICO, DoorDash, and AeroVironment
review.summary: Ganapathi presents shorts in FICO, AeroVironment and DoorDash. Eisman remains short FICO, accepts its competitive threat, and finds the delivery credit-risk argument compelling. Primary evidence supports FICO debt-funded repurchases and expanding VantageScore adoption. It contradicts the asserted national BNPL prevalence and the categorical claim that AeroVironment has been priced out of its market. Numerous valuation, legal and product-comparison premises remain unverified; general BNPL statistics do not establish DoorDash customer exposure.
review.assessment: The most substantiated thesis is erosion of FICO exclusivity and increased leverage. DoorDash and AeroVironment theses rely on unverified exposure, customer economics and product equivalence. Eisman explicitly adopts several claims in the close, while his position disclosures remain distinct from price targets.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 identifies himself as Eisman and introduces Lakshmi Ganapathi of Unicus Research; SPEAKER_00 answers as Ganapathi. Interjections are resolved from dialogue.
framework_points: Classify shorts by structural competition, product economics and credit exposure.
Separate poor contractor economics from company profitability.
Look beyond filings to product quality, warranties and management behavior.
Monitor debt-funded buybacks and acquisition accounting.
Require matching denominators before inferring customer dependence.
tools_and_charts: FICO mortgage score prices and market share
Goodwill as a share of assets and impairment charges
BNPL adoption and grocery or delivery use
transcript_cautions: Nova Credit appears as NOAA Credit.
June fiscal third quarter is clarified after confusion between Q2 and Q3.
VantageScore application share, securitization share and overall scoring share are mixed in the dialogue.
European exposure percentage lacks a clear denominator.
At 1961-2016 captions omit transitions between the AeroVironment and DoorDash classifications; closing summary clarifies intended meaning.
Eisman closing statement converts general BNPL population statistics into a claim about DoorDash customers without supporting platform data.

review.title: Inside AI’s Fragile Ecosystem with Ed Zitron
review.summary: Eisman and Ed Zitron examine concentrated AI financing, frontier-model economics, token spending and data-center delivery. Eisman explicitly shares concern about OpenAI and Anthropic counterparty risk and questions growth durability. Many financial assertions rely on private reports or estimates. Later primary filings support Anthropic growth deceleration and NVIDIA reciprocal financing relationships, while clarifying revenue definitions, operating results and the preliminary nature of financing platforms. Catastrophic outcomes remain scenarios rather than established forecasts.
review.assessment: Useful concentration-risk framework, but substantial unverified private-company arithmetic, causal inference and rhetorical overstatement. Anthropic subsequent filings complicate blanket claims of negative unit economics. Guest claims remain separately attributed.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 self-identifies as Steve Eisman and introduces Ed Zitron; SPEAKER_00 answers as Zitron. Short interjections occasionally sit inside the other speaker block; attribution follows dialogue and the explicit closing endorsement.
framework_points: Trace the final cash payer through an investment supply chain.
Distinguish accounting profit, cash generation, committed financing and paid-in cash.
Separate API list prices from provider serving costs.
Stress concentrated counterparties and refinancing dependencies.
Treat a run-rate snapshot separately from recurring revenue and a forecast.
Check whether capex demand survives removal of the largest customers.
tools_and_charts: Company 10-Q receivable concentration and payment terms
Hyperscaler AI versus total cloud revenue
API token prices and enterprise budgets
Data-center gigawatts, square footage and delivery schedules
transcript_cautions: Recorded August 27 according to Eisman, published September 9.
Captions contain missing phrases and repeated watermark text, including around the opening Microsoft arithmetic and 2300 seconds.
900 billion weekly users is a scale error; official OpenAI disclosure says more than 900 million.
The Abilene area of roughly one thousand square feet is implausible and conflicts with developer plans; do not silently repair the units.
Fable model name is uncertain.
Eisman turns retail token value into actual provider cost in one restatement; that distinction is material.
The closing summary explicitly endorses selected risks but does not adopt every guest claim.

review.summary: The wrap revises Eisman's rate threshold, reviews Treasury buybacks, questions Tesla valuation and compares bullish and bearish AI financing interpretations. He preserves a conditional warning that OpenAI failure within a year would cause a major correction, while acknowledging competition could ultimately benefit users and suppliers. The subsequent Fed hike supports his narrow expectation that political threats would not prevent policy action. Treasury buybacks are officially liquidity operations, and the Qualcomm warrant-value inference requires a proper valuation.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman delivers a solo monologue; inserted advertisements and opening montage are excluded.
framework_points: Separate technological success from investor return and timing.
Consider competing explanations received from readers.
Distinguish earnings fundamentals from stock-price behavior.
transcript_cautions: GameStop EPS sentence is incomplete in captions.
Model name and subscriber claims are retained as attributed, not independently verified.

review.summary: Eisman reunites with Vincent Daniel and Porter Collins for a broad discussion of fiscal constraints, gold, AI funding, hedge-fund leverage and selected equities. He explicitly becomes less dismissive of deficit risks while remaining skeptical of imminent crisis. The guests favor gold, Golar and Glass House and explain why concentrated, leveraged shorts can fail despite plausible fundamentals. Their Carvana discussion includes unverified buyer allegations; the filing contradicts the blanket suggestion that Carvana retains no securitization exposure.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman hosts Porter Collins and Vincent Daniel. Clearly introduced turns are named. Overlapping or ambiguous guest turns use Uncertain speaker with qualifications and must be excluded from Eisman accuracy scoring.
framework_points: Ask exactly what a business, security or portfolio mechanism does.
Track financing needs and concentration behind headline growth.
A correct structural thesis can fail through leverage, timing and forced exits.
Separate physical/product usefulness from the returns earned by original capital providers.
Look for a catalyst and a survivable position size when shorting.
tools_and_charts: Loan-sale gains, retained securitization interests and buyer disclosures.
Gross/net hedge-fund exposure, beta and factor stresses.
Gold versus reserves and fiscal cash flows.

review.title: How to Analyze Bank Stocks (Part 1): Leverage, Accounting, and Loan Losses
review.summary: Eisman builds bank analysis from accounting, leverage, capital rules and credit provisioning, then argues current bank credit is stable while private-credit warnings may appear elsewhere first. His leverage arithmetic and core CECL timing are useful. The audit corrects the deposit-multiplier framing, exclusive reliance on risk-weighted regulation, rating-agency delegation, Tarullo title/date and CECL history. Some absolute statements confuse uncertain estimates with necessarily wrong accounting, and conditional identities with real-world causation. Current stability does not settle future private-credit risk.
review.assessment: The strongest material is explicit leverage and loss arithmetic, with assumptions retained. Historical and regulatory simplifications require substantial correction. Neither accounting changes nor later stock appreciation prove management motive or a guaranteed contrarian investment outcome.
review.speaker_map_notes: The sole SPEAKER_00 self-identifies as Steve Eisman and delivers the full tutorial.
framework_points: Read accounting as a test of the business narrative.
Separate return on assets from leverage-driven return on equity.
Stress loss absorption using capital and asset exposure.
Compare risk weights with actual underwriting changes.
Separate loan growth provisions from deterioration provisions.
Watch credit recognition lags and indicators outside bank statements.
tools_and_charts: Hypothetical $1 billion-equity banks at 1,10 and 100 times leverage
Large-bank CET1 table from Q4 2024 to Q2 2026
Major-bank nonaccrual table across Q2 2025, Q1 2026 and Q2 2026
transcript_cautions: Captions repeatedly substitute ROA for ROE: the 100% return at 100 times leverage is ROE, while assumed ROA remains 1%. The surrounding arithmetic resolves the intended identity; no separate false ROA forecast is created.
The compensation sentence says ROE versus ROE; adjacent explanation clearly contrasts ROA with ROE.
Cecil is CECL, chewing up istrueing up, and Tarula is Tarullo.
A JPMorgan stock price appears as $84 million; this is not accepted literally, and the price-date comparison remains unverified.
Chip accounting is called semiconductor profits even though depreciation concerns users of capitalized chips; no issuer is specified.
The four-bank nonaccrual chart itself is absent from the transcript.

claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

claims.claim: An initial deposited dollar is repeatedly lent and redeposited, creating a multiplier of money that powers the economy.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Trace the accounting of loan origination, deposits, settlement and constraints.
claims.reason: Bank lending does create deposits, but the fixed initial-deposit multiplier reverses the operational sequence emphasized by the central bank explanation.

evidence.title: Money creation in the modern economy
evidence.finding: Commercial-bank lending creates matching deposits; banks do not simply multiply a fixed initial quantity of deposited money.

claims.next_check: Trace the accounting of loan origination, deposits, settlement and constraints.

claims.claim: Banking distress signals or coincides with major economic trouble because banks are central to credit creation.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Test bank-stress measures against recession and market timing across episodes.
claims.reason: No calibrated signal, lead time or false-positive rate is provided; universal wording exceeds the evidence.
claims.next_check: Test bank-stress measures against recession and market timing across episodes.

claims.claim: Citi has become a successful bank and attractive investment after years of mediocrity.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare sustained returns with cost of equity and the entry valuation.
claims.reason: Recent operating improvement is verified, but no price target or required-return benchmark establishes investment attractiveness.

evidence.title: Citi Q2 2026 results
evidence.finding: Citi reports 13% RoTCE and 45% net income growth; evidence of improvement does not by itself establish an attractive stock price.

claims.next_check: Compare sustained returns with cost of equity and the entry valuation.

claims.claim: Extending chip useful lives lowers annual depreciation and raises reported earnings without changing the original cash expenditure.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare straight-line expense with equal asset cost and salvage value over different useful lives.
claims.reason: For depreciable base B and life N, annual expense B/N falls as N rises, raising pre-tax income all else equal; total depreciable cost is unchanged.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

proof.derivation: For depreciable base B and life N, annual expense B/N falls as N rises, raising pre-tax income all else equal; total depreciable cost is unchanged.

claims.claim: Chips appear to last longer and a growing secondary market can justify longer depreciation schedules.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect actual reuse, resale prices, performance and service-life disclosures by chip cohort.
claims.reason: No matched chip-cohort or audited residual-value evidence was inspected.
claims.next_check: Inspect actual reuse, resale prices, performance and service-life disclosures by chip cohort.

claims.claim: Companies extended chip lives to smooth earnings before they knew resale usefulness, a warning of subsequent AI difficulties.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect contemporaneous management estimates, internal evidence and timing of life revisions.
claims.reason: Motive cannot be inferred merely from an estimate change; no internal or contemporaneous evidence proves the claim.
claims.next_check: Inspect contemporaneous management estimates, internal evidence and timing of life revisions.

claims.claim: Energy constraints, local opposition and Chinese price competition are now material headwinds to AI companies.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Quantify delayed capacity, power costs, customer pricing and margin impact.
claims.reason: No company-specific magnitude or causal earnings bridge was inspected.
claims.next_check: Quantify delayed capacity, power costs, customer pricing and margin impact.

claims.claim: The real reasons for accounting adjustments are almost always hidden, so ignoring them is dangerous.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Define a sample of adjustments and compare disclosed reasons with established evidence.
claims.reason: The almost-always frequency assertion has no supporting sample; skepticism is a process preference.
claims.next_check: Define a sample of adjustments and compare disclosed reasons with established evidence.

claims.claim: Regulatory limits constrain bank leverage and deposit insurance emerged after Depression-era runs to restore confidence.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect historical statutes and current capital/deposit insurance framework.
claims.reason: Current constraints are documented, but the historical claim that regulation began only then is too broad and not independently verified.

evidence.title: Departing thoughts on regulation
evidence.finding: Tarullo describes the previous and continuing US use of complementary leverage and risk-weighted requirements, with higher post-crisis standards.

claims.next_check: Inspect historical statutes and current capital/deposit insurance framework.

claims.claim: Ultimate loan losses are unknown at origination, so reported bank profit depends on forward-looking loss estimates.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect allowance accounting and subsequent realized losses.
claims.reason: CECL requires estimates using available history, conditions and forecasts, with actual outcomes arriving later.

evidence.title: Interagency CECL FAQs
evidence.finding: CECL replaces incurred/probable loss recognition with expected contractual-life losses using historical, current and forecast information. Origination allowances and reporting-date updates apply; calendar-year SEC filers initially adopted in 2020.

claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

claims.claim: Because provisions are estimates, bank net income is necessarily wrong in every reporting period.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Distinguish valid GAAP estimates, expected values and later realized outcomes.
claims.reason: An estimate can coincide with realization; uncertainty does not logically imply every reported amount is false. A probabilistic expectation can also be correct while an outcome differs.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

proof.derivation: An estimate can coincide with realization; uncertainty does not logically imply every reported amount is false. A probabilistic expectation can also be correct while an outcome differs.

claims.claim: With $1 billion equity and $1 billion assets, simple assets/equity leverage is 1 times; deposits would be debt owed to customers.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Apply assets=liabilities+equity and the stated leverage definition.
claims.qualifications: Hypotheticals hold after-funding-cost ROA fixed. They do not prove real borrowing leaves ROA unchanged.
claims.reason: With zero liabilities, assets equal equity and A/E = 1; a repayable deposit is a liability under the assumed contract.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

proof.derivation: With zero liabilities, assets equal equity and A/E = 1; a repayable deposit is a liability under the assumed contract.

claims.claim: ROA is net income divided by assets and includes the effect of estimated credit losses, making it a useful operating-profitability comparison.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compute consistent annualized net income over average assets and compare risk/mix.
claims.reason: The ratio is defined by NI/A and includes provision expense through net income. Average balances and consistent annualization are needed for real comparisons.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

proof.derivation: The ratio is defined by NI/A and includes provision expense through net income. Average balances and consistent annualization are needed for real comparisons.

claims.claim: A 1% ROA is respectable for a bank; JPMorgan exceeds it while Citi has remained below it for decades.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare long-run annualized ROA series with consistent denominators.
claims.reason: The broad decades claim and universal quality benchmark were not checked.
claims.next_check: Compare long-run annualized ROA series with consistent denominators.

claims.claim: ROE equals ROA multiplied by assets/equity leverage when numerators and average-balance conventions match.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Multiply NI/A by A/E with compatible period and equity definitions.
claims.qualifications: Hypotheticals hold after-funding-cost ROA fixed. They do not prove real borrowing leaves ROA unchanged.
claims.reason: The assets denominator cancels: (NI/A)*(A/E)=NI/E. It is an identity rather than proof that borrowing itself raises net income.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

proof.derivation: The assets denominator cancels: (NI/A)*(A/E)=NI/E. It is an identity rather than proof that borrowing itself raises net income.

claims.claim: Bank management compensation focuses on net income and ROE, creating incentives to increase leverage rather than asset productivity.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect compensation contracts and changes in risk-adjusted incentives across banks.
claims.reason: No representative proxy-statement sample or causal test was inspected.
claims.next_check: Inspect compensation contracts and changes in risk-adjusted incentives across banks.

claims.claim: At fixed 1% ROA, $1 billion equity supports 1%,10% or 100% ROE at 1, 10 or 100 times leverage respectively.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Hold after-funding-cost ROA fixed and compute net income/equity.
claims.qualifications: Hypotheticals hold after-funding-cost ROA fixed. They do not prove real borrowing leaves ROA unchanged.
claims.reason: Assets of $1, $10 and $100 billion produce $10 million, $100 million and $1 billion income; dividing by $1 billion equity gives 1%,10%,100%. This is explicitly a hypothetical, not a permissible bank balance sheet.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

proof.derivation: Assets of $1, $10 and $100 billion produce $10 million, $100 million and $1 billion income; dividing by $1 billion equity gives 1%,10%,100%. This is explicitly a hypothetical, not a permissible bank balance sheet.

claims.claim: At 100 times leverage, a 1% net loss on $100 billion assets wipes out the bank's initial $1 billion equity.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Subtract a $1 billion loss from $1 billion equity, with no offsetting earnings or issuance.
claims.qualifications: Hypotheticals hold after-funding-cost ROA fixed. They do not prove real borrowing leaves ROA unchanged.
claims.reason: A100 billion*(-1%)=-1 billion, so remaining equity is zero under the stated conditions.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

proof.derivation: A100 billion*(-1%)=-1 billion, so remaining equity is zero under the stated conditions.

claims.claim: Only regulators can restrain managers' overwhelming incentive to increase leverage.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Examine market funding, shareholder governance and internal risk limits as additional constraints.
claims.reason: The exclusive only-regulators assertion is not supported; the interview's model omits other constraints.
claims.next_check: Examine market funding, shareholder governance and internal risk limits as additional constraints.

claims.claim: Severely limiting bank leverage would require very high loan rates to preserve returns and could halt lending.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Model required returns, funding costs, competition and nonbank substitution under different equity shares.
claims.reason: The thought experiment fixes ROA rather than endogenizing lower funding risk/cost; it does not prove economy-wide lending cessation.
claims.next_check: Model required returns, funding costs, competition and nonbank substitution under different equity shares.

claims.claim: For most nonbank businesses, 1% ROA implies likely failure without repeated equity injections.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Test cash generation, asset intensity and capital needs rather than ROA alone.
claims.reason: A profitable steady-state business can earn positive 1% ROA, fund replacement depreciation from operating cash and require no new equity. Low accounting ROA is not a sufficient insolvency condition.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

proof.derivation: A profitable steady-state business can earn positive 1% ROA, fund replacement depreciation from operating cash and require no new equity. Low accounting ROA is not a sufficient insolvency condition.

claims.claim: Hyperscaler valuations face dilution from continued data-center capital requirements and competition from cheaper Chinese alternatives.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect financing sources, share counts, capex needs and unit economics.
claims.reason: Capex does not necessarily require equity issuance, and no quantified dilution or pricing scenario is specified.
claims.next_check: Inspect financing sources, share counts, capex needs and unit economics.

claims.claim: Large-bank leverage fell by more than half after the crisis; nearly every major bank had been about 40 times levered beforehand.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare consistent assets/common-equity measures across a defined large-bank sample.
claims.reason: The broad deleveraging direction is documented, but JPMorgan's 2007 simple ratio was 12.68 times, illustrating how the 40 times generalization and changing denominators can mislead.

evidence.title: JPMorgan 2007 annual report
evidence.finding: 2007 assets $1,562,147 million and common equity $123,221 million imply 12.68 times simple leverage, far below 40 times.

evidence.title: Departing thoughts on regulation
evidence.finding: Tarullo describes the previous and continuing US use of complementary leverage and risk-weighted requirements, with higher post-crisis standards.

claims.next_check: Compare consistent assets/common-equity measures across a defined large-bank sample.

claims.claim: Regulation is loosening, but banks will never return to pre-crisis extreme leverage.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Track finalized requirements and consistent actual leverage over a defined horizon.
claims.reason: Never has no finite test horizon; current loosening does not establish an enduring leverage ceiling.
claims.next_check: Track finalized requirements and consistent actual leverage over a defined horizon.

claims.claim: Risk-weighted assets distinguish portfolios with equal total assets but different regulatory risk; weighted assets can be above or below accounting assets.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Apply RWA=sum(exposure*weight)with specified risk weights.
claims.reason: Equal asset totals yield different RWA when weights differ; average weights over 100% produce RWA above assets and under 100% produce less. Actual rules include off-balance-sheet and other adjustments.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

proof.derivation: Equal asset totals yield different RWA when weights differ; average weights over 100% produce RWA above assets and under 100% produce less. Actual rules include off-balance-sheet and other adjustments.

claims.claim: A capital ratio is the inverse of leverage when both use exactly the same equity and asset definitions.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Invert A/E or RWA/Ewith nonzero positive values.
claims.reason: 1/(A/E)=E/A. Regulatory capital definitions cannot be interchanged with tangible book without reconciliation.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

proof.derivation: 1/(A/E)=E/A. Regulatory capital definitions cannot be interchanged with tangible book without reconciliation.

claims.claim: Regulators focus only on risk-weighted capital ratios, and assigning risk weights is mostly delegated to credit-rating agencies.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect US standardized, internal-model and leverage rules and their historical evolution.
claims.reason: US leverage requirements coexist with RWA requirements; post-Dodd-Frank rules removed reliance on external ratings. The current categorical description is wrong even though ratings mattered historically.

evidence.title: Departing thoughts on regulation
evidence.finding: Tarullo describes the previous and continuing US use of complementary leverage and risk-weighted requirements, with higher post-crisis standards.

evidence.title: 2013 regulatory capital rule
evidence.finding: Regulation Q removed references to and reliance on external credit ratings, consistent with Dodd-Frank 939A.

claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

claims.claim: Low risk weights can permit accounting leverage to rise without proportionately worsening a risk-weighted capital ratio.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Add assets with sufficiently low weights while holding equity and other exposures fixed.
claims.reason: Adding zero-weight assets leaves RWA/Eunchanged while A/E rises; low positive weights produce a smaller RWA increase. Independent leverage limits can bind.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

proof.derivation: Adding zero-weight assets leaves RWA/Eunchanged while A/E rises; low positive weights produce a smaller RWA increase. Independent leverage limits can bind.

claims.claim: Historical loss experience can understate future risk when underwriting weakens, letting losses emerge after apparently safe balance-sheet expansion.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare loan-vintage underwriting and subsequent loss performance, controlling for macro conditions.
claims.reason: A coherent mechanism, but no inspected vintage dataset quantifies it in this episode.
claims.next_check: Compare loan-vintage underwriting and subsequent loss performance, controlling for macro conditions.

claims.claim: From 1997 to 2007 European bank leverage rose from 11 to 33 times and ROE tripled, showing unchanged ROA rather than better management.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect defined European-bank sample, accounting netting and all three ratio series.
claims.reason: No underlying time series or sample is supplied. The identity is valid if premises hold, but the historical premises are not verified.
claims.next_check: Inspect defined European-bank sample, accounting netting and all three ratio series.

claims.claim: Rising leverage and pay made bank executives overconfident and resistant to warnings before the crisis.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect contemporaneous decisions, pay arrangements and evidence distinguishing beliefs from incentives.
claims.reason: The imagined CEO response is illustrative psychology, not direct evidence of a universal motive.
claims.next_check: Inspect contemporaneous decisions, pay arrangements and evidence distinguishing beliefs from incentives.

claims.claim: CET1 is roughly tangible common equity adjusted under regulation divided by risk-weighted assets.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconcile GAAP common equity, regulatory deductions/adjustments and RWA.
claims.reason: The broad structure is useful, but calling all adjustments small can be misleading; the inspected filing distinguishes regulatory and accounting amounts.

evidence.title: JPMorgan Q2 2026 Form 10-Q
evidence.finding: Nonaccrual disclosures distinguish consumer, wholesale, retained, held-for-sale and fair-value loans; some cash-basis interest is recognized, and collateralized loans may lack allowances. Tier 1 leverage and supplementary leverage requirements remain distinct from RWA.

claims.next_check: Reconcile GAAP common equity, regulatory deductions/adjustments and RWA.

claims.claim: Daniel Tarullo first held the vice-chair-for-supervision office until April 2016 and forced major post-crisis deleveraging.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect official title, tenure and policy record.
claims.reason: Tarullo chaired the supervision committee and left in April 2017, not April 2016. His major supervisory influence does not make the formal title and date correct.

evidence.finding: Tarullo describes the previous and continuing US use of complementary leverage and risk-weighted requirements, with higher post-crisis standards.

claims.claim: Stress tests estimate capital depletion under severe scenarios and constrain banks' buffers, dividends and repurchases.

claims.reason: Tarullo's primary account describes stress testing added to the capital framework; capital resilience and distributions are linked, though it is not the only leverage constraint.

evidence.title: Departing thoughts on regulation
evidence.finding: Tarullo describes the previous and continuing US use of complementary leverage and risk-weighted requirements, with higher post-crisis standards.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Specify systemic spillovers and social-risk objectives for calibration.
claims.reason: A policy rationale rather than a numerical causal forecast; regional failures can still generate contagion.
claims.next_check: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconcile consistent capital ratios, buybacks, earnings and RWA changes with stress-buffer revisions.

claims.test: Inspect allowance roll-forwards and forecast assumptions rather than expense alone.

claims.reason: The previous model used incurred/probable loss recognition, not a general mandated two-to-three-year reserve horizon.

claims.reason: Historical figures and causal attribution were not reconstructed; prices alone do not identify allowance adequacy.
claims.next_check: Verify share-price adjustments, shares outstanding, capital actions and loss chronology.

claims.reason: Interagency guidance confirms an origination allowance for expected losses over contractual life using historical/current/forecast information; this is credit loss, not every future business cost.

evidence.finding: CECL replaces incurred/probable loss recognition with expected contractual-life losses using historical, current and forecast information. Origination allowances and reporting-date updates apply; calendar-year SEC filers initially adopted in 2020.

review.summary: Eisman acknowledges his earlier 4.5% Treasury threshold was wrong, then discusses a 5% threshold, FICO competition and AI leadership's safety rhetoric. He sees a regulatory-moat motive but offers no evidence proving intent. His unqualified tax-deferral suggestion via shorting appreciated shares is contradicted by constructive-sale rules and is partly corrected in the following week. Defensive portfolio suggestions and insurance pricing observations are mechanisms, not verified excess-return forecasts.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman delivers a solo monologue; inserted advertisements and opening montage are excluded.
framework_points: Admit failed thresholds rather than erase them.
Investigate pricing power and regulatory risk.
Treat safe-sector allocation separately from stock selection.
transcript_cautions: Regulatory allegations and AI motive claims are Eisman's own theories, not established facts.
The following week partially corrects this episode's tax omission.

evidence.title: Publication 550 (2025): Constructive Sales
evidence.finding: Shorting the same appreciated stock generally creates a taxable constructive sale. The closed-transaction exception requires close by 30 days after tax-year-end, 60 days continued ownership and no reduction of risk during those 60 days.

review.transcript_hash_basis: Normalized source metadata records the underlying full transcript hash. All normalized segments were read.
review.summary: A September 2 recorded conversation with George Noble, published September 21, connects AI funding risk, heavy debt issuance, Japanese capital flows and narrative-driven valuations. Eisman stresses borrower profitability and customer concentration; Noble supplies the strongest AI-collapse and Tesla/SpaceX short claims. The review preserves Eisman's explicit statement that Noble may be more bearish than he is.
review.assessment: Empirical premises and forecasts are assessed separately. Guest assertions are not Eisman forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal attribution remain unresolved.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman hosts George Noble. SPEAKER_00 generally denotes Eisman and SPEAKER_01 Noble, but speaker markers contain obvious turn-boundary errors. Guest short targets remain guest claims; the host's closing summary is not a wholesale endorsement.
framework_points: Trace supplier revenue to end-user economics and financing sources.
Circular financing is a warning signal, not automatic default.
Account for macro factors and currency exposure in stock selection.
Separate long-run investment value from daily price moves and technology usefulness.
Distinguish receivables concentration from revenue concentration.
tools_and_charts: Debt-to-GDP versus yield chart is described but not reconstructed.
Tesla Q3 financial summary and operating/FCF distinctions.
FIMA repo mechanics compared with the guest's swap-line account.
transcript_cautions: All 1,201 normalized transcript segments were read in full.
Noble explicitly dates the recording September 2, 2026 at about 1938 seconds; publication is September 21.
Publisher speaker markers sometimes assign both sides of an exchange to one label. Attribution follows question-and-answer context; short confirmations are not separate predictions.
Eisman's 40-basis-point AI rate effect is explicitly an invented illustrative number.
Tesla PDF financial table was inspected via primary-source search extraction; PDF screenshot output was not usable, and no claim of a complete PDF read is made.
No verified short-entry records or total trading returns were available.
review.materiality_note: Major investment theses are distinguished from supporting factual premises. No overall accuracy percentage is appropriate.

review.title: How to Analyze Banks (Part 2): Deposits, Valuations, and Silicon Valley
review.summary: Eisman explains deposit franchises, SVB's duration and funding failure, bank income statements and tangible-book valuation. He favors large banks but avoids adding them at rich valuations and with AI financing exposure. The central SVB mechanism and conditional arithmetic are useful. Material errors concern securities accounting, liquidity-rule maturity restrictions, SVB closure timing and OZK consumer lending. Current credit data is broadly stable, but not uniformly benign. Claims of zero systemic risk and inevitable consolidation are substantially less established.
review.assessment: A useful bank-analysis framework with several consequential factual and accounting simplifications. Distinguish book, regulatory and economic capital; liquidity from duration; and reported returns from stock-valuation judgments. The solo presentation means all extracted substantive views are Eisman's.
review.speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_00 self-identifies as Steve Eisman at the beginning and delivers the entire solo tutorial.
framework_points: Analyze deposit composition and correlation, not merely total balances.
Separate funding cost, asset duration and credit risk.
Decompose pre-provision earnings from credit provisions.
Compare tangible-book multiples with sustainable returns and cost of equity.
Treat good valuation logic as insufficient to predict merger execution.
Assess indirect portfolio exposure through investment-banking clients.
tools_and_charts: Net interest margin and earning assets
SVB deposits, securities marks and VC funding chronology
Q2 2026 large-bank ROTCE and price/tangible-book table
transcript_cautions: SVB and SIVB refer to bank and holding-company ticker; their asset totals and capital measures differ.
Captions name Basel IV endgame; the official proposal is Basel III endgame.
The spoken JPMorgan quarter and $16.9 billion figure do not match the inspected Q1 release; charts are not included in the text.
Bank of the Ozarks is the former name of Bank OZK; no-consumer lending is a substantive false claim, not a harmless name correction.
The spoken flat/nonaccrual generalization does not include a bank-by-bank data table in the transcript.

claims.claim: Stable deposits can let a bank hold performing bonds to maturity, making duration losses an income problem instead of a forced-sale crisis.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.deductive_proof: Assume contractual bond payments are made, deposits remain available through maturity, and all other cash obligations can be met. With no required sale, the bank collects contractual principal and coupons rather than selling at the lower market price. However, present value still falls when the discount rate rises, and stable deposits alone do not prove the other liquidity or solvency assumptions. Thus the conditional funding insight is valid but incomplete as a general solvency claim.

proof.derivation: Assume contractual bond payments are made, deposits remain available through maturity, and all other cash obligations can be met. With no required sale, the bank collects contractual principal and coupons rather than selling at the lower market price. However, present value still falls when the discount rate rises, and stable deposits alone do not prove the other liquidity or solvency assumptions. Thus the conditional funding insight is valid but incomplete as a general solvency claim.

claims.claim: Massive deposit withdrawals are necessary for duration exposure to become a solvency problem.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

review.summary: The episode warns that higher rates and complex AI financing may expose balance-sheet risks. Eisman distinguishes visible Nvidia vendor financing from Meta's unconsolidated venture, but his interpretation of EY's audit work contradicts the procedures he reads aloud. He also considers agentic commerce, streaming competition and a qualified correction to his earlier short-against-the-box discussion. The rate threshold and market-correction timing are not tightly defined enough for a clean forecast score.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman delivers a solo monologue; inserted advertisements and opening montage are excluded.
framework_points: Trace legal recourse and off-balance-sheet support commitments.
Separate vendor financing from economic end-demand.
Revisit a prior claim when listeners identify a technical problem.
transcript_cautions: The audit interpretation conflicts with the audit procedures read earlier in the same episode.
SIV and VIE terminology is garbled in captions, but the referenced structures are clear.

review.summary: Cisco IR chief Sam Badri explains accelerating networking demand, a campus refresh cycle and expected fiscal-2027 growth. Eisman accepts the reality of AI-related sales while concentrating on lab dependence and price competition. Badri presents advanced workflows as a source of future token growth and a reason frontier models can retain a premium. Verified financial disclosures support current growth and NVIDIA receivables concentration, but they do not settle final-user returns, long-run supplier profitability or the competitive outcome.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman interviews Cisco investor-relations chief Sam Badri. Guest operational assertions and forecasts are kept separate from Eisman's questions and explicit final synthesis.
framework_points: Separate genuine supplier revenue from durable final-user economics.
Distinguish customer mix effects from vendor competitive performance.
Map premium and inexpensive models to the tasks that require them.
Track token volume alongside price, cost, retention and cash collection.
tools_and_charts: Cisco revenue, guidance, AI orders and campus refresh indicators.
NVIDIA receivables and direct versus indirect customer disclosures.
Quality-adjusted token prices and workflow productivity comparisons.
Power interconnection queues, rack density and resource accounting boundaries.
transcript_cautions: Badri represents Cisco and discusses company guidance; these are not independent realized forecasts.
His investor-conversation sample does not establish the claimed 90% beginner share.
NVIDIA 70% refers to receivables, not revenue.
The concluding summary adopts conditional durability, not every guest numerical or technical assertion.

review.title: Inside the Disruptive New World of Prediction Markets with Edwin Dorsey
review.summary: Dorsey argues prediction exchanges improve information, distribution and hedging, threaten sportsbooks, and may eventually replace parts of insurance. Eisman shifts from skepticism to explicit enthusiasm. Contract mechanics and Robinhood distribution are documented, but superior forecasting and low insider-trading risk remain unproven. Kalshi-only-US eligibility and Left conviction-count claims are wrong. The discussion also understates the deception theory of Left's prosecution and blurs a soldier's charges with a completed penalty. Insurance disruption has a genuine long horizon and acknowledged basis risk.
review.assessment: Strong conceptual distinction between trading an event and a correlated proxy, but numerous legal, access, taxation and competitive assertions need qualification. DraftKings has its own expanding prediction business, complicating the extinction analogy. Eisman's final endorsement is recorded separately from guest claims.
review.speaker_map_notes: Introduction and dialogue map SPEAKER_00 to Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_01 to Edwin Dorsey. Short interviewer interjections are sometimes embedded in guest segments, but main claims are attributable. Closing name Adam is a caption error.
framework_points: Compare forecasts against realistic alternatives rather than perfection.
Separate vote share from probability of victory.
Specify resolution criteria before assessing event contracts.
Distinguish direct event hedges from asset proxies and geographic basis risk.
Do not equate enforcement anecdotes with total insider incidence.
tools_and_charts: Binary yes/no contract prices and $1 payouts
Courtroom stock charts and split adjustment
transcript_cautions: Kalshi is repeatedly rendered Calci, CalShe or Cauchy; names normalized.
Andrew Left is repeatedly rendered Leff or Loft; Cronos rendered Kronos.
A gap at about 7:42-8:06 interrupts the election example and another at 31:11-31:40 interrupts trial discussion.
The caption near 34:58 says a good newsletter attracts no readers; context suggests a missing negation, so it is not extracted literally.
Dorsey corrects Eisman: he sold The Bear Cave and did not write the recent Walter-group article.
Publication date is known; references to yesterday do not independently establish recording date.

review.summary: Eisman links FICO's loss of exclusivity to regulator antagonism and examines software buyouts financed in a low-rate era. His residual-equity example is arithmetically sound if enterprise value halves and debt is unchanged, but it does not establish that public equity drawdowns proxy private enterprise values. The precise refinancing cash demand is not a mathematical necessity. He also distinguishes oil supply shocks from the Fed's broader inflation role and describes the vintage-delinquency work behind his crisis trade.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman delivers a solo monologue; inserted advertisements and opening montage are excluded.
framework_points: Model residual equity and refinancing explicitly.
Distinguish operating performance from multiples.
Use vintage credit data rather than stories to identify deterioration.
tools_and_charts: Five software buyout purchase prices and debt ratios
transcript_cautions: Captions render Anaplan, Thoma Bravo, Permira and Galcap inconsistently; entity names were normalized only when context is clear.
The hypothetical equity arithmetic does not establish the assumptions for the actual named deals.
