metadata.title: 5% Rates, Bessent's Failed Gamble & What Comes Next w/ Krishna Guha | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 78

review.summary: Krishna Guha explains the new Fed regime, the September hike, rising long yields and the distinction between firm forward commitments and useful policy communication. He links AI investment and fiscal borrowing to rates while separating AI capex from housing sensitivity. Eisman repeats his QE skepticism and concludes Treasury buybacks failed. The official record supports the policy shifts and buyback scale, while the strongest causal claims about QE, credibility and yield suppression require counterfactual analysis.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman interviews Krishna Guha. Guha supplies most policy analysis; Eisman explicitly states QE skepticism, an exploratory liquidity-regulation theory and the closing buyback-failure judgment.
framework_points: Separate short policy rates, neutral rates and long-term risk premia.
Separate stock and flow, liquidity support and yield control.
Different sectors have different financing sensitivities.
Distinguish conditional guidance from promises.
tools_and_charts: FOMC decisions, speeches and balance-sheet task-force output.
Ten-year yields, issuance by maturity, term-premium estimates and buyback results.
PCE, labor-market data, AI capex and wealth-sensitive consumption.
transcript_cautions: Auto-captions repeatedly render Warsh as Walsh and misspell names.
The phrase 40 trillion deficit refers in context to a debt stock or Treasury-market scale, not an annual deficit; do not score it as a separate thesis.
Guha's expectations are not automatically Eisman forecasts.
Closing recap merges repetitions; advertisements excluded.

review.title: The AI Bull Case with Joseph Carlson
review.summary: Carlson argues AI utility and incumbent distribution support a bullish hyperscaler case, especially Meta, while distinguishing software with embedded workflows from tax and travel intermediaries. Eisman accepts utility but questions model moats and capital returns. Meta results support growth and adoption, not proof of full AI investment payback. Apple documents contradict a necessary customer-data transfer to Google. Most company disruption theses remain unverified; the six-month agentic-commerce forecast has an unfinished horizon.
review.assessment: The episode usefully separates useful technology from investor returns and differentiates company exposure. Strong strategic assertions about moats, software disruption, product superiority and Apple dependence need more evidence. Eisman does not adopt every guest thesis merely by summarizing it.
review.speaker_map_notes: Self-introduction and direct dialogue map SPEAKER_01 to Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_00 to Joseph Carlson. Closing paraphrases of Carlson are not independently attributed as Eisman forecasts.
framework_points: Separate product usefulness from economic rent and capital returns.
Distinguish consumer model switching from enterprise workflow switching.
Compare infrastructure-only suppliers with vertically integrated distribution owners.
Assess software exposure by workflow depth and physical fulfillment.
Distinguish an exposure thesis from a price target.
tools_and_charts: Forward price/earnings comparisons for Meta and Google
Hyperscaler capital spending and supplier value capture
Software stock compensation and operating discipline
Personal coding, tax-document and shopping workflows
transcript_cautions: The conversation refers to Meta Connect as yesterday; recording date is not independently established by publication metadata.
Private Apple-Google payments and hypothetical future license pricing must not be treated as audited terms.
The latest model in the financial-document example is unnamed.
Closing summary omits context around a promotional transition; it remains explicitly a summary of guest views.
Personal anecdotes and counterfactual programmer superiority are not controlled product tests.

review.summary: Gary Marcus separates demonstrated agent-security failures from speculative extinction narratives. Eisman adopts his skepticism about near-term AGI and advances a central hypothesis that frontier labs are using fear to protect a duopoly against open-weight competition. Concrete incident reports support the security-control critique; they do not establish the claimed commercial conspiracy or extinction probabilities. Marcus favors liability, independent review and targeted restrictions, while acknowledging uncertainty about safer architectures.

review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman interviews Gary Marcus. Short acknowledgments are not wholesale endorsement; the closing monologue explicitly adopts selected conclusions.
framework_points: Distinguish demonstrated mechanisms from alarming analogies.
Assess expected loss using probability and severity together.
Examine whether public-interest narratives also serve financing and competitive incentives.
Treat security as layered controls, not a verbal instruction.
tools_and_charts: Incident postmortems, sandbox and monitoring logs.
Capability, reliability and matched-cost model benchmarks.

Marcus's forecasts and policy proposals remain attributed to Marcus; Eisman's explicit concluding adoption is separately captured.

review.title: How the Owner of the LA Dodgers Built an Empire on Policyholder Money
review.summary: Gober and Morgenson examine Walter-group affiliate reporting, state oversight, A-CAP proceedings, guaranty protection and mutual-insurer preferences. Eisman adopts the regulatory-failure and asset-sale concerns. Primary records confirm material affiliate reclassification and negative rating outlooks, but not a rating downgrade or a blanket breach of a universal affiliate cap. Official biography contradicts the claim of no insurance background. Several stronger allegations remain unverified, and the discussion must not collapse investigations, rehabilitation petitions and bankruptcy into the same event.
review.assessment: Material reporting failure is documented, but legal conclusions, specific financing paths and broad insolvency claims need further evidence. The episode has valuable questions about related parties and liability protection, alongside overstatements about regulatory background, rating actions and guaranty recovery mechanics.
review.speaker_map_notes: Introduction and named handoffs map SPEAKER_02 to Eisman, SPEAKER_01 to Tom Gober and SPEAKER_00 to Gretchen Morgenson. The spelling Morgensen in captions is normalized. Several interviewer questions are appended to guest segments; main expositions are clear.
framework_points: Trace affiliated exposure through legal entities instead of accepting labels.
Compare invested-asset percentages with surplus percentages without confusing denominators.
Separate statutory accounting capital from economic risk and risk-adjusted capital.
Distinguish ratings from outlooks, investigations from guilt, and rehabilitation from liquidation.
Examine protection transfer in pension buyouts and present-value guaranty limits.
tools_and_charts: Statutory annual statements and affiliate schedules
Affiliated investments as percentage of assets and surplus
State examiner staffing and tax revenue
transcript_cautions: Metadata audience is everyone despite assignment grouping with subscriber episodes.
Captions alternate 3% to 40% and later 3% to 10%; later statement conflicts with the repeated restatement account and must not be silently selected as fact.
Receiver petition versus entered order is blurred in the dialogue, then described as bankruptcy in Eisman's closing summary.
Captions $180 appears to mean a 180-degree contrast, not a monetary claim.
The commentator identifies Delaware Life as formerly Guggenheim Life; legal entity histories require separate verification and are not silently merged.

review.summary: Danny Moses and Eisman examine higher rates, AI financing concentration, private-market incentives and fiscal risk. Moses favors diversified cash-generating technology on pullbacks but avoids weak neocloud balance sheets. Eisman stresses concentration and a long difficult period for leveraged PE. Both distinguish technological progress from investable returns. Moses's QE certainty and reserve concerns remain his own views, not Eisman predictions; Eisman emphasizes the lack of a comparable Treasury substitute.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Danny Moses supplies most cycle, private-credit and gold/QE claims. Eisman is separated where he adds the higher-for-longer, housing and concentration arguments.
framework_points: Compare financing structures and incentives across cycles.

review.title: AI, FICO & the Next Big Risks in Financial Services
review.summary: Eisman and Collins survey FICO competition, AI risks to insurance and idle cash, payment networks, bank mergers, software refinancing, rates, life insurers and crypto regulation. Eisman explicitly endorses several concerns in his closing summary. FHFA verifies pricing parity; Senate records verify CLARITY's procedural defeat. The claim that no direct-lending index exists is incorrect. Eisman's leveraged-equity arithmetic is valid under fixed-debt assumptions, while the broad software markdown premise is unverified and the refinancing forecast is still ahead.
review.assessment: The episode has many separable theses, with conditional AI risks and refinancing arithmetic distinct from observed outcomes. Recording date is September 30, three weeks before publication. Permanently dead legislation is not established by one failed vote.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve introduces Dwight Collins. SPEAKER_01 usually Eisman and SPEAKER_00 Collins; short questions and interruptions are frequently mislabeled. Closing monologue explicitly converts selected themes into Eisman endorsements, while KKR and Rowan views remain reported guest material.
framework_points: Distinguish current earnings from future franchise erosion.
Examine granular idle balances rather than assume all low-cost deposits migrate.
Separate payment interfaces from network rails.
Separate operating earnings, enterprise multiples, debt and residual equity.
Use regulatory incentives and merger economics rather than management narrative alone.
tools_and_charts: Tangible-book dilution and merger integration economics
Yield curve, SOFR spreads and asset-liability mismatch
Senate cloture vote and stablecoin legislation
transcript_cautions: Recording date explicitly September 30; publication October 21 should not be substituted for the observation date.
VantageScore comparison says 814 FICO in an 800 FICO example; likely intended VantageScore but not silently treated as verified numerical equivalence.
Captions render LLPA as LOPA and SVB as Civ B.
The guest questions whether a Stripe bid for PayPal existed; retain that correction.
Some short turns and the 24:08 phrase have uncertain speaker markers; substance of Eisman's later software example is clear.

Eisman argues that cash-intensive AI expansion makes neocloud financing a market bottleneck, critiques a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger, and turns increasingly bearish on housing wealth creation. review.summary: Benn Steil discusses persistent inflation, Fed communication, Treasury financing, reserve currencies and French fiscal vulnerability. Eisman questions repeated debt-crisis forecasts and emphasizes structural Treasury demand. The distinction between liquidity management and QE matters, while exclusive-Treasury claims are overstated. Steil's October-hike concern did not become the actual policy outcome. The latter half explores monetary history and explicitly counterfactual Wallace-era geopolitics, kept separate from contemporary forecasts.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Benn Steil answers macroeconomic and historical questions; Eisman asks and occasionally endorses. Distinct guest claims are not counted as Eisman forecasts.
framework_points: Compare currencies with feasible alternatives rather than in isolation.
Separate timing uncertainty from structural fiscal arithmetic.
Use historical institutions to explain reserve-currency persistence.
tools_and_charts: Treasury buybacks relative to debt stock
Archival and declassified sources discussed by Steil
transcript_cautions: Recording date is explicitly October 14, earlier than release.
Speakers repeatedly say deficit when they mean the roughly $40 trillion debt stock.
Historical Manchuria invasion date is transcribed as 1944 and would require checking before quotation; not used to grade a modern forecast.

review.title: The Energy Crisis, World War III & the Future of Power with Doomberg
review.summary: Doomberg explains diesel scarcity through refinery and trade bottlenecks, advances a broad World War III and Western-retrenchment thesis, and favors gas midstream infrastructure over refiners. Eisman challenges crude pricing, Russian military performance and Chinese leadership, while predicting no Trump strategic retreat. Primary energy data supports product-market stress but qualifies several quantities and price claims. Russia's claimed rare-earth production rank is contradicted by USGS. Most military-intent and capability assertions lack inspected primary corroboration; they remain guest claims, not Eisman endorsements.
review.assessment: Useful product-versus-crude distinction is mixed with highly confident geopolitical explanations. Quantitative errors, unverified causal assertions and genuine future horizons are kept separate. No overall episode accuracy percentage is appropriate.
review.speaker_map_notes: Introductions establish SPEAKER_01 as Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_00 as the anonymous Doomberg representative. Speaker-marker mistakes occur in short interjections. The long technical and geopolitical answers belong to Doomberg; Eisman's questions and explicit disagreements are retained.
framework_points: Analyze the specific refined product and marginal tradable supply, not only headline crude.
Distinguish physical flows from financial-market narratives.
The guest uses an explicit adversarial, resource-attrition geopolitical model.
Prefer contracted volume exposure to commodity-price exposure, subject to valuation and contract details.
tools_and_charts: Global crude and diesel mass balance
Diesel crack spreads and refinery utilization
Taiwan LNG inventory and generation mix
Midstream volume contracts and MLP structures
transcript_cautions: 800,000 barrels a year conflicts with daily denominators; the 11% calculation requires common time units.
US diesel exports rising to 1.9% is a corrupted unit in context; not silently corrected.
Kaliningrad is initially called landlocked then described as having sea access, and once captioned Leningrad.
F-15s and F-14s may be caption or speaker errors; no weapon-platform fact is inferred from them.
The 31:31 Iran-war political judgment carries a SPEAKER_01 label within an otherwise continuous Doomberg answer; attribution is inferred from context.

claims.claim: Wars and attacks on energy infrastructure have produced chronic global energy undersupply, making geopolitical resolution the dominant market driver.
claims.speaker: Doomberg
claims.test: Compare supply-demand balances, inventory draws and identified wartime outages.
claims.qualifications: No specified end date.
claims.reason: Primary inventory and product-supply data support shortages; dominance across all energy markets is broader than the evidence.

evidence.title: Oil Market Report, October 2026
evidence.finding: Oil stocks fell 509 million barrels from end-February. September diesel exports were 700 kb/d lower year over year. Diesel benchmarks exceeded $200, with highs around $220 in Europe and the US. European diesel cracks fell from $100 to about $60 by early October. Global seaborne net gasoil/diesel exports averaged 4.7 mb/d in the first nine months. G7 committed October 2 to accelerate reserve delivery.

claims.next_check: Compare supply-demand balances, inventory draws and identified wartime outages.

review.summary: The October 30 wrap links weaker AI financing and several earnings disappointments to possible capex deceleration. Anthropic growth and compute ratios support a narrow slowdown observation, but the token-maxing cause is unproven. Microsoft identifies delayed capacity delivery and Amazon reports accelerating AWS growth, important counterweights to the bearish cycle inference. Eisman clarifies fixed-coupon versus new-debt cost and presents conditional 2027 power constraints.
review.assessment: Empirical premises and forecasts are assessed separately. Guest assertions are not Eisman forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal attribution remain unresolved.
review.speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman solo, quoting two viewers. A Doomberg promotional excerpt and sponsor message are excluded.
framework_points: Separate sequential growth from absolute growth.
Compare revenue with compute expense, but do not treat the ratio as a complete profit model.
Distinguish GAAP EPS from investment gains and adjusted measures.
Distinguish fixed coupon cash payments from market funding cost.
Separate capex delivery delays from end-demand weakness.
Treat viewer field reports as hypotheses requiring broader validation.
tools_and_charts: Anthropic quarterly revenue, compute expense and efficiency ratio table

Recorded October 29 for October 30 publication.

review.summary: Eisman and Lemonade Stand hosts discuss entry-level jobs, housing affordability, AI concentration, automated cash management, leveraged software buyouts and insurance regulation. Eisman remains supportive of long-horizon S&P saving despite near-term risks. He overstates the impossibility of higher-level zoning reform and Schwab's dependence on cash spreads. Guest anecdotes are kept separate from Eisman's assertions; severe housing declines are attributed to Melody Wright rather than adopted as Eisman's target.
review.assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
review.speaker_map_notes: Eisman is identifiable by questions, first-person history and long analytical answers. The two Lemonade Stand guests are often not distinguishable from text alone, so their claims use Uncertain speaker rather than fabricated names.
framework_points: Separate housing consumption from expected investment gains.
Trace AI effects into deposits and financial intermediation.
Use residual-equity arithmetic, but state valuation assumptions.
Keep long-horizon savings distinct from near-term cyclical risk.
transcript_cautions: Guest turns are not consistently labeled; individual Aidan McCaig versus Brandon Ewing attribution is uncertain.
The 30%-50% housing decline belongs to reported guest Melody Wright.
Specific Mark Walter allegations require primary documentary corroboration.

review.title: AI, Data Centers, & the Narratives Driving Wall Street with Herb Greenberg
review.summary: Greenberg challenges data-center, restaurant and industrial-compounder narratives and explains his AI-assisted research process. Eisman probes the claims, agrees that writing tests understanding, and highlights NVIDIA customer concentration despite continuing ownership. The strongest verified premise is NVIDIA receivables concentration; its translation into revenue concentration is invalid. Recent Modine growth and mixed restaurant and ESAB results qualify the guest's operating criticism. No crash timing or universal adoption of guest short theses is attributed to Eisman.
review.assessment: Mostly guest-led skepticism and research principles. Primary filings verify the NVIDIA concentration premise and reveal material distinctions between growth, margins, stock returns and narrative criticism. Several subjective or underspecified theses remain unresolved rather than automatically too early.
review.speaker_map_notes: Introduction identifies SPEAKER_01 as Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_00 as Herb Greenberg. Short interjections are sometimes assigned the wrong marker; attribution follows question-answer continuity. Main substantive stretches are clear.
framework_points: Separate a marketing narrative from realized organic growth and returns on capital.
Inspect customer concentration and financing terms in filings after headline earnings.
Use writing and primary-source verification to test understanding.
Do not confuse recognition of risk with liquidation of a position.
tools_and_charts: Organic growth and return on invested capital
Stock performance relative to the market
Gemini, Tenzing Memo, AlphaSense, Quartr, FinTool and Fiscal AI
Cross-model answer comparisons and source footnotes

Captions render Nordson ticker as DSN and Enovis with several spellings; claims retain company identities without treating caption spellings as facts.
Short interviewer questions at 4:58, 14:35 and 21:55 are marked SPEAKER_00 but context identifies question-answer turns.

review.summary: Eisman organizes the AI boom into probability-weighted scenarios and five risks: capital intensity, power constraints, customer concentration, OpenAI fragility and weak model switching costs. He favors infrastructure suppliers while warning that an early major-model failure could hit the economy and multiple sectors. His distinctions between technology success and investor returns are useful. Several numerical premises require further verification; the EY interpretation is contradicted by the audit report and a quoted Oracle drawdown fails its own arithmetic.
review.assessment: Strong financing and moat framework, but risks are scenarios rather than realized calls. The Meta audit-work allegation is wrong; Oracle drawdown arithmetic is wrong. Negative quarterly cash flow is supported, while recession exposure, market-share claims and several headline totals remain unverified.

claims.test: Establish whether the stated loss ratio arithmetic proposition holds using matched primary disclosures; retain its conditions and separate causal explanations from price movements.
claims.reason: Assume matching exposures and periods, positive premium P and claims L. If P grows by p and L by l with p>l, new L/P equals old L/P times (1+l)/(1+p), which is lower. Selection and claim frequency can invalidate the comparable-risk assumption.

evidence.finding: Investigative evidence documents fragile leverage/funding, fee and ROE incentives, deteriorating underwriting, and securitization dependence. Pages 61-64 describe pay incentives; pages 89 and 125 describe the origination chain; page 281 reports Bear near 38:1 and balance-sheet window dressing. Findings are not proof of a single exclusive cause.

claims.claim: JPMorgan trades around 2.4 times tangible book and Citi around 0.7 because JPMorgan earns higher returns.

claims.test: Use the same date and denominator for market value, tangible equity and profitability.
claims.reason: The prices and return measures are date-sensitive, and ROE must not be confused with ROTCE. No matched snapshot establishes these exact multiples or the complete causal explanation.
claims.next_check: Use the same date and denominator for market value, tangible equity and profitability.
claims.unit_title: Steve Eisman’s Masterclass on Financial Literacy | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 24

claims.claim: DCF values a business by discounting expected future cash flows to present value.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: This is the valuation identity, not a claim that distant forecasts can be known precisely.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: Present value = sum over t of expected cash flow at t divided by (1 + discount rate)^t, plus any consistently defined terminal value.

claims.claim: He prefers researching business fundamentals to building precise decades-long DCF forecasts.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: This is an explicit methodological preference. DCF sensitivity is a reason to use scenarios, not a mathematical invalidation of discounting.

claims.claim: Sector specialists collectively determine the metrics and valuation conventions that markets use for long periods.

claims.claim: Choose valuation tools by business model: P/E for many sectors, tangible book for banks, reserves for oil, pipeline economics for drugs and sometimes DCF for unprofitable growth.

claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.reason: The stated bridge conflates FFO with other measures. Nareit FFO begins with GAAP net income, and is expressly not GAAP operating cash flow; interest income is not a universal FFO subtraction.

evidence.title: 2025 supplemental definitions: FFO and FAD
evidence.finding: Nareit FFO starts with GAAP net income, adjusts real-estate depreciation and sale gains/losses, and is not GAAP operating cash flow. The FAD reconciliation deducts recurring capital and leasing costs.

claims.next_check: Use the issuer’s reconciliation to the Nareit definition and distinguish cash-flow statements.

claims.reason: AFFO is not standardized. Recurring capex is commonly deducted from FFO-based measures; capital spending is not generally an expense already removed from FFO that can simply be added back.

evidence.title: Q2 2026 definitions: AFFO
evidence.finding: AFFO deducts recurring capital expenditures and leasing costs from adjusted FFO. Nareit has not standardized AFFO, so company definitions differ.

claims.next_check: Inspect the individual issuer’s AFFO bridge and avoid double-counting capex.

evidence.title: Ample-reserves monetary-policy implementation
evidence.finding: The Fed sets administered reserve-interest and reverse-repo rates to guide the federal funds market rate. The discount rate is also administered; long-term yields are not directly fixed by the funds target.

claims.claim: A steeper yield curve increases bank net interest margins because banks fund short and lend long.

claims.next_check: Model asset and liability repricing rather than use slope alone.

proof.derivation: Suppose the market short rate is unchanged and the long rate rises 1 point, steepening the curve. If a bank raises previously low deposit rates by 2 points to retain funding while asset yield rises 1 point, its spread falls 1 point. The claimed result requires assumptions about deposit pricing and asset repricing.

proof.derivation: For each positive future cash flow C at time t, C/(1+r)^t declines as r rises; summing preserves the direction.

proof.derivation: The proportional sensitivity of a single discounted cash flow is -t/(1+r); later t means larger sensitivity at the same rate.

assumptions: Use the linear single-market regression definition.
proof.proof: Return_i = alpha + beta*Return_market + residual. Beta describes the fitted sensitivity; the residual is not generally zero, and beta alone does not determine realized daily return.

assumptions: All component betas use the same market factor and period.
proof.proof: Cov(sum(w_i R_i),R_m)/Var(R_m) = sum(w_i beta_i). Equal dollar long and short positions can have unequal factor sensitivity.
proof.derivation: Cov(sum(w_i R_i),R_m)/Var(R_m) = sum(w_i beta_i). Equal dollar long and short positions can have unequal factor sensitivity.

claims.claim: The yen carry trade earns a positive cross-currency interest spread if exchange rates are sufficiently stable, but yen appreciation can erase accumulated profits and leverage amplifies losses.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Establish whether the stated yen carry mechanics proposition holds using matched primary disclosures; retain its conditions and separate causal explanations from price movements.
claims.qualifications: The 100-to-one example is illustrative, not a measured market leverage estimate.
claims.reason: Assume unhedged yen funding, a higher-yield foreign asset, fixed borrowing terms and no defaults. Return in yen equals foreign asset return plus currency conversion change minus funding cost. Yen appreciation reduces the yen value of foreign assets while yen debt remains due; leverage multiplies equity sensitivity. A fully hedged trade also pays hedge costs.
